items.title: Kod
items.text:
Kod is a toy language that compiles to AArch64 (Apple Silicon) machine code for macOS. The self-hosted compiler (sh_kodc) compiles Kod programs, including itself.

func main() -> int64 {
    print("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

$ ./kod build hello.kod
$ ./build/apps/hello/hello
Hello, world!

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Compiled to native ARM64 machine code (via as + clang)
  • Static types: int64, str, bool, arrays [T], structs, enums, optionals T?, generic types T[U, V] and functions f[T]
  • Union types: int64 | str, taken apart with n: int64 patterns
  • Pattern matching via match, plus if X is .Variant(bindings) sugar
  • F-string interpolation (f"hello {name}"), auto-to_str for non-string interpolands
  • Interfaces with vtable dispatch; primitives implement them via implicit boxing
  • Error handling via T or Error, try / must / throw
  • test "description" { ... } syntax with assert <expr> (source captured)
  • Modules and imports (import "kod/ast", import "./helper")
  • Self-hosted ARM64 codegen written in Kod itself

items.title: Status
items.text: The self-hosted compiler (sh_kodc) is the only implementation. A checked-in snapshot of it builds the current sources (see Self-hosting).

items.title: Writing an API client
items.text:
examples/github_repo.kod reads a repository's details and its open issues from the GitHub API. It is about a hundred lines and uses every piece of the standard library that a client needs; this page walks through it.

kod run examples/github_repo.kod anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python

anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python
  (no description)
  language: Python
  stars: 4030, forks: 901
  license: Apache-2.0
open issues:
  #2050 fix(streaming): keep compaction metadata when a delta omits encrypted_content
  #2049 fix(decoders): close the response when JSONL decoding fails
  #2048 fix(tools): don't coerce a non-object tool input in the session runner

Set GITHUB_TOKEN to send a bearer token (private repositories need one), and GITHUB_API to talk to something other than https://api.github.com. The tests use that to run the example against a local stand-in server (tests/support/github_api.kod), so they need no network.

items.title: The pieces
items.text:
Arguments and environment. main(argv: [str]) receives the command line, with the program's name first. env.get("GITHUB_TOKEN") returns a str?, and x? or default handles a missing variable (Built-ins).

The client. What every request to the service needs goes on a Client once: its headers, its deadline. The example wraps it in a small GitHub type, so main reads as github.repo(name) and github.open_issues(name, limit: 3). One Client serves both requests, which keeps the connection from the first and uses it for the second (HTTP client).

let client = Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15))
client.headers.add("Accept", "application/vnd.github+json")
client.headers.add("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)

let response = try client.get(url)

A single request can override any of that with Options, for instance client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration(seconds: 2))). Client.get follows redirects, enforces the size limits and the deadline, and picks TCP or TLS from the URL.

Query strings. Build them with Query, which encodes names and values, rather than by joining strings:

let query = Query()
query.add("state", "open")
query.add("per_page", "3")
let url = with_query("/repos/" + name + "/issues", query)

Reading JSON. json.parse returns Value or Error. The accessors never fail, so a missing or null field is a fallback, not a crash:

func text_of(anon v: json.Value, key: str, fallback: str) -> str {
    return v.get(key).as_str()? or fallback
}

license.get("spdx_id") on a null license is Null, and as_str of that is none, which ? or "none" turns into the text none.

Errors. A non-2xx response is not a Kod error; fetch hands it back so you can read what the API said. The example turns it into its own ApiError and throws it, so that callers see one failure path for "the request failed" and "the API refused":

type ApiError = struct {
    status: int64
    reason: str
    detail: str

    func to_str(self) -> str { ... }
}

Network failures arrive as an IoError with a kind (ConnectionRefused, TimedOut, HostNotFound, Tls, Protocol, ...); see Streams. main here turns every failure into error: ... on standard error and an exit status of 1, and a bad command line into 2.

items.title: Sending JSON
items.text:
Writing to an API is the same, with a body. ObjectBuilder keeps the keys and values in step, and post sets the length and the content type:

import "json"
import "net/http" { post }

let body = json.ObjectBuilder()
body.put_str("title", "It crashes")
body.put_str("body", "Steps to reproduce: ...")
body.put("labels", json.array_of([json.str_value("bug")]))

let payload = kod_str_to_bytes(body.build().emit())
let response = try post(
    "https://api.example.com/issues",
    payload,
    content_type: "application/json",
)

items.title: What to know before relying on it
items.text:
• get, post and fetch open a connection for each request and close it. A program that makes many requests to one host should create a Client and call its get, post and fetch instead, which keep connections for reuse (Connection reuse).
  • timeout applies to the connect, the TLS handshake and each read or write. Set deadline to bound a request as a whole (Deadlines).
  • TLS is Kod's own TLS 1.3; a server without it is refused (TLS).
  • Numbers with a fraction or an exponent come back as Decimal text: as_int() is none for them, as_number_text() gives the digits, and .parse_float() on those turns them into a float64.

items.title: Arrays
items.text:
Arrays in Kod are resizable, homogeneous sequences. The type is [T] where T is the element type.

An array is a value, like an int64 or a str: assigning it, passing it or storing it in a field gives the other place the array as it is, and changing one of them later leaves the others alone (see Arrays are values).

items.title: Literals
items.text:
let nums: [int64] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let words: [str] = ["hello", "world"]
let empty: [int64] = []

A literal with no type to go to takes its first element's type, and every other element must have that type: let xs = [1, "a"] is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), and so is [Sq(s: 1), Circle(r: 1)] even when both implement Shape. Annotate the array to mix structs behind an interface: let shapes: [Shape] = [Sq(s: 1), Circle(r: 1)], which the error suggests when the module has an interface both implement.

items.title: Indexing
items.text:
let first: int64 = nums[0]
let last: int64 = nums[-1]    // negative index counts from end
let third: int64 = nums[2]

Negative indices wrap around: arr[-1] is equivalent to arr[len(arr) - 1]. An index out of range either way panics. An index must be an int64: nums["a"], nums[true] and an int64? index such as nums[m.get(k)] are errors.

An array never shrinks, so in for i in 0..len(xs) (from any literal of 0 or more) xs[i] is always in range, and the compiler leaves out the check when xs is a let or a parameter, which nothing can point at another array.

Arrays nest: an element of a [[int64]] is an [int64], so grid[i][j] and for row in grid { for x in row { ... } } work, and an element of a [bool] is a bool.

A literal takes its element type from where it goes, at any depth: a let, an assignment, an argument, a field, an enum payload, a return value (including a match arm's), the rest of an array + chain (see Concatenation), or an element or Map value it's stored as. In let g: [[Shape]] = [[Sq(s: 3)]], shapes += [Sq(s: 4)], [Sq(s: 1)] + shapes or return [none, 3] from a -> [int64?] function, each struct is boxed as the interface and each value wrapped as the optional. In a [Direction], [.North, .South] builds Direction variants even when another enum declares variants of those names, and in a [Maybe[int64]], [.Just(value: 1), .Nothing] builds Maybe[int64] ones.

Arrays, str and bytes can be indexed, and so can a struct that declares an op_index method (Map does). Element assignment needs an array or a struct with op_index_set, slicing needs an array, str or bytes, and for … in needs an array, str, bytes, Map, Set or a..b (see Control flow). Anything else is a compile error.

An array can be changed, by assigning an element or appending, only through a name that could be assigned: a mut binding or a mut parameter. On a let array, a parameter not declared mut, a for variable or a pattern binding, xs[0] = 1 and grid[i][j] = 1 are errors (cannot change `xs`, an immutable binding; declare it with `mut`), as xs += [1] is. An array kept in a field is changed through the field, so self.xs[i] = v and p.items += [x] work however self or p is bound.

An assigned element must have the array's element type, with the same conversions as a let: names[0] = 5 on a [str] is an error, while xs[0] = 42 on an [int64?] and pets[0] = Cat() on a [Pet] wrap and box the value. On a struct, the key of m[k] and the key and value of m[k] = v must have the types of op_index's and op_index_set's parameters (see Indexing a struct), so m[5] on a Map[str, int64] is an error.

An element or a slice is read once its index or bounds have been worked out, so xs[add(mut xs)] reads the array that add leaves.

A store evaluates its parts left to right: in rows()[i()] = v() and m[k()] = v() the receiver comes first, then the index or key, then the value, and f().x = v() calls f before v. A compound rows()[i()] += v() evaluates the receiver and the index once, reads the element and then evaluates v(), so rows and i are each called once. Indexing a struct calls its op_index, so it counts as a call too: xs[a[k]] += b[k] calls a's op_index once, before b's.

items.title: Length
items.text: let n: int64 = len(nums)

items.title: Slicing
items.text:
let sub: [int64] = nums[1..4]   // elements 1, 2, 3
let prefix: [int64] = nums[..3]  // first three
let suffix: [int64] = nums[3..]  // from index 3 onward
let all: [int64] = nums[..]      // all of it

A negative bound counts from the end, as an index does: nums[..-1] is all but the last and nums[-2..] the last two. Then both endpoints clamp to [0, len], so [1, 2, 3][1..10] is [2, 3] and [1, 2, 3][-9..1] is [1]. An end before the start yields an empty slice. Both bounds must be int64.

items.title: Concatenation
items.text:
Use += to append elements or extend with another array:

mut a: [int64] = [1, 2]
a += [3, 4]          // a is now [1, 2, 3, 4]

Or + to produce a new array; neither operand is modified:

let b: [int64] = [5]
let c: [int64] = a + b   // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; a and b are unchanged

Every literal and match in a chain of + is built as the type the whole chain goes to, or, without one, as its first operand that isn't a literal or match. So [Sq(s: 1)] + [Sq(s: 2)] + shapes boxes both squares as Shape, and let ms: [Maybe[str]] = [.Just(value: "a")] + [.Nothing] builds Maybe[str] variants. The other operands must all have that one type: squares + shapes (a [Sq] and a [Shape]) and nums + names are errors, and so is names + [1], whose literal's element isn't a str.

+= grows the array's buffer geometrically, so appending in a loop is amortized O(1) per element. + always copies both operands, so xs = xs + [x] costs O(len(xs)); prefer xs += [x] in loops. xs += [x] with one element builds no array for the literal: x goes straight onto the end of xs.

items.title: Arrays are values
items.text:
Each name, field and element holds an array of its own. After let a = xs, xs += [3] leaves a as it was, and so does xs[0] = 9; the same goes for an array stored in a field or in another array, or passed to a function:

mut xs = [1, 2]
let a = xs
xs += [3]              // xs is [1, 2, 3], a is still [1, 2]

mut grid = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
let row = grid[0]
grid[0][1] = 5         // grid is [[0, 5], [0, 0]], row is still [0, 0]

None of this copies anything until it has to: assigning or passing an array shares its elements, and they are copied the first time one holder changes them while another still has them. An array nobody else holds is changed in place, so appending in a loop stays amortized O(1). A function changes its caller's array only through a mut parameter.

A for x in xs loop goes over xs as it was when the loop started: what the body appends or assigns to xs is in xs afterwards, but the loop doesn't reach it.

items.title: Repetition
items.text:
* with an int64 repeats an array, in a new array, which is the way to make one of a given size:

mut seen = [false] * 1000      // 1000 times false
let zeros: [int64] = [0] * n
let ab = [1, 2] * 3            // [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2]

The count comes second, and zero or less gives an empty array. It is one allocation and a copy, much faster than appending in a loop. Each element is a value of its own, so the rows of mut grid = [[0] * 3] * 3 can be changed one at a time.

items.title: Comprehensions
items.text:
[elem for x in xs] makes an array of what elem is for each x:

let words = ["pear", "fig", "apple"]
let sizes = [len(w) for w in words]               // [4, 3, 5]
let long = [w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 3]
let pairs = [(i, j) for i in 0..3 for j in i + 1..3]    // [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]

The for goes over what a for loop does, and binds what that does: for i, x in xs, for k, v in m, for (a, b) in pairs. Any number of fors and ifs may follow each other, each inside the one before it. An if can bind names and narrow them as an if statement's condition does:

let nums = [n for f in fields if f.parse_int() is Some(n)]     // [1, 3]
let next = [n + 1 for n in maybe if n is not none]             // [2]
let table = [
    (i, f)
    for i, f in fields
    if i > 0
]

The names are the comprehension's own. elem is worked out after the fors and ifs, in their order, as if it were appended in the loops' body, and what it is converts to the type the array goes to: let ids: [int64?] = [i for i in 0..3]. Where the array goes nowhere that says its type, it's an array of elem's.

items.title: Comparing
items.text:
== and != compare two arrays of the same type element by element: they are equal when they have the same length and each element is == to the one at the same place in the other.

[1, 2] == [1, 2]             // true
["a"] != ["a", "b"]          // true
[[1], [2, 3]] == [[1], [2, 3]]

The elements must have an == of their own, so an array of interface values, functions or shared structs without op_eq doesn't compare (see Operators). An array literal compared with an array of optionals or of a union is built as that type, so with opts: [int64?], opts == [1, none] compares the two.

items.title: As text
items.text:
An f-string, str(xs) and print(xs) show an array as its elements in brackets, separated by ,, each as an f-string would show it:

print([1, 2, 3])             // [1, 2, 3]
print(f"{["a", "b"]}")       // [a, b]
print([[1], []])             // [[1], []]

A str element shows as its text, without quotes. The elements must have a text of their own: an array of functions can't be shown.

items.title: Iterating
items.text:
Index-based:

mut i: int64 = 0
for i < len(nums) {
    print_int(nums[i])
    i = i + 1
}

Foreach:

for n in nums {
    print_int(n)
}

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
Arrays are represented as a header struct on the heap:

{ void* ptr, int64 len, int64 cap }

The ptr field points to a block of elements, each 8 bytes wide except in a [bool], whose elements are a byte each (a 1000-element [bool] takes 1000 bytes, not 8000). len is the number of live elements; cap is the allocated capacity, in elements.

The header is counted like any other object, and the count says how many places hold the array. Before changing an array, generated code checks that the count is 1; if it isn't, _kod_arr_unique copies the header and the elements, stores the copy where the array was, and lets go of the original.

xs = xs[..n], which keeps the first elements of the array in xs, drops the rest where the array is (a field written the same on both sides, as in s.items = s.items[..n], too), through _kod_arr_truncate_at, rather than making a copy; arrays.pop uses it.

Appending (+=) goes through _kod_arr_concat in the runtime, which writes into the existing buffer and reallocates it with doubled capacity only when cap runs out. + goes through _kod_arr_concat_new, which allocates a fresh header and buffer, and * through _kod_arr_repeat. Each takes the element width from the compiler, which knows the type.

items.title: Helpers
items.text:
The arrays module has what's the same for an array of any type:

import "arrays"

arrays.contains(["a", "b"], "b")     // true
arrays.equal([1, 2], [1, 2])         // true

Elements compare with ==, so strs by content, and a type that == doesn't take is an error (see Generic functions).

Function Gives sum(xs), sum_floats(xs) what int64s, or float64s, come to; 0 for none min(xs), max(xs) the first of the smallest, or largest, elements by <; a T?, none when there are none any(xs), all(xs) whether one of some bools, or all of them, are true index_of(xs, x) where the first element == to x is; a T?, none when none is reversed(xs) the elements, last first, in a new array pop(mut xs) the last element, taken off xs; a T?, none when there are none

With a comprehension, these are over anything:

let total = arrays.sum([len(w) for w in words])
let longest = arrays.max([len(w) for w in words])? or 0
assert arrays.all([w != "" for w in words])

items.title: Sorting
items.text:
The sort module's functions return a new array and leave the argument as it is. They take O(n log n) comparisons and are stable: elements that compare equal keep their order.

import "sort"

sort.sorted([3, 1, 2])       // [1, 2, 3]
sort.sorted(["b", "a"])      // ["a", "b"]

sorted orders by <, so it takes numbers, strs (by byte), and structs that declare op_lt. sorted_by takes the order as a function that says whether its first argument goes before its second:

sort.sorted_by(people, less: func(a: Person, b: Person) -> bool {
    return a.age < b.age
})

sorted_by_key orders by what a function gives for each element, by <, and calls it once per element:

sort.sorted_by_key(people, key: func(anon p: Person) -> int64 { return p.age })

items.title: Heaps and deques
items.text:
Heap[T] from the heaps module keeps its elements so that the smallest by < comes out first, as a priority queue does. push and pop take O(log n), and peek gives the smallest without taking it out. Both pop and peek give a T?, none when the heap is empty. Elements that compare equal come out in no particular order.

mut todo = Heap[(int64, str)]()
todo.push((3, "c"))
todo.push((1, "a"))
todo.push((2, "b"))
assert (todo.pop()? or (0, "")) == (1, "a")
assert len(todo) == 2

A tuple compares its elements in order, so (distance, node) pairs come out nearest first, as a shortest-path search wants them. For the largest first, push the negated number or give the element type an op_lt that says so.

Deque[T] from the deques module is a queue open at both ends: push_back and push_front add, pop_front and pop_back take an element out and give it as a T?, and front and back look without taking. Each takes O(1), counting the occasional doubling of its storage.

mut queue = Deque[int64]()
queue.push_back(1)
queue.push_back(2)
queue.push_front(0)
assert queue.pop_front() == 0
assert queue.pop_back() == 2
assert len(queue) == 1

Both are values, like arrays: a copy, let saved = queue, keeps what the queue held when it was made. len(h) and h.is_empty() say how much is in either, h.values() gives the elements as an array (a heap's in no particular order, a deque's front to back), which is what for x in d goes over.

items.title: Built-ins
items.text:
These names live in stdlib/builtins.kod and are available in every Kod program without an explicit import.

A call without a module name, f(args), goes to the first of these that exists:

  1. a struct named f that the module sees (Pt(x: 1) constructs);
  2. the innermost binding of f in force, when it holds a function value;
  3. a function the module declares or lists in an import;
  4. the builtin of that name.

A binding that holds anything else doesn't hide a function, so let len = len(xs) and a later len(ys) both call the builtin. It does hide any outer binding of its name: after let g = double, a call g(1) in a block that binds let g = 5 goes to the module's or the builtin g. With neither, it is an error: `g` is a local of type `int64`, not a function.

A function value declared in a block hides an outer one only inside that block; after the block, f(args) calls the outer one again. With no binding of f in force and no function of that name, the call is an error: `f` is called before its `let` or `f` is declared in a block that has ended; declare it outside the block to call it here.

The same holds for len, str, hash and panic: a module can declare its own func hash(anon p: Point) -> int64, and its hash(...) calls use it, while another module's dep.hash(x) names that one. An f-string always converts its values with the builtin str. Only the builtin panic counts as a call that never returns; a module's own or imported panic, or a local function value of that name, is an ordinary call. A local named panic that holds anything else doesn't hide the builtin, so panic(msg) after let panic = 5 never returns.

items.title: Output
items.text: Function Signature Description print (x) -> none Print x, followed by a newline. Takes whatever f"{x}" does (see Strings). print_int (int64) -> none Print an integer followed by a newline. Equivalent to print(n.to_str()). kod_puts (str) -> int64 Write a string and a newline to stdout. What print calls; embedded NULs are written as-is. putchar (int64) -> int64 C putchar: write a single byte to stdout. Shares libc's stdout buffer with print.

items.title: Length
items.text:
Function Signature Description len (str) -> int64 String length in bytes. len ([T]) -> int64 Number of elements in an array. len (SomeStruct) -> int64 Dispatches to the struct's func len(self) -> int64 method if one exists (e.g. Map.len); a len method of any other shape is an error.

As a value, len is its string form: let n: func(str) -> int64 = len.

items.title: Smaller and larger
items.text:
min(a, b) and max(a, b) give the smaller and the larger of two values of one type that < compares: numbers, strs, bytes and structs that declare op_lt. When neither is smaller, as with equal values or a NaN, both give a.

min(3, 5)                  // 3
max("pear", "apple")       // "pear"

items.title: Bytes
items.text:
Function Signature Description kod_str_to_bytes (str) -> bytes The same bytes, typed bytes; nothing is copied. kod_bytes_to_str (bytes) -> str The same bytes, typed str; nothing is copied. kod_bytes_from_array ([int64]) -> bytes One byte per element, from its low 8 bits. kod_bytes_le64 (bytes, int64) -> int64 The 8 bytes from at as one int64, the first byte lowest (little-endian). An at below 0, or fewer than 8 bytes left, panics with the index of the first missing byte.

kod_bytes_le64(b, at) is what reading the 8 bytes one at a time and shifting them together gives, in one load: a decoder reading many bits at a time uses it to fill its bit buffer.

items.title: String conversion
items.text:
There is no int_to_str builtin — primitives carry their own to_str methods:

let s: str = 42.to_str()      // "42"
let t: str = true.to_str()    // "true"
let u: str = "hi".to_str()    // identity

F-strings interpolate non-str values by calling to_str automatically:

print(f"n = {42}")            // n = 42

items.title: Hashing
items.text:
let h: int64 = "hello".hash()
let g: int64 = 99.hash()

int64.hash is the identity function; str.hash is djb2; bool.hash is 0/1. Used internally by Map[K, V].

The hash(x) builtin takes a hashable value: an int64, str, bytes or bool, a value of an enum whose payloads' fields are hashable, an optional of a hashable type, an array of hashable elements, a plain struct whose fields are hashable (see Structs are values), or a value of a union whose members are all hashable, such as int64 | str. Hashing anything else, such as a float64 or an enum with a float64 in a payload, is an error (cannot hash a value of type `float64`), as is hashing a union with a member that can't be hashed, which the error names (cannot hash a value of type `float64 | int64`; its member `float64` can't be hashed). It gives what the methods above give, a bytes value hashes like the str with the same bytes, an enum value without a payload hashes to its variant's position, counting from 1, one with a payload mixes that with its fields' hashes, an optional hashes what it holds, and a union value hashes the member it holds, mixed with which member that is, so the int64 0 and the bool false don't collide. An array's hash is made of its elements', in order, and a struct's of its fields' unless it has a hash method.

items.title: Map[K, V]
items.text:
A built-in generic. Open-addressing hash map (PEP 468 dense + sparse).

A map is a value, like an array: let n = m gives n the map as it is, and m.set(...) afterwards changes only m. So set, remove and m[k] = v need a map that may be changed, a mut binding, a field, or a mut parameter, and a function that fills a caller's map takes it as a mut parameter. Nothing is copied until a map another holder still has is changed. Set[T] (in sets) is a value the same way.

mut m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()
m.set("a", 1)
m.set("b", 2)
match m.get("a") {
    Some(v) -> print(v.to_str())
    none -> print("miss")
}
print(len(m).to_str())   // 2
Method Description set(k, v) Add k with value v, or replace the value k has. m[k] = v is the same. get(k) -> V? k's value, or none when k isn't in the map. m[k] is the same. m[k, default: d] k's value, or d when k isn't in the map; m[k, default: d] += v changes it in place (see Indexing a struct). get_or_set(k, v) -> V k's value; when k isn't in the map, v, which becomes k's value. One search either way, as for numbering names: ids.get_or_set(name, len(ids)). contains(k) -> bool Whether k is in the map. remove(k) -> V? Take k out of the map, giving the value it had, or none when it wasn't there. keys() -> [K] / values() -> [V] The keys, or the values, in the order the keys were first set, as a new array. len(m) How many keys the map holds. f"{m}", str(m), print(m) The entries in order as text, {a: 1, b: 2}, each key and value as an f-string shows it; {} when empty. The key and value types must have a text of their own.

The entries keep the order their keys were first set in: setting a key again changes its value but not its place, and a key that is removed and set again goes last. for k in m and for k, v in m go over them in that order (see for / in). set, get, contains and remove take constant time on average.

A lookup finds the entry whose key is == to the one it's given, so key equality depends on the key type: str and bytes keys match by content, int64 and bool keys by value, enum keys by variant and payload, optional keys by what they hold, array keys by their elements, struct keys by their fields (or their op_eq), and union keys when they hold the same member and those are equal, so in a Map[int64 | str, V] the keys 1 and "1" are two keys.

The key type must be hashable, as for hash(x): int64, str, bytes, bool, or an enum, an optional, an array, a plain struct or a union of those. Any other key type, such as Map[float64, int64] or a shared struct, is an error at the type argument that names it, in whichever module it's written (`float64` can't be a `Map` key), reported once per key type. A key that comes from another generic type's parameter is reported at the argument of that type that is or holds the key: with type Index[V, K] = struct { m: Map[K, V] }, a parameter of type Index[int64, Pt] is an error at Pt (`Pt` can't be a `Map` key in `Index[int64, Pt]`). A Map[T, V] in a generic type's method names the instance whose T is the bad key (`Pt` can't be a `Map` key in `Box[Pt]`); any other bad key in a method, such as a Map[Pt, int64] written out in Box[Pt], ends with the instance it's compiled for, as other errors there do ((in `Box[Pt]`)). The same holds for the element type of a Set[T] from the sets module, which shows as its elements in braces, {a, b}, in the order they were first added.

items.title: Indexing a struct
items.text:
m[k] calls the struct's op_index and m[k] = v its op_index_set, which is how Map supports both (m[k] is a V?, like m.get(k)). op_index must take one key besides self, and op_index_set a key and a value:

func op_index(self, anon key: K) -> V? { ... }
func op_index_set(mut self, anon key: K, anon value: V) -> none { ... }

The key and value must have those parameters' types, like a method's arguments. m[k] = v evaluates m, then k, then v before the call.

m[k, default: d] is k's value, or d when there is none, through the struct's op_index_or; for a Map it is a V, not a V?:

mut counts = Map[str, int64]()
mut groups = Map[int64, [str]]()
for word in words {
    counts[word, default: 0] += 1
    groups[len(word), default: []] += [word]
}

A change to an entry, such as m[k] += v, m[k][i] = v, m[k].x = v or the same with default:, changes the value where the struct keeps it: m, k and v are evaluated first (in that order), then op_index_take (or op_index_take_or with the default) takes the value out, the change is made to it, and op_index_set puts it back. Since nothing else holds the value meanwhile, appending to an array in a map doesn't copy it. Without default: the key must be there; a Map panics when it isn't (key not in map). A struct that declares neither take method gets m[k] += v as op_index and then op_index_set, each with the same m and k:

func op_index_or(self, anon key: K, default: V) -> V { ... }
func op_index_take(mut self, anon key: K) -> V { ... }
func op_index_take_or(mut self, anon key: K, default: V) -> V { ... }

items.title: Error handling
items.text: Name Description Error (interface) Marker for types that can be thrown. Requires to_str(self) -> str. ExitCode (interface) exit_code(self) -> int64, declared but not consulted yet: an Err that main returns exits with status 1 whatever it implements. panic Print panic: <msg>\n to stderr and exit(1), unless it is caught. Used by must and by assert outside a test. kod_eprint (extern) Write to stderr without exiting.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Name Description fail(msg) Mark the current test "..." {} as failed; outside a test, no-op. assert <expr> Statement form. Inside a test, flag on false; outside, panic. Source text is captured at parse time. See Testing.

items.title: I/O
items.text:
The io module wraps the filesystem primitives. Both calls require import "io" — touching the filesystem is explicit at the import line.

import "io"

// Read the whole file. Pipes and FIFOs (e.g. "/dev/stdin") are read
// until EOF. A file that can't be opened or read gives an IoError that
// says why, so `must` panics with the reason.
let contents: str = must io.read_file("data.txt")

// Write a file, replacing it if it exists. Returns 0 on success,
// -1 on failure. The parent directory must already exist.
let rc: int64 = io.write_file("out.txt", "hello\n")

For subprocess support, see stdlib/process.kod:

import "process"

let r: process.ProcessResult = process.run(["echo", "hello"])
assert r.status == 0
assert r.stdout == "hello\n"

process.output(argv) runs argv[0], looked up on PATH, to the end and returns what it wrote, as a process.Output or an Error:

import "process"

func branch() -> str or Error {
    let out = try process.output(["git", "branch", "--show-current"], dir: "/src/kod")
    if out.status != 0 {
        throw process.ProcessError(message: f"git: {out.stderr}")
    }
    return out.stdout.trim()
}
  • out.status is the exit code, and out.stdout and out.stderr are what the program wrote to each, read together, so a program that writes a lot to both can't stall.
  • input: is written to the program's stdin while its output is read, then stdin is closed. Without it, stdin is empty. A program that exits without reading all of its input is not an error.
  • dir:, env: and add_env: work as for start, below.
  • It fails as start does when the program can't be run, and with a process.ProcessError when a signal ends it.

process.start(argv) starts argv[0], looked up on PATH, without waiting for it, and returns a process.Child or an Error:

import "process"

func shout(anon text: str) -> str or Error {
    let child = try process.start(["tr", "a-z", "A-Z"], stdin: .Pipe, stdout: .Pipe)
    try child.stdin.write_str(text)
    try child.stdin.close()                 // the child sees the end of its input
    let out = try child.stdout.read_all()
    try child.stdout.close()
    let status = try child.wait()           // the exit code
    if status != 0 {
        throw process.ProcessError(message: f"tr exited with {status}")
    }
    return str(out)
}
  • stdin:, stdout: and stderr: each take a process.Stdio: .Inherit (the default) shares this process's stream, .Null gives the child /dev/null, and .Pipe connects it to this process. A piped stream is a posix.Fd field of the same name on the Child, for this process to write to (stdin) or read from (stdout, stderr) and to close. A stream that isn't piped has the Fd -1, which fails on every call.
  • dir: starts the child in that directory instead of the current one.
  • env: replaces the child's environment with a list of NAME=value strings; without it, the child gets this process's environment. argv[0] is looked up on this process's PATH either way.
  • add_env: sets variables on top of that, as NAME=value strings: each replaces a variable of the same name or adds one, so add_env: ["DEBUG=1"] runs the child with this process's environment plus DEBUG. An entry without a =, or with nothing before it, is a process.ProcessError.
  • start fails with an IoError when the program can't be run, as for a missing program (.NotFound) or directory.
  • child.wait() closes child.stdin if it is a pipe, waits for the child to end, and returns its exit code. A child ended by a signal is a process.ProcessError that names it, as in tr was killed by SIGTERM. A child can be waited for once.
  • child.try_wait() is wait without the waiting. It returns the exit code (int64?) if the child has ended, which counts as its one wait, or none if it is still running. It doesn't close stdin.
  • child.kill() sends it SIGTERM and returns without waiting; wait then collects it. kill(signal: .Kill) sends another process.Signal: .Hup, .Int, .Quit, .Kill, .Term, .Usr1 or .Usr2.
  • child.pid is its process id.

A child that is never waited for stays a zombie until this process exits. process.run and process.kill are shorthands for common cases:

process.run(argv) captures stdout and stderr; unlike output, it can't fail: a program that can't be run, or that a signal ends, has the status -1. process.kill(pid) ends a child by its process id (a Child's pid), with SIGTERM, waits for it, and returns whether it was signalled; a child that is never waited for stays a zombie until the parent exits. process.exec(argv) instead replaces the calling process with argv[0], looked up on PATH: the new program has the same terminal, stdin and process id. Stdout is flushed first. If stdin is a pipe, input the program has already read into its buffer (as io.read_stdin_line does, beyond the line it asked for) is not handed on; a file or a terminal loses nothing. exec returns, with -1, only if argv[0] could not be run.

import "process"

func main() -> int64 {
    process.exec(["echo", "hello"])
    return 127  // not reached unless `echo` could not be run
}

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
stdlib/env.kod reads and changes the process's environment. A program's arguments come from main(argv: [str]) (see Functions).

import "env"

func main() -> int64 {
    let token = env.get("API_TOKEN")
    print(token? or "no token")
    must env.set("MODE", "test")
    env.unset("API_TOKEN")
    return 0
}
Function Meaning get(name) -> str? the value, or none if the variable isn't set; a variable set to the empty string is "", not none set(name, value) -> none or Error set or replace it; the change is seen by programs started afterwards with process.run and process.exec; an empty name, one containing = or a NUL byte, and a value with a NUL byte are InvalidInput errors unset(name) -> none remove it; unsetting a variable that isn't set does nothing

items.title: Extern (C runtime)
items.text:
Available for re-declaration in any module if needed:

Symbol Description _strlen C strlen. _rc_alloc Allocates an object with a reference count of 1; see Memory layout. _kod_str_concat, _kod_str_slice String operations the runtime exposes to codegen. _kod_sb_new, _kod_sb_append, _kod_sb_append_byte, _kod_sb_append_int, _kod_sb_len, _kod_sb_clear, _kod_sb_to_str The growable buffer behind StrBuilder and the str methods join, repeat, replace, lower and upper; a handle is typed as a str so that it is counted, but isn't one. _kod_array_concat, _kod_array_concat_new Array append in place (+=) and concatenation into a new array (+). _kod_test_fail, _kod_test_summary Test runner internals.

Direct use is rarely needed — the language-level operators cover most cases.

items.title: CLI reference
items.text: The CLI is kod, the native tool build/apps/kod/kod (built from tools/kod.kod). Run it as ./kod ... from the repository root: ./kod is a link there to that tool, and started through it the tool first refreshes the toolchain with make (step 1 below). Build it once with make kod (see Install); until then ./kod fails with the shell's no such file or directory. From another directory it works on the project there, with the checkout's toolchain and standard library (Using kod in other projects).

items.title: kod build [-o PATH] <file>
items.text:
Compile a Kod source file to a native ARM64 binary.

./kod build hello.kod
./build/apps/hello/hello

In a project outside the checkout the program is also written to the working directory, named after the file: kod build cmd/server.kod writes ./server. -o PATH writes it to PATH instead (relative to the working directory), in the checkout too. The program is written beside PATH and renamed into place, so one that is running is replaced whole; its directory is made if it is missing. A directory at PATH is an error.

Build pipeline:

  1. Refresh the toolchain, when started any way but by the tool's own path build/apps/kod/kod (through ./kod, or a link on PATH; the checkout is found by following the links to the executable): under a lock on build/.toolchain.lock, make -s -q stage1 kod checks it (a few milliseconds), and when the compiler, the C runtime, an always-linked stdlib module or the tool itself changed, make -s stage1 kod rebuilds it, its output on stderr, and the freshly built tool takes over with the same arguments. An outer make's MAKEFLAGS, MFLAGS and MAKELEVEL are not passed on. If the rebuild fails, kod prints kod: failed to rebuild the toolchain and exits with make's status; when make is not installed, the step is skipped. Invoking build/apps/kod/kod directly, as the tests do, skips it.
  2. Parse the entry and walk its transitive imports. A missing entry file (path:1:1: error: no such file) or a missing import (importer:line:col: error: no such module ...) is an error. Then read the comment lines at the top of each module for the C files, link arguments and required files it declares (Link inputs); a mistake in them, or a required file that isn't there, stops the build before anything is compiled.
  3. Compile each module that isn't prebuilt in build/stage0/ to a .o with sh_kodc _compile, the entry first, stopping at the first that fails, and then each C file the modules name, once. A module compiled before is taken from build/cache/ instead: its object there is named by a SHA-256 of sh_kodc, the module's path, and the path and text of each module it loads (what it imports, directly or not, and the STAGE0_KOD modules), which is all its object depends on. So an unchanged module isn't compiled again, whichever program it's in. Only modules named by a relative path, inside the project, are kept there. A failing module's errors follow those in the declarations of the modules it loads, such as an import that names no file, an unknown return type, a field declared twice or a parse error, since its own may be only their cascades.
  4. Generate and assemble the _main runtime shim that calls the user's main.
  5. Link everything against the prebuilt build/stage0/ objects with the LINK command of link.cfg (clang, see Self-hosting), followed by the arguments the modules give with kod:link. The driver reads link.cfg, and link.local.cfg if there is one, from the checkout.

Step 1 happens only through ./kod; the tool runs steps 2–5 however it is started.

A syntax error is reported once: the parser skips the rest of the statement, struct field, parameter or declaration it is in, and carries on with the next, so a later mistake is still found. A missing , between parameters, or a missing : before a field's type, is taken as written. Type errors inside a declaration (a function, a type, a constant) that has a syntax error aren't reported, since they may come from what the parser skipped; the other declarations are checked as usual.

On a terminal, errors are coloured: the location and message in bold, error: and the caret under the column in red. Set NO_COLOR to any non-empty value, or TERM=dumb, to turn colour off. When stderr is a file or a pipe there is none.

items.title: kod run <file>
items.text:
kod build + execute. Arguments after the file are passed to the program.

./kod run hello.kod

kod replaces itself with the program (execvp), so the program has your terminal. Its stdin, stdout and stderr are yours, its output appears as it is written, and its exit status, or the signal that killed it, is what your shell sees. (stdout is block-buffered when it is not a terminal; call io.flush_stdout() where the order of the two streams matters; a panic flushes it before its message.) If the program cannot be executed, kod says so and exits 127.

items.title: kod test <path>
items.text:
Run test "..." { ... } blocks. Path can be a file or a directory.

  • File: builds the file + all transitively-imported modules that contain tests, runs everything in one binary, prints a rolled-up summary.
  • Directory: walks for *_test.kod and builds them all into one program, with no temporary module, so two test files may share a file name. A file with a path component below the directory that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files) and a build directory directly below it are skipped; a *_test.kod that cannot be read (a link to nothing) stops the run. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.
./kod test stdlib/map_test.kod
./kod test stdlib            # everything under stdlib/
./kod test .                 # everything in the project

Both replace kod with the test binary, as kod run does with a program: its output appears as it is written and its exit status is kod's. The test reporter flushes stdout around every result line and before a failure's detail goes to stderr, so the ok/FAIL lines and the assertion failed detail stay in order on a pipe or in a CI log too; output a test prints itself is flushed with them.

See Testing for the syntax.

items.title: kod check <file>
items.text:
Run the full compile pipeline through codegen, report errors, but write no artifacts and skip the link step. Exits non-zero on any error. It also checks the link directives at the top of each module (see Link inputs), but compiles no C file and does not look for a kod:require file. An error already shown for one module isn't shown again for another.

./kod check src/foo.kod

items.title: kod fmt <path>...
items.text:
Format Kod source files in place: each path is a .kod file or a directory, whose .kod files are formatted at any depth (directories whose names start with ., and build/, are skipped). Each file that changes is printed. With --check nothing is written: the files that would change are printed, and the exit status is 1 if there are any.

./kod fmt stdlib/json.kod tools
./kod fmt --check .

A file with a syntax error is left as it is; its errors are printed and the exit status is 1. kod fmt needs no build: it runs anywhere, not only in the repository root.

The formatter keeps the line breaks it is given; it only reorders import lines and adds blank lines between declarations, as below. It decides everything else:

  • Indentation is four spaces per level. A line is one level deeper than the line that opened the innermost bracket ((, [ or {) still open at its start; a line that starts by closing brackets is at the level of the line that opened the last of them.
  • Spaces separate tokens, one each, except: none after ( and [, and none before ), ], , and ?; none around ., .. and ...; none before ( or [ that follows a name, a literal or a closing bracket (a call or an index), nor in func(; none before : and one after, except after a :name shorthand argument; none after a prefix -; none in {}. A . that starts an implicit variant (= .Red) has a space before it.
  • A comment at the end of a line keeps the space before it.
  • Inside a { … } that closes on the same line, a gap of two or more spaces stays two, so the arms of a one-line match stay apart.
  • Blank lines: at most one in a row, none at the start or the end of the file and none before a line that closes a bracket. The file ends with one newline, and no line has trailing spaces or tabs.
  • A top-level declaration that follows one spanning several lines (a function, a type, a test) has a blank line before it, or before the comments just above it.
  • Imports are sorted in each group of import lines with no blank line between: the standard library's first, then those whose path starts with ./, each by path, and imports of one path in the order they were. A comment line between two imports moves with the one below it; one above a group stays where it is.
  • A list whose closing bracket starts a line ends with a comma: the arguments or parameters of a call or a func, and an array literal.
  • A multi-line string's lines move with the line it starts on, so its value stays the same (see multi-line strings).

Formatting a formatted file changes nothing.

items.title: Build outputs
items.text:
Path Description build/stage0/ The objects sh_kodc, kod and every app share: the C files and Kod modules link.cfg lists as RUNTIME_C and STAGE0_KOD (arena.o, rc.o, runtime.o, _<name>.o; see Self-hosting) and the compiler library the two tools link. build/stage1/ The self-hosted compiler sh_kodc and the objects it is linked from (kodc.{s,o}, runtime_main.{s,o}). build/apps/<stem>/ The final executable, <stem> (or <stem>_test for kod test). <stem> is the entry's file name without .kod; for kod test <dir> it is the directory with every byte outside letters, digits, _ and - replaced by _ (its last 200 bytes, when it is longer), then _tests. A file whose name without .kod is empty, . or .. has no program name and is refused. An entry named kod or lsp (other than tools/kod.kod and tools/lsp.kod, however they are spelled) is refused, because its executable would replace the tool. So is one whose directory the volume takes for the tool's, such as KOD on a case-insensitive volume. build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/ The program's objects, in a tree that mirrors the source tree: each module's .o (lib/json.kod is <stem>.obj/lib/json.kod.o), with its .s beside it only when KOD_ASM_TEXT is set or link.cfg's AS is another assembler and the module was compiled rather than taken from the cache, the object of each C file a module names (<stem>.obj/lib/json.c.o) and the _main shim (<entry>.main.{s,o}, or <first entry>.testmain.{s,o} for tests). So json and ./json, or a/util and b/util, are different objects.

| build/cache/ | Module objects by key (step 3), <sha256>.o. Rebuilding sh_kodc empties it, since every key names the compiler. |

In a project outside the checkout, what is under build/apps/ above goes to the project's .kod-build/apps/ instead, and kod build copies the program to the working directory (or -o PATH); the cache is the checkout's.

make clean-apps (which also empties build/cache/), make clean-stage1, make clean give scoped cleanup.

items.title: Internal / debug commands
items.text: These exist for the build and for debugging. Their shape may change: sh_kodc has the internal subcommands _compile, _emit-runtime-main and _emit-test-runtime-main.

items.title: Concurrency (design)
items.text: Status: step 1 is built: spawn, Task[T] and wait(), a function waiting for its tasks, channels and for v in ch, tasks waiting for I/O, cancellation, select, generators, the helpers, HTTP and TLS in tasks with a server, backtraces that say where a task was spawned, module variables initialized once across tasks, and preemption (Tasks describes what works); step 2 is a proposal. It describes what Kod would add for doing several things at once, in two steps, and what it promises now so that those steps stay possible. The building blocks are Go's (tasks, channels, select), used in a structured way (a task belongs to the function that starts it), on one thread: Kod doesn't share memory between threads.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
Programs that wait: an HTTP server answering several clients, a client fetching several URLs at once, a language server that stays responsive while it checks a file, a tool that runs subprocesses and reads their output as it comes. These need concurrency: many things in progress, each spending most of its time waiting for I/O.

Using several cores for one computation, parallelism, is a second and smaller need. Today processes cover it: kod test and the test runner run files in parallel, and testing.run forks.

Not a goal: threads sharing objects, locks around shared data, or an async keyword.

items.title: What the runtime decides already
items.text:
Four facts of today's runtime rule out the usual answer, threads that share memory:

  • A count that reaches zero frees the object at once. If threads shared objects, one could read a reference out of a field while another stores over it and releases the old object, freeing it before the reader retains it: a use-after-free from ordinary code, which Kod has none of outside unsafe. Copy-on-write has the same gap: an array whose count is 1, in a field two threads reach, is changed in place while the other reads it. Go is spared this because its garbage collector frees nothing still reachable. Atomic counts don't close the gap, and they are not the cost they are often said to be: with stadd and ldaddal they measured 0% compiling codegen.kod, +1% on trees and +2% on words (cycles, 2026-11-23), as long as one core owns each object. An object many cores retain at once would move its count's cache line between them on every retain and release.
  • The allocator's free lists are one global (rc_free_lists in stdlib/rc.c), and the stdlib keeps state in module variables (posix._read_buf, time._ts, testing's counters).
  • Arrays, Maps and plain structs are values with copy-on-write: one can be handed to other code without being shared.
  • shared struct marks every type that is shared by reference, so the compiler can tell a value that holds one from one that doesn't.

The first two say: never let two threads reach one object. The last two say Kod is well placed to live with that.

items.title: Step 1: tasks on one thread
items.text:
A task is a call running on a stack of its own. All tasks run on the program's one thread, one at a time; a task runs until it would wait, then the next ready one runs. Nothing is shared between threads, so there are no data races, and reference counts, the allocator and module variables stay as they are.

The building blocks are Go's: tasks, channels, select. How they are used is structured, as in Kotlin, Swift and Trio: a task belongs to the function that started it, gives back its result, and is cancelled when that function gives up on it. That takes the place of Go's WaitGroup, errgroup and Context, and no task is left running by mistake.

items.title: spawn, and a task's result
items.text:
let user = spawn fetch_user(id)          // Task[User or Error]
let orders = spawn fetch_orders(id)
show(try user.wait(), try orders.wait())

spawn takes a call: the function and its arguments are evaluated where it is, and the call then runs as a new task. It gives a Task[T], T the call's result, and wait() gives that result once the task has ended, so try, must and ? or default work on it as on the call. A call that gives back none can be spawned as a statement; one that gives back a value has its task kept, as any value must be (let _t = spawn f() to drop it on purpose).

items.title: Tasks belong to the function that starts them
items.text:
A function doesn't return while a task it spawned is running: at its end it waits for each one it hasn't waited for. When the function returns an error, by throw or a try that passes one up, the tasks it hasn't waited for are cancelled first; a plain return just waits, so that spawn log(x) before one still logs. A cancelled task carries on until it next waits, and that wait gives up: one that can fail gives an IoError of kind .Cancelled, which try passes up as any error, so it ends; a sleep ends, a receive gives none, a send isn't made; wait() and give_way() go on, as they can't fail. What such a task gave back is dropped.

It is the function a task belongs to, not the block it was spawned in: a loop that spawns a task each time leaves them running until the function ends, unless it waits for them. That is simpler to follow than a wait at the end of every block (as Kotlin's coroutineScope has).

func dashboard(anon id: int64) -> Page or Error {
    let user = spawn fetch_user(id)
    let orders = spawn fetch_orders(id)
    return Page(user: try user.wait(), orders: try orders.wait())
}   // when fetch_user fails, fetch_orders is cancelled, not left running

A Task can be kept, returned or stored like any value: the function that spawned it has waited for it by the time it returns, so a Task that has left that function holds a result, and nothing needs checking.

A task that should outlive its function, such as a server's connection handler, is started with spawn detached: it gives no Task, nothing waits for it, and it runs until its call returns or the program ends.

for true {
    let conn = try listener.accept()
    spawn detached serve(conn)
}

main is a function like any other: it waits for its tasks before the program ends; detached ones end with the program.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text:
tasks.within(d, f) runs f as a task and gives back what it gives back, or an IoError of kind .TimedOut after d, when it cancels f and so the tasks f started:

let page = try tasks.within(Duration(seconds: 5), func() -> Page or Error {
    return dashboard(id)
})

items.title: Channels
items.text:
Channel[T] is tasks.Channel[T], as Task[T] is tasks.Task[T]: the scheduler they call can't move into the builtins, whose module would then have variables, which stops the compiler inlining any builtin into other modules. for v in ch is the language's, as chan is Go's.

let jobs = Channel[str]()                 // unbuffered: a send waits for a receive
let results = Channel[int64](capacity: 8) // buffered: a send waits only when full
jobs.send("a.txt")
let n = results.receive()                 // int64?: none once closed and drained
jobs.close()
for job in jobs {                         // receives until the channel is closed
    work(job)
}

A channel carries any value, shared structs included: everything is on one thread. Sending on a closed channel, or closing one twice, panics, as in Go. A wait on a channel is a wait like any other: cancelling a task that waits in send or receive ends that wait with .Cancelled.

items.title: select
items.text:
Waiting on whichever of several channel operations is ready first needs syntax, and takes the shape of match:

select {
    receive(results) is r -> total += r
    send(jobs, next) -> sent += 1
    after(Duration(seconds: 5)) -> throw Timeout()
    else -> idle()
}

receive(ch) is v binds what was received (and takes the arm with none once the channel is closed), send(ch, v) takes the arm once the value is taken, after(d) once d has passed, and else at once when no other is ready. When several are ready, one is picked at random, as in Go, so none starves.

items.title: Generators
items.text:
A function with yield in it is a generator: it gives back a Channel[T], and calling it starts its body as a task, which each yield v sends v on:

func lines(anon r: Reader) -> Channel[str] {
    for not r.at_end() {
        yield r.read_line()
    }
}

for line in lines(conn) {
    handle(line)
}

The channel is unbuffered, so the body runs only as far ahead as the reader reads, and it is closed when the body ends. The task belongs to the caller, not to the generator, which returns at once: a caller that stops reading early cancels it when it returns, as with any task. yield is allowed only in a function that gives back a Channel, and a generator's return takes no value.

As built, the body's task belongs to no function, and ends once nothing holds the channel: its hold on the channel is weak, so a reader that lets go of it early frees it, and the body's next yield finds it gone and ends the body. One already waiting in a yield ends when the next generator starts, which wakes those whose channel is gone. Belonging to the caller instead would cancel the body where the caller returns, which goes wrong for a function that hands a generator's channel on to its own caller.

items.title: Actors
items.text:
A task that owns some state and serves messages needs nothing new; an enum with payloads says what it can be asked:

type Msg = enum {
    Add(n: int64)
    Total(reply: Channel[int64])
}

func counter(anon inbox: Channel[Msg]) -> none {
    mut n = 0
    for msg in inbox {
        match msg {
            .Add(k) -> n += k
            .Total(reply) -> reply.send(n)
        }
    }
}

Only counter touches n, so nothing guards it.

items.title: Helpers
items.text:
In tasks, written with the above:

  • tasks.all(fs) runs calls together and gives back their results in order, or the first error, cancelling the rest;
  • tasks.first(fs) gives back the first to succeed and cancels the others;
  • xs.map_concurrently(f, limit: n) maps over an array with at most n calls running at once;
  • tasks.Mutex, for logic that holds a value across a wait (below);
  • tasks.give_way() lets the other tasks run.

Outside tasks nothing changes: a program that never spawns one runs exactly as today.

items.title: When a task gives way
items.text:
At the points where it would wait:

  • reading or writing a descriptor that isn't ready (posix.Fd, tcp, tls, and so http, stream and jsonrpc above them), accepting, connecting;
  • waiting for a child process (process.Child.wait);
  • sleeping (time.sleep), sending, receiving, select, waiting for a task (wait(), and the wait at a function's end);
  • tasks.give_way().

These are also where cancellation reaches a task.

A task that runs long without waiting is preempted (below). Waiting works the same through every layer, because the stack is the task's own: when C code calls back into Kod and the callback has to wait, it gives way with the C frames still on the task's stack, and carries on when what it waits for comes. Stackless designs (async/await) cannot do that, and would also split every function into the kinds that may wait and those that may not.

When no task can run and none waits for anything that can come (a descriptor, a timer, a child), the program panics with all tasks are asleep: deadlock, as Go does, instead of hanging.

items.title: Preemption
items.text:
A task that runs long without waiting is also made to give way, as in Go, so one busy loop can't keep the others waiting. The compiler puts a check at the top of every loop iteration: a load from a polling page, the JVM's way, with no branch. While more than one task is ready, a timer makes that page unreadable every 10 ms; the next check then faults, and the fault handler sends the task into the scheduler from there. The point is a known one, the top of a loop: no reference count is half changed, and a stub that keeps every register makes the switch, so the loop goes on as it was once the task runs again. The handler tells the page from a real fault by its address, and makes it readable again.

Measured on the benchmarks (cycles, 2026-11-23; the experiment is kept out of the tree), against no check, and against a flag that each iteration loads and branches on:

check at each loop iteration qsort sieve loop words trees fib load a flag, branch if set +17% +11% +5% 0% 0% +1% load from the polling page 0% +9% 0% 0% 0% +2% as built (2026-11-24) +16% +10% 0% 0% 0% 0% as built, a local's copy-on-write check hoisted +16% +8% 0% 0% 0% 0%

The branch is what costs, in tight loops. The experiment left out what the check must stop the optimiser doing: reusing after the check a value loaded from the heap before it, or hoisting a heap load out of the loop, or a loop's copy-on-write check, since at the check another task may change (or free) what was loaded, or take a reference to the array. As built, the check is opaque to load reuse, and a loop with one isn't hoisted from: qsort's inner loops load self.xs's buffer and length again after each check (+8%) and on each iteration (+8% more): self is a shared struct, so that is the price of reading what another task may have stored. A loop's copy-on-write check on a local's array is still hoisted, since no other task can reach the frame or take an array a local holds alone (sieve: +10% to +8%); one on a field isn't. What is left of sieve's cost is the check's own load, in a loop of a few instructions. The compiler, with the check in its own loops, is about 1% slower, within the noise. Loads, unlike the copy-on-write check, aren't told apart by where they come from: a slot may hold a shared struct as well as an array, and the passes that would reuse or hoist them see no types.

As built until 2026-11-27, every 10 ms a thread made the page unreadable once a program had started a task; the fault handler made it readable again and sent the task to a stub that saves every register a call may change, calls give_way, and goes on past the load. No check is put in the scheduler (tasks), the builtins it uses, or the backtrace printer, which a switch mustn't land in.

A simulation needs more: to preempt a task at a check the seed picks, the same one each time, it must count the checks, which a fault on each would make take microseconds apiece. So the check became a flag after all: a load, and a branch to a call out of line, after the function's ret, which isn't taken until the flag is set. The call goes to a stub that changes nothing a value may be in, so the passes see the check as before: text that may change memory and names no register. The thread sets the flag every 10 ms, and the stub counts a countdown down, 1 outside a simulation, and at 0 has the task give way and clears the flag; a simulation keeps the flag set and the countdown at what the seed says, so that every check calls the stub, a few instructions until the countdown is out. Measured against the page (best of 7 runs, 2026-11-27):

check at each loop iteration qsort sieve loop load a flag, branch out of line if set 0% +1.5% +1%

The branch, measured at +11% to +17% on 2026-11-23, was then in the loop's straight line; out of line, the branch not taken costs next to nothing. Under a simulation, a TLS connection writing and reading 300 KB at once takes 20 ms a seed on average against 13 ms without preemption; a seed that preempts every few checks switches tasks hundreds of thousands of times, so a preemption looks for I/O that has come (a system call per descriptor) only one time in 16. Once the snapshot that builds the compiler's own modules had the flag too, the page and its fault handler went.

Counting alone rarely finds a race whose window is a few checks among hundreds of thousands, such as a writer preempted between queueing records and sending them (a TLS bug, put back on purpose: 0 of 200 seeds). Three things find it, in 55 of 200 seeds (the count moves a little as code changes where seeds preempt):

  • A store to a shared struct's field or a module-level variable sets a word to the struct's address (adrp, str: no branch; for a variable, an address outside the counted heap); the next check that finds it set clears it and, if another task can reach the struct, counts a second, short countdown down. Modules are compiled apart, so which structs other tasks reach is known only at run time: under a simulation, spawn marks what the new task's body refers to, and all it refers to in turn, in a byte map beside the counted heap (one byte for 16 bytes, address space reserved per run), and so does a channel's send for the value sent. Marks stay when an object is freed, so the walk always looks into the object it starts from, which may be new in a marked one's memory. The preemption is at the check, never between the store and the next one, so the simulation interleaves only as a real run could.
  • Under half the seeds tasks run by priority (PCT): the highest ready one, a preempted one dropping below the rest, so that a writer can run on while a reader that is ready waits, as on a busy machine.
  • Every switch looks for I/O that has come (one poll(2) for all of a run's descriptors), as the kernel would have woken those tasks meanwhile.

Without the store bias, or without priorities, none of the 200 seeds found it. While every shared struct's stores counted, 32 did: stores to ones no other task sees, such as a byte buffer's, diluted the bias, half of a run's stores. A mark stays on a freed object's bytes until the run ends, so a new object there counts too; clearing it on reuse, a branch in every allocation, found 56 seeds instead of 54, so it isn't done.

Outside a simulation the store's word costs little: with the address of the struct, which takes a load when it isn't in a register, the compiler takes 367 ms against 365 with a constant, and a loop storing to a shared struct's fields 200 million times is within the noise. A TLS hunt takes 6.3 s for 200 seeds, against 4.2 s before any of this.

The check is in every loop of every program, since a module is compiled without knowing whether the program starts tasks; a program that never does pays for it too, and it is the one thing step 1 costs such a program. Code that loops by recursion, without a loop, needs the check at function entry as well: measured on top of the loop checks, fib +1%, trees +1%, the compiler +1%, the rest 0%, and built.

items.title: The runtime
items.text:
• A task's stack is reserved with mmap (8 MB of address space, as the main thread has, with a guard page below it). Pages are committed as they are touched, so a task that uses 20 KB costs 20 KB, and thousands fit, the way Go's small growing stacks do. Overflowing hits the guard page, as on the main stack.
  • Switching saves the registers a call keeps (x19–x28, fp, lr, sp, d8–d15) and loads the next task's: a few dozen instructions in a naked function in the runtime, like the reference-count stubs.
  • The scheduler keeps a queue of ready tasks. When it is empty it waits in kevent for whatever the waiting tasks wait on: a descriptor to become readable or writable, a timer, a child process to exit (EVFILT_READ/WRITE/TIMER/PROC).
  • Descriptors a task uses are set non-blocking; a read that would block (EAGAIN) registers with kevent and gives way. While no task has been started the calls block as today; checking which applies is one load and branch per call.
  • spawn compiles to a closure over the evaluated arguments, handed to the runtime with a fresh stack; the task ends when the call returns, and keeps what it gave back for wait().
  • Belonging to a function: a function that spawns gets a list of its tasks in its frame, and its exits (each return, and the paths throw and try take) wait for the list, cancelling first when the exit is early. Cancelling sets a flag on the task and wakes it if it waits; each wait point checks the flag. A function that spawns nothing pays nothing.
  • Backtraces walk the frame chain of the task that panicked, which ends at its entry function. A panic ends the program, as now (and as in Go), wherever it happens, unless it is caught.
  • Module variables: a lazy initializer may now give way halfway (it reads a file, say). Another task that reads the variable meanwhile waits for it, instead of starting a second initialization.

items.title: Limits of step 1
items.text:
• One core. Tasks interleave; they don't run at the same time. Step 2 is the way to several cores.
  • DNS: getaddrinfo has no non-blocking form here, so a lookup holds up every task until it returns. Later, a C helper thread could make the call and wake the task; it touches no Kod object, so it needs no changes to reference counting.
  • Regular files are always "ready" to kevent; reading a large file blocks the thread while it does, which is short.
  • Interleaving still happens where a task gives way: code that checks a shared value, waits, then acts on it can see it change in between. No data races, but logic races are still possible, as in Go; tasks.Mutex covers the cases that hold a value across a wait.

items.title: Step 2: workers that share nothing
items.text:
Here Kod departs from Go. Go runs goroutines on every core over one shared heap. For Kod that would take one of three things: data races that may free memory still in use, which gives up memory safety in racy programs (as C++ and Swift 5 do); a compile-time proof that there are none (Swift 6's actors and Sendable, Rust's Send and Sync), the largest language change of the three; or frees delayed until every thread has moved on, with each read of a shared field retaining through an increment-if-not-zero, a cost on every such read. None is worth it yet, so Kod doesn't share memory between threads.

For parallelism inside one process, later: a worker is a thread with its own heap, free lists and module variables, running its own tasks. Workers exchange values only through channels made for it, and only values that contain no shared struct, closure or interface (which could hold one): those are copied into the receiving worker's heap. Reference counts stay non-atomic, because no object is reachable from two threads; the copy is the price, paid only for what is sent. This is the model of Erlang processes and Dart isolates.

Step 2 reuses step 1's channels and scheduler; what it adds is per-thread runtime state and the check of what may be sent. It is a sketch, to be designed when there is a program that needs it.

items.title: What holds from now on
items.text:
• No object is shared between threads, in either step, so a program without unsafe has no use-after-free. That also lets reference counts stay non-atomic, though they could be made atomic for little.
  • spawn, select and yield become keywords when step 1 lands (detached is one only after spawn). No code in the repository uses select or yield as a name. process.spawn, a shorthand for process.start(argv, stdin: .Null, stdout: .Null, stderr: .Null) and its pid, is gone already.
  • IoKind gains .Cancelled, the error a cancelled task's wait gives.
  • New mutable module state in the stdlib is a cost for step 2; keep it to what a worker could have its own copy of.
  • Blocking calls go through a few low-level functions (posix.Fd.read and write, tcp's accept and connect, the TLS callbacks, process.wait_status, time.sleep): step 1 changes those, not their callers, so new I/O code should build on them rather than call libc directly.

items.title: Building it
items.text:
Each step lands with its tests, and the first is measured: the cost of a switch, and that a program without tasks is no slower than the loop checks make it.

  1. Stacks, switching and tasks.give_way in the runtime; spawn, Task[T] and wait(), and the wait at a function's end. Tests of order, of deep recursion inside a task, and of a function not returning before its tasks.
  2. Channel[T], close, for v in ch, and deadlock detection.
  3. kevent: descriptors, timers and child processes; posix.Fd, tcp, process and time.sleep give way inside a task.
  4. Cancellation: an error exit cancels, every wait point gives up, spawn detached, tasks.within.
  5. select, generators and yield, tasks.all, tasks.first, map_concurrently, tasks.Mutex.
  6. TLS and HTTP inside tasks; a demo that fetches several URLs at once, and a small concurrent HTTP server.
  7. Backtraces, and lazily initialized module variables, across tasks.

Preemption comes after them: the loop checks, the polling page and its timer, the fault handler, and the check at function entry, measured before it goes in.

items.title: if / else
items.text:
if x > 0 {
    print("positive")
} else {
    print("non-positive")
}

The else branch is optional. Braces are always required.

The condition must be a bool. There's no truthiness, so if n on an int64 is an error (write if n != 0), and so is if x on an optional (write if x is not none, or if x is Some(v) to bind the value).

items.title: if as a value
items.text:
Where a value goes, an if with an else gives one: that of the branch that runs.

let step = if line.starts_with("L") { -1 } else { 1 }
let size = if n < 0 {
    "negative"
} else if n < 10 {
    "small"
} else {
    "large"
}
print(f"{size}, {if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }}")

A branch is a block whose last statement is an expression (or another if with an else), the branch's value, as in a match's arm. One that ends in return, throw or a call that never returns needs no value. The else can't be left out, and the branches' types follow the rules of match as an expression: they are one type, or convert to the one that the value goes to, and a none makes it optional.

The condition can bind names and narrow them as in an if statement:

let doubled = if text.parse_int() is int64(n) and n > 0 { 2 * n } else { 0 }

At the start of a statement, if is always the statement.

items.title: for (while-style)
items.text:
for with a condition loops until the condition is false:

mut i: int64 = 0
for i < 10 {
    print_int(i)
    i = i + 1
}

This is Kod's general looping construct. There is no while keyword. As with if, the condition must be a bool.

The condition can bind names as an if condition does, alone or joined by and. The loop ends when a pattern fails, and the names are new each time round:

for reader.next_line() is Some(line) and len(line) > 0 {
    print(line)
}

items.title: for / in (foreach)
items.text:
Iterate over an array with for … in:

let names: [str] = ["alice", "bob", "carol"]
for name in names {
    print(name)
}

The loop variable is declared implicitly — no let needed.

for i, x in xs also numbers the elements from 0:

for i, name in names {
    print(f"{i}: {name}")
}

for i in a..b counts from a up to but not including b, like the slice xs[a..b]. Both bounds must be int64 and are evaluated once, before the first iteration, so changing n in the body of for i in 0..n doesn't change how many times it runs. a..b works only here: it isn't a value of its own.

for i in 0..3 {
    print_int(i)    // 0, 1, 2
}

a..=b includes b. step k after the range counts by k instead of 1, and a negative k counts down, while the counter is above the end (or, with ..=, not below it):

for i in 1..=3 {
    print_int(i)    // 1, 2, 3
}
for i in 0..10 step 4 {
    print_int(i)    // 0, 4, 8
}
for i in 3..=0 step -1 {
    print_int(i)    // 3, 2, 1, 0
}

The step is evaluated once too, and must be an int64. A step of 0 is an error when it is a literal and a panic (a range's step is 0) when it isn't. A range may end at the largest or smallest int64: the loop stops there instead of stepping past it. These forms work in a comprehension's for as well. arrays.reversed(xs) gives an array's elements last first.

Either form can take _ for a name it doesn't use.

A str or bytes value is iterated byte by byte, each byte an int64 from 0 to 255, as s[i] gives it; for i, b in s numbers them. For text, iterate over s.code_points() instead.

mut spaces: int64 = 0
for b in "a b c" {
    if b == ' ' {
        spaces += 1
    }
}

A Map is iterated in the order its keys were first set: for k in m gives the keys and for k, v in m each key with its value. The loop goes over the entries the map had when it started, so the body may set and remove entries freely.

for name, age in ages {
    print(f"{name} is {age}")
}

A Set from the sets module is iterated the same way, for x in s, over its elements in the order they were first added.

Arrays, str, bytes, Map, Set and a..b can be iterated, and so can a struct with a values(self) -> [T] method, such as a Deque or a Heap: the loop goes over the array values() gives. Any other kind of value is an error.

items.title: break and continue
items.text:
Both work inside every form of for, and nowhere else; a function literal in a loop's body is outside of it:

mut i: int64 = 0
for i < 100 {
    if i == 5 {
        break
    }
    i = i + 1
}

for x in items {
    if x == skip_value {
        continue
    }
    process(x)
}

Both act on the innermost loop. To leave or go on with an outer one, give it a label, a name and a colon before its for, and name it after break or continue:

mut found = -1
rows: for i, row in grid {
    for x in row {
        if x < 0 {
            found = i
            break rows
        }
    }
}
// found is 1

continue rows goes on with the next pass of the labelled loop. A label names the loop it's on and the loops inside it can use it, so break name for a loop that isn't around it is an error (no loop labelled `rows` around this `break`), and so is a label that a loop around it already has.

items.title: match
items.text:
Pattern matching on enums, integers, and strings. See Pattern matching.

match direction {
    Direction.North -> print("north")
    Direction.South -> print("south")
    else -> print("other")
}

items.title: Blocks and bindings
items.text:
A statement ends at the end of its line or at a }, so two statements can share a line only after a block (if c { a() } b()). Anything else after a statement on its line is an error: let x = 5 print_int(x).

A let or let-else binding lasts from its statement to the end of the block it's in. The bindings of a match arm's pattern, or of if … is, last for that arm. A for … in variable lasts for the loop body, and parameters (self included) for the whole function. Parameter and field defaults follow the same rules.

Every block has its own scope. A binding may take the name of one still in force, whatever kind of binding either is: a let, mut or let-else, a name in a pattern, a for variable, a parameter or self. Inside its block, arm or loop body the new binding hides the old one, and reading or assigning the name there means the new one. When that block, arm or loop ends, the old binding is back with its own value, type and mutability:

func show(anon item: A, anon flag: bool) -> str {
    if flag {
        let item = B(x: 9)   // hides the parameter until the `}`
        return item.show()   // B's show
    }
    return item.show()       // A's show
}

mut total = 0
for x in xs {
