    let total = x * 2        // this loop body's own `total`
    print(f"{total}")
}
total = total + 1            // the `mut total` again

A block may also bind a name again itself. The new binding then replaces the old one for the rest of that block. These count as binding the name again in the same block:

  • a function's top block reusing a parameter's name;
  • an arm reusing its pattern's name;
  • a loop body reusing its for variable's name.

A binding's value, the array of a for … in and the value that if … is tests all see the binding the name had before, even when the type differs: let x = x + 1, let x = f"#{x}", for x in x, if o is Some(o). A let-else's else block runs when the pattern doesn't match, so there the name still has the binding it had before the let-else:

for arg in args {
    let .Some(arg) = parse_num(arg) else {
        print(f"bad: {arg}")   // the str from `args`
        continue
    }
    total += arg               // the parsed int64
}

A name is a local only where a binding of it is in force. Elsewhere it means a function of the module, an imported one or a builtin of that name, as it does in a call (see Function values). Elsewhere means before its let, or after the block, arm or loop that bound it when no outer binding is in force. With none of those functions, reading or assigning the name is an error: `x` is read before its `let` or `x` is declared in a block that has ended. When another module declares a type of that name and this one doesn't see it, reading or calling the name gives the error for that type (unknown type `Mode`; lib/modes.kod declares `Mode`: write `modes.Mode` or list it in the import (`{ Mode }`)), as with no local at all. Assigning the name still gives the errors above. Declare a name before the block to use it after the block:

mut label = "other"
if n > 0 {
    label = "positive"
}
print(label)

A function literal doesn't see the locals of the function it's written in.

items.title: return
items.text:
Return a value from a function:

func abs(n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n < 0 {
        return 0 - n
    }
    return n
}

A bare return (no value) is valid in -> none functions.

A function that returns a value must not be able to run off the end of its body (see Return values). An if without an else, a for over a condition or an array, and a for true loop with a break can all finish, so a return has to follow them; a match whose arms all return, and a for true loop that only leaves through return, can't. Nor can a call that never returns: panic(...), or a -> none function or method without a return whose body can't finish by these same rules, such as one that ends in another such call or in a for true loop without a break. A method counts whatever it's called on, a local included, as long as the receiver's type is known at the call. A call through a function value and a method called through an interface value are taken to return, since what they call is chosen at run time; end such a path with a panic(...) or a return after the call (see Return values).

items.title: Cryptography
items.text:
The modules under stdlib/crypto/ are the pieces TLS 1.3 is built from, written in Kod: hashes, HMAC and HKDF, two AEAD ciphers, a key exchange, checking RSA and ECDSA signatures and certificates, and the operating system's random numbers. Each is checked against the test vectors of the standard that defines it.

import "crypto/sha2"
import "crypto/hmac"
import "encoding/hex"

print(hex.encode(sha2.sha256(b"abc")))
// ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad

let tag = hmac.mac(.Sha256, key: b"key", data: b"The quick brown fox")

The code that handles secrets (the ciphers, the MAC, the key exchange, ECDSA signing and hmac.equal) does the same work whatever the secret is: it doesn't branch on a secret or use one to pick an array element. That is how it keeps secrets from showing in how long it takes. Checking a signature uses only public values, so that code doesn't need to. None of it has been audited.

items.title: Hashes: crypto/sha2
items.text:
SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (FIPS 180-4), named by sha2.Algo:

Algo Digest Block .Sha256 32 bytes 64 bytes .Sha384 48 bytes 128 bytes .Sha512 64 bytes 128 bytes

algo.size() and algo.block_size() give the two numbers.

Function Gives sha256(data: bytes) -> bytes the SHA-256 digest of data; sha384 and sha512 likewise digest(algo: Algo, data: bytes) -> bytes the digest of data with algo

A Hasher takes the data in pieces:

mut h = sha2.Hasher(.Sha384)
h.update(b"hello, ")
let so_far = h.finish()      // the digest of "hello, "
h.update(b"world")
assert h.finish() == sha2.sha384(b"hello, world")

finish doesn't change the hasher, so it can be asked for the digest of what it has seen so far and go on; a copy (let saved = h) goes on from the same point separately. TLS uses both to hash the handshake as it goes.

The blocks go to the CPU's SHA-256 and SHA-512 instructions (sha256h, sha512h and their kin, which every Apple CPU since the M1 has): SHA-256 runs at about 2 GB/s and SHA-384 and SHA-512 at about 1.4 GB/s (OpenSSL's, 3 and 1.8 GB/s).

items.title: HMAC: crypto/hmac
items.text:
Function Gives mac(algo: Algo, key: bytes, data: bytes) -> bytes the HMAC (RFC 2104) of data under key, as long as algo's digest equal(a: bytes, b: bytes) -> bool whether a and b are the same, taking as long for any two values of one length

Compare a MAC with equal, not ==: == stops at the first byte that differs, which tells someone timing it how much of a forged MAC was right.

items.title: HKDF: crypto/hkdf
items.text:
HKDF (RFC 5869) makes keys from a shared secret:

Function Gives extract(algo: Algo, salt: bytes, ikm: bytes) -> bytes a pseudorandom key from the input key material ikm; an empty salt stands for a block of zeros expand(algo: Algo, prk: bytes, info: bytes, length: int64) -> bytes length bytes of key from prk, labelled by info; length is at most 255 digests, and more panics

items.title: ChaCha20-Poly1305: crypto/chacha20poly1305
items.text:
The AEAD of RFC 8439: it encrypts and authenticates a message, and authenticates extra data sent alongside it in the clear (aad).

import "crypto/chacha20poly1305"

let sealed = chacha20poly1305.seal(b"attack at dawn", key: key, nonce: nonce, aad: b"header")
let opened = chacha20poly1305.open(sealed, key: key, nonce: nonce, aad: b"header")   // bytes?
Function Gives seal(plaintext: bytes, key: bytes, nonce: bytes, aad: bytes) -> bytes the ciphertext, as long as plaintext, then the 16-byte tag open(sealed: bytes, key: bytes, nonce: bytes, aad: bytes) -> bytes? the plaintext, or none when the tag doesn't match: the data, aad, key or nonce isn't what was sealed

The key is 32 bytes and the nonce 12; another length panics. A nonce must never be used twice with one key: that gives away both messages and lets anyone forge others. TLS counts records for it.

The two halves are there on their own too: chacha20(data, key:, nonce:, counter:) XORs data with the key stream from block counter, and poly1305(data, key:) is the one-time MAC under a 32-byte key.

items.title: AES-GCM: crypto/aesgcm
items.text:
AES-128 and AES-256 in Galois/Counter Mode (NIST SP 800-38D), the AEAD every TLS 1.3 server has. It works as ChaCha20-Poly1305 does, with a key of 16 or 32 bytes and a nonce of 12:

import "crypto/aesgcm"
import "crypto/random"

let key = aesgcm.Key(random.secure_bytes(16))
let sealed = key.seal(b"attack at dawn", nonce: nonce, aad: b"header")
let opened = key.open(sealed, nonce: nonce, aad: b"header")   // bytes?

A Key holds the expanded key, so a connection makes it once and seals each record with it; aesgcm.seal(plaintext, key:, nonce:, aad:) and aesgcm.open(sealed, key:, nonce:, aad:) make one for a single message. encrypt_block(block, key:) is AES itself, on one 16-byte block.

The AES rounds and GHASH's multiplications are the CPU's own instructions (aese, aesmc and pmull, which every 64-bit Apple CPU has), so they take the same time whatever the key and data are, and AES-GCM is about seven times as fast as ChaCha20-Poly1305 here.

items.title: X25519: crypto/x25519
items.text:
The Diffie-Hellman function of RFC 7748. Each side makes a private key of 32 random bytes and sends its public key; each then gets the same shared secret from its own private key and the other's public key.

import "crypto/random"
import "crypto/x25519"

let mine = random.secure_bytes(32)
let public = x25519.public_key(mine)
// ... send `public`, receive `theirs` ...
let Some(secret) = x25519.shared(mine, theirs) else { return ... }
Function Gives public_key(private: bytes) -> bytes the 32-byte public key of a 32-byte private key shared(private: bytes, peer: bytes) -> bytes? the 32-byte shared secret, or none when it comes out all zeros, which a peer sending a bad public key causes and TLS must refuse scalar_mult(scalar: bytes, point: bytes) -> bytes the function itself, with no check

A key of another length panics. One call takes about 0.16 ms (OpenSSL's, 0.023 ms), the same steps whatever the private key is.

items.title: RSA signatures: crypto/rsa
items.text:
rsa.PublicKey(n:, e:) is a key from its modulus and exponent, big-endian bytes as a certificate holds them; a modulus under 512 bits, an even one, or an exponent that is even or 1 is an error. Two kinds of signature are checked (RFC 8017):

Function Gives verify_pkcs1(key: PublicKey, algo: Algo, message: bytes, signature: bytes) -> bool whether signature is the key's PKCS #1 v1.5 signature of message hashed with algo, the kind most certificates carry verify_pss(key: PublicKey, algo: Algo, message: bytes, signature: bytes, salt_size: int64 = -1) -> bool the same for a PSS signature, with algo for MGF1 too and a salt of salt_size bytes; -1 is the digest's size, which TLS 1.3 requires

key.bits() is the modulus's size and key.size() a signature's length in bytes.

rsa.PrivateKey(der) is a private key from its PKCS #1 form (the DER of an RSA PRIVATE KEY block, which a PKCS #8 PRIVATE KEY holds for RSA). A key whose modulus isn't the product of its primes, or whose exponents don't fit it, is an error.

Function Gives key.sign_pkcs1(algo: Algo, message: bytes) -> bytes the PKCS #1 v1.5 signature, the same each time key.sign_pss(algo: Algo, message: bytes) -> bytes the PSS signature, with MGF1 of algo and a random salt of the digest's size key.public the PublicKey

Signing works by the Chinese remainder theorem, with exponentiations that look at the secret exponents 4 bits at a time and pick each multiplier by masks from all 16, so they take the same steps for every key. Each signature is checked with the public key before it is given out, since a fault in one of the two halves would otherwise give the key away. A 2048-bit signature takes about 3.2 ms, and a 3072-bit one 11 ms (OpenSSL's, 0.4 and 1.2 ms).

items.title: ECDSA signatures: crypto/ecdsa
items.text:
ECDSA (FIPS 186-5) on the curves ecdsa.Curve.P256 and .P384.

Function Gives PublicKey(curve: Curve, point: bytes) -> PublicKey or Error the key whose point is point, uncompressed (0x04, then x and y); a point not on the curve is an error key.verify(algo: Algo, message: bytes, signature: bytes) -> bool whether signature, DER as X.509 and TLS carry it, is the key's signature of message hashed with algo key.verify_rs(algo: Algo, message: bytes, r: bytes, s: bytes) -> bool the same with r and s given as big-endian numbers

key.point() gives the point back, uncompressed.

ecdsa.PrivateKey(curve, scalar:) is a private key from its scalar, big-endian and the curve's size (32 or 48 bytes), above 0 and below the curve's order:

Function Gives key.public_key() -> PublicKey its public key key.sign(algo: Algo, message: bytes) -> bytes the DER signature of message hashed with algo key.sign_rs(algo: Algo, message: bytes) -> (bytes, bytes) r and s, each the curve's size

The nonce is RFC 6979's, made from the key and the message, so the same message always gets the same signature and no random number can be bad enough to give the key away. Signing does the same steps whatever the key and nonce are: the multiplication by the nonce adds one precomputed multiple of the generator for every 4 bits, picked by looking at all 16 and keeping one by masks, with formulas that have no special cases (Renes, Costello and Batina, 2016). It takes about 0.18 ms on P-256 and 0.85 ms on P-384, after a table that the first signature on a curve makes (about 2 ms on P-256).

A signature must be strict DER: a length in long form, an integer with a 0 byte it doesn't need, a negative one, or bytes after the end is refused, so that a signature has one encoding.

Both modules are checked against Wycheproof's test vectors, which aim at the mistakes signature checks are known for. Checking takes about 0.09 ms for an RSA signature of 2048 bits and 0.23 ms for 3072, 0.4 ms for P-256 and 2.5 ms for P-384.

items.title: Certificates: crypto/x509
items.text:
x509.parse(der) reads an X.509 certificate (RFC 5280), and x509.verify checks the chain a server sent:

import "crypto/x509"

let chain = [must x509.parse(d) for d in must x509.pem_certificates(text)]
let path = x509.verify(chain, host: "github.com", roots: must x509.system_roots(), now: now)

chain is the server's certificates in the order TLS sends them, its own first; now is seconds since 1970. verify gives the path it found, from the server's certificate up to the root, or an error that says what is wrong. It checks that:

  • every certificate on the path is valid at now, and signed by the next one's key, with RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) or ECDSA on P-256 or P-384 and SHA-2;
  • each certificate above the server's is a CA (basicConstraints), may sign certificates (keyUsage, if it has one), allows as many CAs below it as there are (pathLenConstraint), and allows a server (extKeyUsage, if it has one);
  • the server's certificate names host in its subjectAltName, as a DNS name (ignoring case and a trailing dot; *.example.com stands for one label, so it matches www.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com) or, for an IPv4 address, as an IP address; the common name isn't used, as browsers don't;
  • the server's certificate allows a server and a signature;
  • no certificate sent has a critical extension this module doesn't know (such as name constraints), which RFC 5280 says to refuse.

The certificates may come in any order after the first, with extra ones; it tries each that could be next. A root is trusted as it is, so only its validity and signature over the certificate below it count. Revocation isn't checked.

system_roots() reads the operating system's trusted roots once: on macOS those in /System/Library/Keychains/SystemRootCertificates.keychain, which keychain_certificates(data) takes out of the keychain file as DER (the /etc/ssl/cert.pem there has fewer), and elsewhere the usual PEM bundles. load_roots(path) reads another PEM file; a certificate in it that can't be read (an unusual key, say) is left out. A Certificate has its fields as read (dns_names, not_after, is_ca, key, ...) and common_name() for messages. crypto/der is the DER reader underneath.

items.title: Random bytes: crypto/random
items.text: random.secure_bytes(n) gives n bytes from the operating system's cryptographic generator (getentropy), for keys and nonces. Under a simulation they come from its seed instead, so that a run repeats; they are then anything but secret.

items.title: Debugging
items.text:
A program kod build makes can be run under lldb, the debugger that comes with Xcode's command line tools: breakpoints on Kod lines, a backtrace with Kod functions, files and lines, and stepping a line at a time.

$ ./kod build hello.kod
$ lldb build/apps/hello/hello
(lldb) b hello.kod:12
Breakpoint 1: where = hello`greet + 20 at hello.kod:12, address = 0x...
(lldb) run
(lldb) bt
* frame #0: hello`greet at hello.kod:12
  frame #1: hello`main at hello.kod:20
(lldb) next

Functions go by their Kod names: b greet stops in greet, and a method is its type's name and its own, b Counter.bump. (b main also finds the C main that starts every program.)

items.title: What the debugger is told
items.text:
Each object the compiler writes carries DWARF, the format debuggers read:

  • a line table: for each statement, where its instructions start, and its file and line;
  • for each function, its name, file and line, and where its instructions start and end;
  • its parameters and locals, with their types, and where each is: its slot in the function's frame, or the register that holds it, and from where to where.

So b file.kod:N, bt, next, step and finish work, and frame variable shows values (below). A panic that would end the program stops it under the debugger first, after printing its message, with its stack: the first frames are the runtime's, then the Kod function that panicked and its callers, which frame select (or up) gets to. continue lets it end.

(lldb) run
panic: index 7 out of bounds for array of length 3
...
* thread #1, stop reason = EXC_BREAKPOINT
(lldb) bt
  * frame #0: ... kod_stop_for_debugger + 116
    frame #1: ... kod_panic_text + 256
    frame #2: ... kod_index_oob + 56
    frame #3: ... pick at boom.kod:5
    frame #4: ... main at boom.kod:11
(lldb) frame select 3

Stopped in a function, frame variable shows its parameters and locals:

(lldb) frame variable
(str) name = (buf = "kod", len = 3)
([int64]) xs = {
  ptr = 0x0000300000000058
  len = 4
  cap = 6
}
(Pet) pet = {
  name = 0x0000000100035780
  age = 3
  tags = 0x0000300000000018
  owner = 0x0000300000000008
  happy = true
}
(lldb) p xs.ptr[3]
(long) 42
(lldb) p *pet.owner
(Counter)  (n = 9)

An int64, bool or float64 shows as a number. A str (and bytes) shows as its buffer and length, an array as its elements' pointer, length and room, and a struct as its fields; a field or element that is one of those holds a pointer to it, which * follows. An optional shows what it holds as value (<parent is NULL> for none). An enum shows its variant by name, as tag, and in payload its fields as each variant would read them, of which the one tag names is the value's:

(Shape) t = {
  tag = Circle
  payload = {
    Circle = (radius = 7)
    Rect = {
      w = 7
      h = NULL
    }
  }
}

Other types (maps, interfaces, functions, ...) show as an address, under their Kod name.

A local the compiler keeps in a register rather than in the frame, which is most small ones, is shown while the register holds it: from where it is set to its last use. Elsewhere, before it is set or once nothing reads it any more, it is <variable not available>, as is one whose value the compiler moved on into another register; never a value that isn't its own. The locals of a function inlined into the one stopped in aren't shown. A value whose last use is past may already be released: a str, array or struct then reads as 0, or as memory lldb can't read. A line inside a function that was inlined into its caller has no instructions of its own; a breakpoint there lands on the call.

The debug information stays in the objects, under build/; the executable only records where they are, as clang's does without -g flags of its own. A program copied elsewhere is debugged with dsymutil first, which gathers it into a .dSYM bundle beside the executable:

$ dsymutil build/apps/hello/hello

The compiler itself (build/stage1/sh_kodc, the snapshot) is linked without that record, so that two builds of it can be compared byte for byte.

items.title: Developer mode
items.text: lldb needs the system's permission to control another process. On a Mac where Developer Mode is off, run stops at "Developer mode is currently disabled" until it is turned on (DevToolsSecurity -enable, as an administrator). Setting breakpoints, image lookup and the other commands that only read the program work without it.

items.title: Base64
items.text:
stdlib/encoding/base64.kod implements RFC 4648 base64, in both the standard alphabet (A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) and the URL-safe one (- _ in place of + /).

import "encoding/base64"

let text = base64.encode_str("Aladdin:open sesame")
// QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==

let raw = must base64.decode("QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==")   // bytes
let back = base64.decode_str("QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==")    // str or Error
Function Meaning encode(data: bytes, url: bool = false, pad: bool = true) -> str the base64 text of data; url: true uses the URL-safe alphabet; pad: false leaves out the trailing = encode_str(s: str, url: bool = false, pad: bool = true) -> str the same for the bytes of a str decode(text: str, url: bool = false) -> bytes or Error the bytes text stands for decode_str(text: str, url: bool = false) -> str or Error the same, as a str (the bytes are not checked to be UTF-8)

Encoding is exact for any bytes, including NUL, and takes linear time.

Decoding is strict, so that two texts never stand for the same bytes by accident and a mangled input is noticed:

  • only the chosen alphabet is accepted: + and / are errors with url: true, and - and _ are errors without it;
  • no whitespace or line breaks are skipped (this is not MIME base64);
  • padding is optional, but if it is there it must be exact: Zg== and Zg are both f, while Zg=, Zg===, Z===, =Zg= and Zg==Zg== are errors;
  • a length that leaves a single character over (Zm9vY) is an error;
  • the unused bits at the end must be zero, so Zh== (whose last character carries bits that f would not set) is an error.

Errors are IoErrors of kind InvalidInput, with op base64 decode and a detail that names the byte offset of the problem where there is one.

items.title: Compression
items.text:
stdlib/compress/deflate.kod compresses into the three formats that compress/inflate reads, written in Kod like it.

import "compress/deflate"

let packed = deflate.gzip(kod_str_to_bytes(text))
let quick = deflate.gzip(data, level: 1)
Function Meaning gzip(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a gzip file (RFC 1952) of one member, with no name and a zero time zlib(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a zlib stream (RFC 1950) raw(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a raw deflate stream (RFC 1951)

level trades speed for size as zlib's does: 0 only frames the data (stored blocks), 1 to 3 take the first good match, and 4 to 9 look further back and put off a match when the next byte starts a longer one; 9 is the smallest and slowest. A level outside 0..9 is taken as the nearest one. Each block is written whichever way is smallest: stored, with the standard codes, or with Huffman codes made for its own data, so data that doesn't compress grows by only about 5 bytes every 16 KB.

items.title: Compressing piece by piece
items.text:
Data that is made a piece at a time, or is too long to hold, is compressed into a Writer as it is written:

let out = try posix.create("rows.gz")
let packed = deflate.gzip_writer(out)
for row in rows() {
    try packed.write_str(row)
}
try packed.finish()
try out.close()

gzip_writer(to: Writer, level: int64 = 6), zlib_writer and raw_writer give a DeflateWriter, itself a Writer. What is written goes to to as it is compressed, 64 KB at a time, and takes a megabyte of memory or less however long it is.

Method Meaning flush() -> none or Error sends all that has been written, so that it can be decompressed, though the stream goes on; each costs a few bytes and some of the compression finish() -> none or Error ends the stream, with its checksum; to isn't closed. Without it the data isn't whole. After it, writing is an InvalidInput error, and another does nothing

items.title: Decompression
items.text:
stdlib/compress/inflate.kod decompresses gzip, zlib and raw deflate data. It is written in Kod, like compressing, so it links no C library.

import "compress/inflate"

let text = kod_bytes_to_str(must inflate.gunzip(data))
Function Meaning gunzip(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a gzip file (RFC 1952); several members one after the other give their output joined, like gunzip does inflate_zlib(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a zlib stream (RFC 1950) inflate_raw(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a raw deflate stream (RFC 1951)

max_output is the most bytes the result may have. Decompression stops as soon as it would be exceeded, so a few kilobytes of input cannot make the program allocate gigabytes; the buffer grows only as output is produced. Errors are IoErrors of kind InvalidInput, with op the function's name and a detail that says what was wrong: output too large, truncated, or the wording zlib uses for corrupt data (incorrect header check, invalid block type, incorrect data check for a checksum that does not match, incorrect length check, invalid distance too far back). Bytes after the last gzip member are an error, and so is a stream that ends before its final block.

items.title: Piece by piece
items.text:
Data that comes from a Reader, or is too long to hold, is decompressed as it is read:

let plain = inflate.gunzip_reader(from)
for true {
    let piece = try plain.read(65536)
    if len(piece) == 0 {
        break
    }
    print(len(piece))
}
Function Meaning gunzip_reader(from: Reader) -> InflateReader a gzip file, as gunzip zlib_reader(from: Reader) -> InflateReader a zlib stream raw_reader(from: Reader) -> InflateReader a raw deflate stream deflate_reader(from: Reader) -> InflateReader a zlib stream, or a raw one when it doesn't begin as a zlib stream does (as HTTP's deflate may be)

An InflateReader is a Reader of the decompressed data, which takes a few hundred KB of memory however long that is. It gives what it has before it waits for more compressed data, so what a sender has flushed isn't held up. There is no max_output: stop reading when there is too much.

A read fails as the functions above do, with the same details and op inflate, once what was good before it has been read, and goes on failing. The checksum comes last, so the data isn't known to be whole until the end has been read. An error of from is given as it is. A gzip file is read to the end of from; after the others, from may have been read past their end, by as much as it gave.

items.title: Hex
items.text:
stdlib/encoding/hex.kod writes bytes as two hex digits each and reads them back.

Function Meaning encode(data: bytes) -> str the lowercase hex text of data: hex.encode(b"\x01\xab") is "01ab" decode(text: str) -> bytes or Error the bytes text stands for; upper and lower case digits are both read, and an odd length or another character is an error

items.title: Percent-encoding
items.text: For URLs and query strings, see HTTP client.

items.title: Enums
items.text: Enums in Kod are tagged unions — each value carries a discriminant identifying which variant it is, plus an optional payload with named fields.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
type Direction = enum {
    North
    South
    East
    West
}

type Message = enum {
    // unit variant (no payload)
    Quit
    // payload variants
    Text(content: str)
    Move(x: int64, y: int64)
}

Comments are allowed inside the body. Variants without parentheses are unit variants; variants with parentheses carry named fields.

A payload field can name the enum itself, e.g. Branch(kids: [Tree]) inside type Tree = enum { ... }.

items.title: Construction
items.text:
let d: Direction = Direction.North
let m: Message = Message.Text(content: "hello")
let q: Message = Message.Quit

The annotation is optional: a constructor has the enum's type, so let m = Message.Text(content: "hello") (or mod.Enum.Variant(...) for an imported enum) can be matched without an else arm.

Payload values go in declaration order, labelled or not: Message.Move(x: 1, y: 2) and Message.Move(1, 2) are the same value. A missing or extra payload value, a label that isn't the field in that position, and a variant the enum doesn't declare (Message.Txt) are errors. Each payload value must have its field's type, with the same implicit conversions as a function argument: Message.Text(content: 5) is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`).

items.title: Implicit variant syntax
items.text:
Inside a match arm, the enum name can be omitted when the type is unambiguous:

match d {
    .North -> print("north")
    .South -> print("south")
    else -> {}
}

The variant must belong to the subject's enum: .Up in a match on a Direction that has no Up is an error, even when another enum declares Up, and so is naming that other enum, Arrow.Up. The same goes for an if d is ... pattern.

Unit variants can also use the implicit .Variant form in expressions:

let d: Direction = .North

A payload variant can use it too. Wherever the enum type is known, the variant belongs to that enum: an annotated let (let m: Message = .Text(content: "hi")), an assignment to a variable, field, element or key, an argument, a struct field, an array element, an array literal in a + chain with an array of the enum (ms += [.Quit], [.Quit] + ms or [.Quit] + [.Text(content: "a")] + load()), a return value (the T of a T or Error function too), the other side of == or != (m == .Quit), in a comparison chain too (.Quit == m == n), or an arm of a match whose value goes to one of these (d == match n { 0 -> .North else .South }). Elsewhere, as in an unannotated let, a match subject, an unannotated array literal or a method call on the variant, it belongs to the one enum that declares a variant of that name among those the module sees: its own, those of the modules it imports and the builtin ones. When several of them declare it, that is an error:

type Figure = enum {
    Square(side: int64)
    Circle(r: int64)
}

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(r: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

let s = .Circle(r: 2)    // error: `.Circle` is ambiguous: `Figure` and `Shape`
                         // both declare it; write `Shape.Circle` or give the value a type

let s: Shape = .Circle(r: 2) and Shape.Circle(r: 2) both work. The error writes an imported enum through its import alias, as in geo.Shape, so when the module's own Shape and an imported geo.Shape both declare Circle, the error names Shape and geo.Shape. It suggests an enum whose variant takes the payload written (a unit variant for a bare .Circle), preferring the module's own enum when several do. Enums of modules a module doesn't import don't count, so a generic method or a default written in an imported module means the same variant whichever program uses it. Only when none of the enums the module sees declares the variant does an enum of another loaded module count. When several of those do, the module can't write any of them, so the error only suggests giving the value a type, as by passing it straight to a parameter of its enum.

In a T or Error function, a returned .Ok(...) or .Err(...) is the result's own variant, unless T declares a variant of that name whose payload fits what is written and the result's doesn't. With type Status = enum { Ok Failed(code: int64) }, return .Ok in a -> Status or Error function returns Status.Ok, while return .Ok(.Failed(code: 1)) returns the result's Ok. When both variants take the one argument written, its type decides: with Ok(n: int64) in Status, return .Ok(5) returns Status.Ok(n: 5), as 5 can't be a Status. An arm of a returned match works the same way, and so does a return type that names the T or Error through an alias.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Declare methods inside the enum body, after the variants. The first parameter is self, the enum value:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(r: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)

    func area(self) -> int64 {
        return match self {
            .Circle(r) -> 3 * r * r
            .Rect(w, h) -> w * h
        }
    }

    func scaled(self, by: int64) -> Shape {
        return match self {
            .Circle(r) -> .Circle(r: r * by)
            .Rect(w, h) -> .Rect(w: w * by, h: h * by)
        }
    }
}

let s: Shape = .Rect(w: 2, h: 3)
print(s.scaled(by: 2).area())    // 24

They take arguments, labels and defaults like struct methods, work through s?.area() on a Shape?, and can be called on any Shape value, including one that came from a function in another module without your module importing the one that declares Shape. A method whose name starts with _ is private to the enum's own methods, as on a struct.

An enum that declares func to_str(self) -> str is printed by it in f-strings and print, instead of by its variant's name.

A generic enum declares methods the same way, and they use its type parameters:

type Either[L, R] = enum {
    Left(value: L)
    Right(value: R)

    func swapped(self) -> Either[R, L] {
        return match self {
            .Left(value) -> .Right(:value)
            .Right(value) -> .Left(:value)
        }
    }
}

As with a generic struct, a method is compiled for an instance when something calls it, only its signature is checked otherwise, and an error in its body names the instance, as in (in `Either[int64, str]`).

An enum gives operators a meaning with the same operator methods as a struct: op_add, op_sub, op_mul, op_div, op_mod, op_eq, op_lt and the reflected op_radd and the rest. An enum that declares op_eq is compared by it, payloads and all, so == and != work on any two of its values, including a .Variant on the right:

type Amount = enum {
    Cents(n: int64)
    Free

    func op_eq(self, other: Amount) -> bool {
        return self.cents() == other.cents()
    }

    func op_lt(self, other: Amount) -> bool {
        return self.cents() < other.cents()
    }

    func cents(self) -> int64 {
        return match self {
            .Cents(n) -> n
            .Free -> 0
        }
    }
}

let a: Amount = .Cents(n: 0)
print(a == .Free)                // true
print(a < .Cents(n: 5))          // true

An enum without op_eq keeps comparing variants, as described under Equality.

An enum that declares an interface's methods is a value of that interface, as a struct is (see Interfaces), and an interface value holding one downcasts to it with if v is Dir(d) or a Dir(d) arm:

interface Named {
    func name(self) -> str
}

type Dir = enum {
    Up
    Down

    func name(self) -> str {
        return match self {
            .Up -> "up"
            .Down -> "down"
        }
    }
}

let n: Named = Dir.Down
print(n.name())                  // down

A generic enum's instance is one too, and downcasts through a type alias such as type IntPick = Pick[int64], as a generic struct's does.

items.title: Generic enums
items.text:
Type parameters go in square brackets after the name, as for structs, and each instantiation is monomorphised:

type Either[L, R] = enum {
    Left(value: L)
    Right(value: R)
}

let e: Either[int64, str] = .Left(value: 1)

A variant of a generic enum needs its type arguments from where it goes: an annotated let, as above, or any other place listed above where the enum type is known, such as an argument, an array element or the other side of ==. Without one, let e = Either.Left(value: 1) (or .Left(value: 1), Result.Ok(5)) is an error, cannot infer the type of `e`; add a type annotation. Type arguments on the enum name, Either[int64, str].Left(value: 1), are an error, since type arguments must be followed by (. A pattern names the enum without them, and its bindings take the matched value's payload types: on an Either[int64, str], Either.Left(n) binds an int64.

items.title: Pattern matching
items.text:
match m {
    Message.Quit -> print("quit")
    Message.Text(content) -> print(content)
    Message.Move(x, y) -> {
        print_int(x)
        print_int(y)
    }
    else -> {}
}
  • Bindings in payload patterns (content, x, y) capture the field values
  • else is the catch-all arm; matches whatever the other arms didn't
  • Arm bodies can be a single expression (after ->) or a block ({ ... })

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
[ offset 0  ] discriminant : int64  (8 bytes)
[ offset 8  ] payload      : max(variant payload sizes) bytes

Variants are assigned discriminants in declaration order starting from 1. Discriminant 0 is reserved as the none sentinel.

items.title: Example: Message
items.text:
Message.Quit  → discriminant 1, no payload
Message.Text  → discriminant 2, content at payload offset 0  (8 bytes)
Message.Move  → discriminant 3, x at offset 0, y at offset 8 (16 bytes)

Total size: 8 (discriminant) + 16 (max payload) = 24 bytes.

items.title: Equality
items.text:
Two enum values are equal if and only if they are the same variant and their payloads' fields are ==, in order, as a struct's fields are. An enum that declares op_eq is compared by that method instead (see Methods).

Direction.North == Direction.North  // true
Direction.North == Direction.South  // false

For an enum without payloads, or against a variant without one, as in m == .Quit, this is a single integer comparison on the discriminant. Otherwise m == .Text(content: "hi") and a == b compare the variant, then each field. A field with no ==, such as a shared struct, makes that an error that names it (cannot compare two `Box` values: `.Of`'s `p`, a `Pt`, has no `==`); test those with is or match. Comparing values of two different enums is an error, and so is a .Variant that the other side's enum doesn't declare.

items.title: match as an expression
items.text:
A match can produce a value when every arm has a value: an expression, or a block ending in one:

let label: str = match d {
    .North -> "north"
    .South -> "south"
    .East  -> "east"
    .West  -> "west"
}

Payload bindings are in scope in the arm's expression:

let dist: int64 = match m {
    .Move(x, y) -> x + y
    else 0
}

items.title: Floating point
items.text:
float64 is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating-point number, the type of every JSON number that is not a whole number.

let price: float64 = 19.99
let total = price * 3.0 + 0.5
print(total.to_str())            // 60.47

items.title: Literals
items.text:
A float literal has digits on both sides of a point, an exponent, or both:

1.5
0.25
2e9
6.02e23
1.5e-3
1 000 000.5          // grouped like an integer

1. and .5 are not literals: a point needs a digit after it, so that 1.to_str() still calls a method on the integer 1. Nothing else turns an integer into a float; 2 is an int64 and 2.0 is a float64.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
Operator Operands Result + - * / two float64 float64 -x a float64 float64 < <= > >= == != two float64 bool

Nothing converts implicitly: 1.5 + 1 and n * 0.5 with n: int64 are errors, and so is % on a float. Arithmetic follows IEEE 754 exactly, so 1.0 / 0.0 is infinity, 0.0 / 0.0 is not a number, and a not-a-number value is unequal to everything, itself included (x != x is how to test for one, or x.is_nan()). There is no trap on overflow or division by zero.

A float64 is an ordinary value: it can be a variable, parameter, field, array element ([float64]), optional (float64?) or a type argument (Box[float64]). It cannot be a Map key or a Set member, because its == is not an equivalence, and it has no literal pattern in a match.

items.title: Conversions and methods
items.text:
Method Result n.to_float64() on an int64 the nearest float64 x.to_int64() x truncated toward zero; a not-a-number is 0 and an out-of-range value saturates to the int64 limits x.to_str() the shortest text that reads back as x (below) s.parse_float() on a str a float64?: none unless all of s is a decimal number, with an optional sign, a point and an exponent; inf, nan and hex are not accepted x.abs() x.floor() x.ceil() x.round() x.sqrt() the float64 they name; round rounds halves away from zero x.is_nan() x.is_inf() bool

to_str gives the fewest digits that parse back to exactly x (rounded half to even from its exact value, when more than one such text has that many digits), and always shows it is a float: 2.0, not 2. Magnitudes from 1e-6 up to 1e21 are written without an exponent (0.000001, 123456789.5); outside that range as 1e+21 and 1.5e-7. The special values are inf, -inf and nan. An f-string uses to_str; print takes a str, so write print(x.to_str()).

parse_float gives the float64 nearest the decimal value, however many digits it has; a value exactly halfway between two floats goes to the one whose last bit is 0. A value beyond the largest float is infinity, and one below half the smallest is zero, with the sign kept. Both directions are Kod, in stdlib/primitives/float_text.kod, with exact arithmetic on integers wider than 64 bits where a float can't be trusted.

print((0.1 + 0.2).to_str())     // 0.30000000000000004
print((1.0).to_str())           // 1.0
print((must "2.5e3".parse_float()).to_str())   // 2500.0

items.title: JSON
items.text:
A JSON number that is not a whole int64 keeps its text in a Decimal, so reading one as a float is parse_float on that text, and writing one is to_str:

let text = must item.get("price").as_number_text()
let price = must text.parse_float()
let out = json.Value.Decimal(text: (price * 1.2).to_str())

to_str gives text that is a valid JSON number for every finite value. Infinity and not-a-number have no JSON form: emit writes a Decimal whose text is not a number as null, so inf and nan come out as null.

items.title: Representation
items.text: A float64 is the 8 bytes of its bit pattern, held in an ordinary register or slot; the compiler moves it to a floating-point register only for the operation. That is why it needs no new calling convention and an array of them is an array of 8-byte words.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
func add(a: int64, b: int64) -> int64 {
    return a + b
}

Parameters are name: Type. The return type follows ->. Functions that return nothing use -> none.

Every argument is passed in a register, so a function can take at most 8 parameters. self takes one of them, so a method or interface method can take at most 7 besides self. The same limit holds for externs, function literals and function types such as func(int64) -> int64, in a type alias too; going past it is an error where the function, literal or type is written (`f` takes 9 parameters, but a function can take at most 8), not again at each call through it. When that is in another module, the error is reported at each call through it instead. To pass more, group them in a struct.

items.title: Calling
items.text:
let result: int64 = add(a: 1, b: 2)

The arguments are worked out left to right, each once, before the body runs. Each is the value it was then, whatever working out a later one changes: in f(xs, add(mut xs)), f's first argument is xs as it was before add.

A small function or method whose whole body is return of an expression made of its parameters, literals, operators and field reads, with int64, bool or float64 parameters (a method's self may be a struct) and result, like add above or a method func area(self) -> int64 { return self.w * self.h }, is compiled in place at each call instead of being called. So is a short body of statements (let of a number or bool, assignments, if, for with a condition, break, continue, return and calls, but no match, for x in, try, is or function literal) whose parameters, none of them mut, are numbers, bools or structs, and whose result is a number, a bool or nothing; a struct argument must then be a local name, as self must. It behaves the same, except that a backtrace from inside it, such as a division by zero, names the caller.

items.title: Call labels
items.text:
Calls use labeled arguments by default; the parameter name is the label:

func greet(name: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
}

greet(name: "Alice")

Labeled arguments go in parameter order: with func move(x: int64, y: int64), move(y: 2, x: 1) is an error (parameter 0 of `move` expected label `x`, got `y`). A label may jump over parameters that have defaults, which are then left out of the call.

anon removes the label requirement for that parameter:

func double(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    return n * 2
}

double(5)

Convention: when calling, label every parameter except 1–2 of a single shared type (e.g. slice(arr, from: 0, to: 3) is fine; passing a label for arr is just noise).

If a passed argument is a bare identifier with the same name as the parameter, the label can be shortened to a leading ::

let name: str = "Alice"
greet(:name)          // shorthand for greet(name: name)

items.title: Long calls and parameter lists
items.text:
A call may be split across lines wherever the arguments are separated, and so may a parameter list. Put each argument on its own line, with or without a trailing comma, and comments between them:

let conn = connect(
    "example.com",
    port: 8443,        // not the default
    timeout_ms: 200,
    tls: true,
)

func request(
    anon method: str,
    anon url: str,
    timeout_ms: int64 = 5000,
) -> none { ... }

This holds for every call: functions, methods, x?.method(...), struct and enum constructors (Point(x: 1, y: 2)), and the argument lists of enum variants in a type declaration. A line break after the callee and before the ( still ends the statement, so f and (1) on two lines are two expressions, not a call. A call that never closes is reported at the first token that cannot continue it, for instance expected `)`, got `let` on the line of the next statement.

items.title: Label / binding split
items.text:
A parameter can have two names — an external label used at call sites and an internal binding used inside the function body:

func greet(who person: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {person}!")
}

greet(who: "Alice")

Useful for prepositions that make call sites read naturally without forcing short variable names inside the function.

Each parameter binds a name of its own, self included, so two parameters can't share one: func f(anon a: int64, b a: str) is an error (parameter `a` is declared twice; give one of them another name). The same holds for methods, interface methods, externs and function literals.

items.title: Default values
items.text:
Trailing parameters may declare a default with = expr, and a call can leave them out:

func retry(anon n: int64, delay_ms: int64 = 100) -> int64 {
    return n * delay_ms
}

retry(3)                  // 300
retry(3, delay_ms: 500)   // 1500

The default is evaluated fresh at each call that omits it. It is evaluated in the module that declares the function and can't see the caller's local variables, so a name in it means the same thing at every call site. Methods and interface methods take defaults the same way. A default must have its parameter's type, like an argument. A function's or method's default has its type checked where it is declared, so func f(x: int64 = "a") is an error even if no call leaves x out. Anything else wrong in it, such as an unknown name or variant, or a wrong field in a constructor, is reported where a call leaves it out, and an interface method's default is checked only at each call that leaves it out.

A label can jump over parameters that have defaults, so that a later one can be set without writing out the ones in between:

func connect(anon host: str, port: int64 = 80, timeout_ms: int64 = 5000, tls: bool = false) -> none { ... }

connect("example.com")                          // all defaults
connect("example.com", timeout_ms: 200)         // port and tls by default
connect("example.com", port: 8443, tls: true)   // timeout_ms by default

The labels still go in parameter order, and a parameter that is jumped over must have a default; connect(port: 1) is an error because host has none (parameter 0 of `connect` is anon; remove label `port`). An anon parameter with a default can be jumped over the same way, by labeling a later argument. Unlabeled arguments fill the parameters strictly in order, so only a label can skip.

Each default is evaluated afresh at the call, in the order of the parameters, along with the arguments you did give: in f(a: x(), c: z()) for func f(a: int64, b: int64 = y(), c: int64 = 0), the calls run x, then the default y, then z. It works the same for methods, interface methods and functions of other modules.

items.title: Argument types
items.text:
Each argument must have its parameter's type: print(5) is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`), and so is passing a Gen[int64] where a Gen[str] is declared, or an int64? where an int64 is. The only implicit conversions are the ones an annotated let makes (see Bindings and mutability):

  • a T becomes a T?;
  • a struct, int64, str or bool becomes an interface value;
  • .Variant and Enum.Variant(...) are built for the parameter's enum;
  • an array literal or + chain is built for an array of enums, interfaces, optionals or arrays.

An array value is never converted element by element. With func take(anon xs: [Shape]), take([Sq(s: 1)]) is fine, but passing a [Sq] variable is an error. The same rules apply to extern functions, to calls through a function value, and to the arguments of a method, an interface method and x?.method(...).

items.title: mut parameters
items.text:
A parameter declared mut is the caller's variable: the function can assign it, change its elements or append to it, and the caller's variable has the new value when the call returns. The argument says so with mut, which takes a mut local or another mut parameter of the calling function:

func count(anon s: str, mut seen: [str]) -> int64 {
    seen += [s]
    return len(seen)
}

mut names: [str] = []
count("a", seen: mut names)     // names is ["a"]

Writing the mut at the call site is required, and only there: passing names without it to a mut parameter is an error (`seen` is a `mut` parameter of `count`: pass `mut names`), and so is mut before an argument whose parameter isn't mut. The argument must be a name the caller could assign, a mut local or a mut parameter, and one name can't go to two mut parameters of one call. A field, an element, a let, or a mut a function literal captures is an error; copy it into a mut local and assign it back after the call.

Inside the function, a mut parameter is used like a local. The caller's variable gets the parameter's value when the function returns, however it returns, including through try. A function with a mut parameter is called by name: it can't be used as a function value, and an interface method can't have one. A method that changes its struct declares mut self (see Methods).

items.title: Return values
items.text:
A returned value must have the function's return type, with the same conversions as an argument: func f() -> str { return 5 } is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`), and so is returning a [Sq] variable from a -> [Shape] function. A -> none function returns no value; it can end with a bare return, return none, or return of a call that itself returns none. Any function can return a call that never returns (see below), such as return self.fail("bad") or return log.die("bad").

In a -> T or Error function, a returned T becomes a successful result. A returned T or Error value must have the same T, so returning an int64 or Error from a -> str or Error function is an error.

A function with a return type other than none must end every path with a return, a throw, or a call that doesn't return, like panic(...). One that can reach the end of its body is an error at its name, or at the func of a function literal (`pick` can reach its end without returning a value), and that includes a -> T? function: write return none at the end. Only a -> none or Error function may run off its end, which returns Ok(none). The error isn't reported for a body that already has other errors, or in a file that doesn't parse, since those may hide the missing return. Whether a path can reach the end is decided from the statements alone:

  • return, throw, break and continue end a path, and so does a call of a function or method that never returns;
  • an if ends every path only if it has an else and both branches do;
  • a match does if each of its arms does;
  • a for true loop does unless it can break out of itself; any other for loop, including for … in, may finish.

Code after a statement that ends every path is never run and isn't considered, so a break placed after a return or panic(...) doesn't let a for true loop finish.

The builtin panic(...) never returns, and neither does a function or method that returns none, has no return, and can't reach the end of its body by these rules. A function of the module or one it imports named panic, or a local function value of that name in force at the call, hides the builtin (see Built-ins). A local named panic that holds anything else doesn't, so panic(msg) after let panic = 5 never returns. So a helper that ends in panic(...) never returns, and nor does one that ends in a call of another such helper (self.fail(msg), log.die(msg), or a function declared further down), or in a for true loop it can't break out of. A call that leads back to the function itself doesn't count: func spin() -> none { spin() } is taken to return.

This holds for a call of:

  • a function of the module or one it imports (die(msg)), or a function of an imported module (log.die(msg));
  • a method of a struct, whatever it's called on: self, a parameter, any local, a field or a call's result (self.fail(msg), self.log.fail(msg), r.fail(msg), self.reps[i].fail(msg), reporter().fail(msg)), as long as that expression's type is known at the call. A local has the type of its binding in force there, whether a let, let-else, match arm, if … is or for binds it, so r.fail(msg) never returns after let r = Reporter(), even where r is also a parameter of another type.

Two kinds of call are always taken to return, because what they call is chosen at run time:

  • a call through a function value (a local, parameter or field of a function type);
  • a method called through an interface value.

End such a path with a panic(...) or a return after the call.

A call in a value's place, as a returned value, a match arm's value or an x? or ... default, is decided where it is written by the same rules, so return r.fail(msg) never returns after let r = Reporter(), and nor does return die(msg) when die ends in that call. When what it calls ends in a call taken to return, the error names that call and its line: return die(msg) is an error when die ends in r.fail(msg) after let r: Failer = Reporter(), for an interface Failer (as `die` ends in `r.fail(msg)` (line 19), or (line 19 of lib/log.kod) when the call is in another module), and it says to put a panic(...) after it. The can reach its end error names that call too when the body ends in a call of such a function, and says so when the body itself ends in a call through a function value or a method called through an interface value. Such a call is taken to return wherever it is written: call it as a statement and end the path with panic(...).

items.title: main
items.text:
Every executable must define main. It can take no arguments or receive the command-line argument list:

// no args
func main() -> int64 {
    return 0
}

// with argv
func main(argv: [str]) -> int64 {
    print_int(len(argv))
    return 0
}

main can also return int64 or Error, directly or through an alias. A returned value is the exit status, and an error that reaches the end of main prints panic: <message> and exits with status 1.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Functions inside a struct type declaration are methods. The first parameter must be self:

type Counter = struct {
    value: int64

    func increment(mut self) -> none {
        self.value = self.value + 1
    }

    func get(self) -> int64 {
        return self.value
    }
}

Call with dot notation:

mut c: Counter = Counter(value: 0)
c.increment()
print_int(c.get())

items.title: Function values
items.text:
Functions are values. Use func(T1, T2) -> R as a type to store, pass, or return them. A function value is an 8-byte reference, not a C function pointer (see Function values).

func double(x: int64) -> int64 { return x * 2 }
func triple(x: int64) -> int64 { return x * 3 }

func apply(anon f: func(int64) -> int64, anon x: int64) -> int64 {
    return f(x)
}

let g: func(int64) -> int64 = double
print_int(g(21))             // 42 — indirect call through g
print_int(apply(triple, 14)) // 42 — function passed as callback

A function literal, func(anon n: int64) -> int64 { return n + 1 }, is a value of its function type too.

A bare identifier in value position resolves to the function's address when no local of that name is in force there. A call f(args) goes to a struct named f first, so Pt(x: 1) constructs. Otherwise it does an indirect blr when the innermost binding of f in force holds a function value, and a direct bl of the module's, an imported or the builtin function named f when no binding of f is in force or it holds anything else. A function value declared in a block, such as an if or loop body, is called that way only from its let to the end of the block, and after the block f(args) calls an outer function value of that name again. Elsewhere f(args) calls the module's or an imported function, or the builtin, named f, and f as a value is that function; with none of those it is an error: `f` is declared in a block that has ended after the block, and `f` is called before its `let` (or read) before the declaration (see Blocks and bindings and Built-ins).

A function of an imported module is a value written through its module, let f = vec.dot. A name the module doesn't declare is an error with a did-you-mean hint (module `vec` has no function or constant `dott`).

An indirect call has the function type's return type wherever the function value comes from: a local, an array element (fs[i](x)), a struct field (h.fn(x)) or another call (get_fn()(x)). It must pass exactly as many arguments as the function type has parameters, since a function type carries no defaults.

items.title: Closures
items.text:
A function literal can read the locals and parameters in force where it's written, including self. It keeps their values, so it can outlive the function that made it:

func adder(anon n: int64) -> func(int64) -> int64 {
    return func(anon x: int64) -> int64 {
        return x + n
    }
}

let add5 = adder(5)
print_int(add5(1))           // 6

A literal captures the value a name has when the literal is evaluated. Each pass of a loop makes its own closure, with that pass's for variable and pattern bindings. Literals nest, and an inner one can capture what the outer one can see.

A variable declared mut is shared instead: the literal and the function it's in use the same variable, so what one assigns the other sees, even after the function has returned:

func make_counter() -> func() -> int64 {
    mut n = 0
    return func() -> int64 {
        n += 1
        return n
    }
}

let next = make_counter()
next()
print_int(next())            // 2

A mut declared in a loop's body is a new variable on each pass, so each pass's closure has one of its own. Any other name the literal captures keeps the value it had when the literal was evaluated, and can't be assigned in it: a function literal can't assign to `x`, which it captures. That holds for a let, a parameter, a for variable and a pattern binding. A mut parameter can't be captured: a function literal can't capture `p`, a `mut` parameter; copy it into a `mut` local to share it.

A captured mut lives in a counted cell from its declaration on, and each read and assignment of it goes through the cell, in the function too; a mut that no literal captures stays in the frame.

Other limits:

  • A literal can't see its own let, so it can't call itself through it. Declare a local function to recurse: unknown function `fact`; a function literal can't see its own `let`, so declare it `func fact(...)` to recurse.
  • A default value sees no locals, so a literal used as one captures nothing.
  • A closure kept in a struct that it captures is a cycle, and a cycle is never freed (see Reclaiming memory).

items.title: Local functions
items.text:
A function declared in a function's body is a local function. It can call itself, and it reads the locals around it the way a closure does:

func count_ways(coins: [int64], total: int64) -> int64 {
    func ways(anon left: int64, from: int64) -> int64 {
        if left == 0 {
            return 1
        }
        mut n = 0
        for i in from..len(coins) {
            if coins[i] <= left {
                n += ways(left - coins[i], from: i)
            }
        }
        return n
    }
    return ways(total, from: 0)
}

print_int(count_ways(coins: [1, 2, 5], total: 5))   // 4

func ways(...) -> T { ... } is let ways = func(...) -> T { ... } whose body can also see ways. It is a function value like any other: it can be passed and returned, and it's called only from its declaration to the end of its block. A local function sees the ones declared before it, not those after, so two can't call each other. It can't take type parameters.

Inside its body, ways is the function value the call came through, so calling itself makes no new closure and keeps no extra reference. A call to itself makes a call even as the last thing it does; only a module's own functions jump back to their start (see Recursion).

items.title: Generic functions
items.text:
Type parameters in brackets after the name make a function generic. They can be used in its parameters, its return type and its body:

func first[T](anon xs: [T]) -> T? {
    if len(xs) == 0 {
        return none
    }
    return xs[0]
}

func map_all[T, U](anon xs: [T], f: func(T) -> U) -> [U] {
    mut out: [U] = []
    for x in xs {
        out += [f(x)]
    }
    return out
}

let a = first([1, 2])                                      // a: int64?
let b = map_all([1, 2], f: func(anon n: int64) -> str {    // b: [str]
    return f"#{n}"
})

Like a generic struct, a generic function is monomorphised: it's compiled once for each list of type arguments a module calls it with.

items.title: Inference
items.text:
A call usually leaves the type arguments out, and the compiler works them out from the arguments:

  • Arguments are read in parameter order. Each one is matched against its parameter's declared type: T takes the argument's whole type, [T] an array's element type, Box[T] an instance's type argument, and func(T) -> U a function's parameter and return types. T? takes the inner type of an optional or else the argument's own type, so int64? and int64 both make T an int64.
  • The first argument to settle a type parameter decides it. Later arguments are then converted to the parameter's type as in any call, and one that can't be is an error at that argument. With func pick[T](a: T, b: T), pick(a: 1, b: "x") reports expected `int64`, got `str`, and arguments of two structs that share an interface need the type written out, as in pick[Shape](a: sq, b: circle).
  • An argument with no type of its own (none, [], .Red) settles nothing, but takes its type from the parameter once the others have settled it: with func add[T](xs: [T], x: T), add(xs: [], x: 1) makes T an int64.
  • A parameter left to its default settles nothing either.
  • Only arguments count. Neither the return type nor where the result goes matters, so a type parameter that no argument settles is an error, even in let xs: [int64] = empty(): cannot infer `T` in the call to `empty`; write the type arguments: `empty[T](...)`.

items.title: Explicit type arguments
items.text:
Type arguments can be written after the function's name, all of them or none:

let xs = empty[int64]()
let c = util.first[str](names)

They are spelled as for a generic struct's constructor (str, [str], int64?, Box[int64]). The wrong number is an error, and so is giving them to a function that isn't generic.

items.title: Checking
items.text:
There are no bounds on a type parameter: the body may do anything the type arguments allow, and is compiled for each instance. A signature is always checked. A body is checked only for the instances that are called, so the body of a generic function nothing calls isn't checked. An error in a body is reported once, for the first instance that hits it, and names that instance:

func largest[T](a: T, b: T) -> T {
    if a < b {               // with Color: `<` doesn't take `Color` operands; … (in `largest[Color]`)
        return b
    }
    return a
}

A generic function may call itself and other generic functions. The chain of instances has to end: one that keeps making a bigger type, like f[[T]] inside f[T], is an error once it is 64 instances deep, also when the chain runs through a generic struct's methods. A chain that branches into new types is stopped earlier, when a module passes 4096 instances.

Parameter defaults and the body resolve names in the module that wrote them, as for a generic struct's methods, and T means the instance's type in both.

A function literal in a generic body, or in a method of a generic type, is compiled for each instance too: it can name T and capture, as anywhere else.

func repeater[T](anon x: T) -> func(int64) -> [T] {
    return func(anon n: int64) -> [T] {
        return [x] * n
    }
}

print(repeater("ab")(3))     // ["ab", "ab", "ab"]

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A generic function is a value once it has its type arguments, as in let f = first[int64] or sorted_by(xs, less: before[T]). Without them, let f = first is an error, and they aren't inferred from where the value goes. A value's type arguments must fit on one: pair[A, B] is only read as a call, so wrap a call of it in a function literal.
  • Only top-level functions can be generic. A method can use its struct's type parameters but can't declare its own, and neither can an interface method, a function literal, an extern or main. A module-level constant can't either.
  • A type parameter's name can't repeat in one list, and hides a type of the same name for the length of the function.

items.title: Extern functions
items.text:
Declare external C functions with extern:

extern func labs(anon n: int64) -> int64     // compiled programs only
extern func putchar(anon c: int64) -> int64

A C function that takes a variable number of arguments, such as fcntl, open or printf, ends its parameters with ...:

extern func fcntl(anon fd: int64, anon cmd: int64, ...) -> int64
extern func snprintf(anon buf: int64, anon size: int64, anon format: int64, ...) -> int64

fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK)
  • Only an extern can take ..., and it comes last.
  • The parameters before it must be int64 or bool; pass a pointer as an int64 from unsafe.
  • A call gives at least those, then any number more. Each extra argument is an int64 or a bool, without a label. On arm64 macOS each goes in an 8-byte slot on the stack, where C's va_arg looks for it.
  • A float can't be an extra argument, and neither can a str; pass unsafe.c_str(s) for C's %s.

A C global variable of 8 bytes, such as a pointer or a long, is an extern let:

extern let __stdoutp: int64     // C's `stdout`, a FILE *

fflush(__stdoutp)

Each read loads the variable's value as it is then; Kod can't assign it. The type must be int64. A name that starts with _, as most of libc's globals do, is private to the module that declares it.

An extern func is a C symbol, resolved at link time against the C runtime and whatever the modules of the program declare (see Link inputs): labs is in libc, and a module can name a C file of its own or a library to link. A str argument reaches C as a KodStr *, not as a char *; to call a libc function that takes a C string, a buffer or a pointer to write to, pass addresses from unsafe as int64.

items.title: Recursion
items.text:
Mutual recursion between functions is supported as long as all functions are declared in the same module.

func fib(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n <= 1 {
        return n
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
}

A function that calls itself as the last thing it does, in a return f(...) or, for a function that returns nothing, as its last statement, jumps back to its start instead of making a call, so that recursion takes no stack however deep it goes:

func gcd(a: int64, b: int64) -> int64 {
    if b == 0 {
        return a
    }
    return gcd(a: b, b: a % b)
}

The arguments are all worked out before any parameter changes, as for a call. Some calls stay ordinary calls, each with a frame of its own:

  • a call to another function, or one whose result the function still uses (fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2), 1 + f(n - 1));
  • a call from inside a loop, or from a function with mut parameters, captures or more than eight parameters;
  • a function returning a T?, a T or Error, an interface or a union;
  • a call that passes a newly made string, array, map or struct (walk(xs[1..])), since the function's own values are let go of before the jump. Passing one of its parameters on as it is (count(xs, i: i + 1)) is fine, and numbers and bools can be anything.

items.title: HTTP
items.text:
stdlib/net/http.kod makes HTTP/1.1 requests over TCP or TLS (see TCP and TLS), and answers them. Its parts that don't touch the network, URLs, headers, writing a request to a Writer and reading a response from a BufReader, work on their own too.

import "net/http" { get }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let r = try get("https://example.com/")
    print(f"{r.status} {r.reason}")
    print(r.text())
    return 0
}

get, post and fetch open a connection for each request and close it afterwards (Connection: close). To make several requests over the same connection, use a Client. There is no pipelining, no cookies and no proxy support.

items.title: Requests
items.text:
A Client carries the settings that describe the service you talk to (its headers, its certificate roots, its deadline) and makes the requests:

import "net/http" { Client }
import "time" { Duration }

let client = Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15))
client.headers.add("Accept", "application/json")
client.headers.add("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)

let user = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
let made = try client.post("https://api.example.com/users", payload, content_type: "application/json")
Method of Client Meaning get(url, options = Options()), delete(url, options = Options()) GET, DELETE post(url, body, content_type, options = Options()), put(...), patch(...) the method with a bytes body and a Content-Type fetch(method, url, options = Options()) any method; the body is options.body open(method, url, options = Options()) as fetch, without reading the body: see Bodies that don't fit in memory close() close the idle connections (see Connection reuse)

All return Response or Error. The functions get, post, put, patch, delete, fetch and open of the module do the same with a new Client for each call, which is closed again afterwards: one request, one connection.

A Client has these fields, each with the default shown:

Field Default Meaning headers none headers sent with every request (Headers) trust_file "" PEM roots for https, as for net/tls timeout Duration(seconds: 30) limit for the connect, the TLS handshake, and each single read or write; a server that keeps sending slowly never trips it (see deadline) deadline Duration() limit for the whole request (connect, handshake, every redirect and reading the whole body); zero means none, a negative one is an InvalidInput error max_redirects 5 redirects to follow; 0 returns the redirect response as it is accept_gzip true send Accept-Encoding: gzip, and decode a gzip response (see Compression) limits see below caps on what a response may send max_idle_per_host, idle 2, Duration(seconds: 30) connection reuse (see Connection reuse)

Options is for one request. Its fields are the same, plus the body, and each one that you leave out means the Client's value:

Field Meaning headers added to the client's; where both have a header of the same name, the request's wins body the request body (bytes); empty by default body_from, body_length instead of body, a Reader to send it from, and its length when that is known trust_file, timeout, deadline, max_redirects, accept_gzip, limits replace the client's for this request, including with 0 or false 
let r = try client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration(seconds: 2)))   // this one is quicker
let q = try client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration()))              // and this one has none

A Host header, Connection: close and a Content-Length (for any body, and for an empty POST, PUT or PATCH) are always set by the library and replace any you give. User-Agent: kod and Accept: */* are added when you don't give them.

URLs are http:// or https://, a host (a name, an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets), an optional port, and an optional path and query. The scheme is case-insensitive, the default ports are 80 and 443, and a missing path is /. A fragment is dropped. Credentials in the URL (user@host), other schemes, spaces and control characters are errors.

items.title: Connection reuse
items.text:
A Client keeps the connections it has finished with and uses them again for the next request to the same scheme, host and port, which saves the TCP connect and the TLS handshake each time:

import "net/http" { Client }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let client = Client()
    let a = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
    let b = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/2")   // same connection
    client.close()
    return 0
}

max_idle_per_host (2) is how many idle connections are kept for each scheme, host and port; 0 turns reuse off, so every request opens and closes its own. idle (30 seconds) is how old an idle connection may be before it is closed instead of reused.

A connection goes back to the Client after a response only when nothing about the exchange makes it unsafe: the response is HTTP/1.1 (or HTTP/1.0 with Connection: keep-alive), has no Connection: close, has a length (a Content-Length, chunked encoding, or no body at all, as for HEAD, 204 and 304), and left nothing unread. A response that ends where the connection ends is never reused. After any error the connection is closed.

Before an idle connection is used, the Client checks that the server has not closed it, and discards it if it has. A server can still close one in the instant between that check and the request. When a request on a reused connection then fails before any of the response arrives, and its method is GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE or TRACE (the ones that are safe to repeat), the Client makes it once more on a new connection. A POST or PATCH is not repeated, and the error is returned as it is.

Redirects use the Client too, so a redirect within one host goes over the same connection. The timeouts and the deadline apply to a reused connection exactly as to a new one. A Client is not meant to be shared by two requests at the same time, and there is only one thread.

items.title: Deadlines
items.text:
timeout bounds each wait, so a server that sends one byte every few seconds can keep a request open for as long as it likes. deadline bounds the request as a whole: the time is counted from the start of fetch and shared by every redirect, and every read and write is given only what is left of it. When it runs out the call throws an IoError of kind TimedOut whose detail is deadline exceeded, however the wait ended, and the connection is closed.

Two things can overrun it: resolving a host name is not interruptible, and a TLS connection spends up to the time left on the TCP connect and then up to the same on the handshake. Neither is by more than one timeout.

items.title: Compression
items.text:
With accept_gzip on, requests carry Accept-Encoding: gzip (unless you set an Accept-Encoding yourself), and a response whose Content-Encoding is gzip, x-gzip or deflate is decoded before you see it: Response.body holds the decoded bytes, the Content-Encoding header is removed, and Content-Length is the decoded length. This happens whenever the response says it is compressed, even from a server that was not asked to compress, and with accept_gzip off. A deflate body is meant to be zlib data, but some servers send raw deflate instead; both are read.

The decoded body is held to limits.max_body like any other, so a response that inflates past it fails with a Protocol error body too large instead of filling memory. A body that is not valid gzip is a Protocol error bad gzip body with the reason (bad deflate body for deflate), and Content-Length of the compressed data was already checked as usual. Any other Content-Encoding (br, zstd, or a list of codings) is left alone: the body comes back as received, with its header, for you to handle. A response with no body, such as one to HEAD, is not decoded.

An opened response's body is decoded as it is read, to any length. Its Content-Encoding and Content-Length headers are removed, as the decoded length isn't known. That the body is not valid is an error of a read.

items.title: Redirects
items.text: 301, 302 and 303 are retried as GET without a body (HEAD stays HEAD); 307 and 308 repeat the method and the body. A Location may be an absolute URL, //host/path, /path, ?query or a path relative to the request's, with . and .. segments resolved. A redirect from https to http is an error, never followed. When the redirect goes to another host or port, the Authorization, Cookie and Proxy-Authorization headers are not sent on. More than max_redirects redirects is an error.

items.title: Responses
items.text:
type Response = struct {
    status: int64
    reason: str
    headers: Headers
    body: bytes

    func text(self) -> str
    func ok(self) -> bool          // 200..299
    func header(self, anon name: str) -> str?
}

headers keeps the order the server sent and any repeated names. Headers has get(name) -> str? (the first value), all(name) -> [str], has(name), add(name, value) and set(name, value) (replaces every value of that name), and compares names without regard to case.

The body is framed as RFC 9112 says: none for HEAD, 1xx, 204 and 304; chunked when Transfer-Encoding is chunked (extensions are ignored and trailers are read and dropped); else Content-Length; else everything up to the end of the connection. 100 Continue and other 1xx responses before the real one are skipped.

Bad responses are errors, not guesses. All of these throw an IoError of kind Protocol, with op http and a detail saying what was wrong: a status line that isn't HTTP/1.x and a three-digit status, a header without a :, whitespace before the :, a header continuation line, a NUL in a header, a Content-Length that is not plain digits or that repeats with a different value, a Transfer-Encoding other than plain chunked (the client doesn't undo gzip or any other coding), a bad chunk size or a chunk without its closing line break. A connection that ends before the announced length or the last chunk is UnexpectedEof.

items.title: Bodies that don't fit in memory
items.text:
open gives the response once its headers have come. resp.reader() is a Reader of the body, which is read as it is asked for, so it takes no more memory than one piece:

func download(anon url: str, to: str) -> int64 or Error {
    let resp = try http.open("GET", url)
    if not resp.ok() {
        resp.close()
        throw http.HttpError(status: resp.status, message: resp.reason)
    }
    let out = try posix.create(to)
    let copied = resp.reader().copy_to(out)
    resp.close()
    try out.close()
    return try copied
}

The connection goes back to the Client, or is closed, once the body has been read to its end or a read has failed. resp.close() ends it before that, and does nothing after; a response that is neither read to its end nor closed keeps its connection open. resp.body is empty, and limits.max_body doesn't hold. timeout is for each read, and deadline goes on until the last.
