A compressed body is decoded as it is read. When the connection ends before the body does, a read fails with UnexpectedEof. Redirects are followed as by fetch. For a response that has been read already, reader() reads its body.

Options(body_from: r) sends what the Reader r gives until its end, in chunks, or with body_length as its Content-Length; a body of another length than that is an InvalidInput error. It works with fetch and open, always on a new connection:

func upload(anon path: str, anon url: str) -> http.Response or Error {
    let f = try posix.open_read(path)
    let sent = http.fetch("PUT", url, options: http.Options(body_from: f, body_length: io.file_size(path)))
    try f.close()
    return try sent
}

A Reader can't be read twice, so a 307 or 308 redirect of such a request is an error. An error of the Reader ends the request and is given back. When the server answers and stops reading before all has been sent, the answer is given back if it can still be read.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limits bounds what one response may make the client read, so a hostile or broken server can't use up memory:

Field Default Exceeding it max_body 16777216 Protocol, body too large max_header_bytes 65536 Protocol, headers too large (the status line, all header lines and trailers together) max_headers 100 Protocol, too many headers

A Content-Length over max_body fails before any of the body is read.

items.title: Query strings and percent-encoding
items.text:
Put user input into a URL through Query, never by concatenating it:

import "net/http" { Query, with_query }

let q = Query()
q.add("q", "kod language")
q.add("page", "2")
let url = with_query("https://api.example.com/search", q)
// https://api.example.com/search?q=kod%20language&page=2
Function Meaning percent_encode(s) every byte except A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ becomes %XX (uppercase hex); UTF-8 text is encoded byte by byte percent_decode(s) the reverse; %XX is a byte, and + stays a +; a % not followed by two hex digits is an InvalidInput error; str or Error Query add(name, value) appends a pair, to_str() joins them as name=value&name=value, with names and values encoded; no pairs give "" with_query(url, q) url plus ? and the query, or & if url already has a ?; an empty query returns url as it is; a #fragment stays at the end

items.title: Basic authentication
items.text:
basic_auth(user, password) returns the value for an Authorization header, Basic and the base64 of user:password (RFC 7617). The text is taken as bytes, so UTF-8 passes through unchanged. A user containing : is an InvalidInput error, because the colon is what separates the two.

import "net/http" { basic_auth, Options }

let options = Options()
options.headers.add("Authorization", try basic_auth("aladdin", "open sesame"))

items.title: Requests at the same time
items.text:
Inside tasks, a request waits for the network while the other tasks run, so requests spawned together are made together, over TLS too:

func status_of(anon url: str) -> int64 or Error {
    return (try get(url)).status
}

func check_all(anon urls: [str]) -> none {
    mut checks: [tasks.Task[int64 or Error]] = []
    for url in urls {
        checks += [spawn status_of(url)]
    }
    for i, check in checks {
        match check.wait() {
            Ok(status) -> print(f"{urls[i]}: {status}")
            Err(e) -> print(f"{urls[i]}: {e.to_str()}")
        }
    }
}

Timeouts and deadlines hold for each task as they do without tasks. A Client can be shared between tasks; each request takes a connection of its own, from the idle ones or a new one. Looking up the host's address still holds up every task (see Tasks).

items.title: Serving
items.text:
A Router says which handler answers which requests, and a Server answers them: each connection is handled by a task of its own, and each request on it by a handler, which takes the Request and gives back a Response.

import "net/http"
import "net/http" { Request, Response }

type User = struct {
    name: str
}

func find_user(anon id: int64) -> User or Error {
    if id != 7 {
        throw http.HttpError(status: 404, message: f"no user {id}")
    }
    return User(name: "Ada")
}

func show_user(anon req: Request) -> Response or Error {
    let Some(id) = req.param("id").parse_int() else {
        throw http.HttpError(status: 400, message: "an id is a number")
    }
    let user = try find_user(id)
    return http.json(f"\{\"name\": \"{user.name}\"}")
}

func main() -> none or Error {
    let routes = http.Router()
    routes.get("/", func(anon req: Request) -> Response or Error {
        return http.text(f"hello, {req.query("name")? or "you"}\n")
    })
    routes.get("/users/{id}", show_user)
    try http.Server(port: 8080, :routes).run()
}

A handler that waits, for a request of its own or a sleep, lets the other connections go on meanwhile. One that fails fails only its own request:

  • an HttpError is a response with its status, and its message as the body;
  • any other error, and a panic, is a 500, and the error, or the panic's message and backtrace, is logged. (A task the handler spawned detached is nobody's, so a panic in one still ends the program.)

items.title: Routes
items.text:
routes.get(pattern, handler), and likewise post, put, patch and delete, or routes.add(method, pattern, handler) for any other method, say who answers the requests of that method whose path fits pattern:

In a pattern Fits /users/all just that /users/{id} any one part that isn't empty: req.param("id") is the part, percent-decoded /files/{path...} all the rest, with at least one part: req.param("path") is a/b.txt for /files/a/b.txt (and may have .. in it: check it before it names a file)

A written part goes before a {name} at the same place, and that before a {name...}: with the first two above, /users/all is the first's. Adding a pattern that fits the same paths as one added before for that method, or isn't one at all, panics.

A path no pattern fits is a 404. One that only patterns of other methods fit is a 405, with the methods it has in Allow. HEAD is answered by GET's handler, without the body, where there is no handler for HEAD itself.

items.title: Request
items.text: method, target as sent; target is the path and the query headers, body Headers, and the body's bytes remote the client's address, such as 127.0.0.1:50123 secure whether it came over HTTPS path() target up to ?; of a whole URL, as a proxy may send, its path param(name) the part of the path {name} in the pattern stands for; panics when the pattern has no such name query(name) the first value of name in the query, decoded (+ is a space); str? queries(name) all its values, [str] header(name) a header's value; str? text() the body as text reader() a Reader of the body: see Streaming

items.title: Response
items.text: http.text(body, status = 200) plain text http.html(body, status = 200) HTML http.json(body, status = 200) JSON, given as text: see json for making it http.redirect(to, status = 302) a redirect to to http.status(code) only a status, with its reason as the body where it can have one respond(status, body, content_type = "text/plain; charset=utf-8") any of them http.stream(write, status = 200, content_type = "application/octet-stream", length = none) a body that write writes piece by piece http.file(path, req = none, content_type = none) a file's content, streamed; Response or Error, a 404 HttpError when there is no such file (or it is a directory). Its type is the one its name's ending says, when left out resp.with_header(name, value) resp, with a header added

items.title: HTTPS
items.text:
With an identity, a certificate and its key, a Server speaks HTTPS, and nothing else, on its port:

let identity = try tls.load_identity("cert.pem", "key.pem")
try http.Server(host: "", port: 443, :routes, :identity).run()

The handshake is part of what header_timeout limits; a client that fails it is closed, after an alert when it can't speak TLS 1.3 (see TLS). Everything else is as over plain HTTP. req.secure says which it was. Setting server.identity to a newly loaded one, as when a certificate is renewed, is for connections from then on.

items.title: Files
items.text:
routes.files(prefix, dir) serves the files below the directory dir, for paths below prefix:

routes.files("/static", "public", max_age: Duration(hours: 1))   // /static/css/a.css is public/css/a.css
routes.files("/", "site")                                        // and everything no other route fits
  • A directory is its index (index.html when left out), and a 404 when it has none; its path without the slash at the end is redirected to the one with it.
  • A part of the path that starts with a dot, such as .. or .git, is a 404, and so is an empty one or one with a \ or a NUL in it. (/.well-known needs a routes.files of its own.) Symbolic links are followed, out of dir too.
  • max_age is sent as Cache-Control: max-age.

Files have Last-Modified, and a request with If-Modified-Since that is as new gets a 304. A GET with a Range of bytes (one range, in any of its three forms) gets those as a 206, or a 416 when the file is shorter; If-Range with a date makes that depend on the file being unchanged. Anything else in a Range is ignored, and the whole file sent. There is no ETag. http.file(path, req: req) does the same in a handler; without req it always sends the whole file.

When the response would be compressed for the client, a Range is ignored: it would be of the bytes compressed, which aren't kept.

items.title: Streaming
items.text:
A response's body needn't be in memory as a whole. http.stream takes a function that writes it, which is called once the handler has given the response back:

func rows(anon _req: Request) -> Response or Error {
    return http.stream(func(anon w: http.BodyWriter) -> none or Error {
        for i in 0..1000000 {
            try w.write_str(f"{i},{i * i}\n")
        }
    }, content_type: "text/csv")
}

A BodyWriter is a Writer. What is written goes out once there are 64 KB of it, or at w.flush(), as for a stream of events. A write waits while the client is slow to read, so the body takes no more memory than that. length is the body's length when it is known, sent as Content-Length; writing more or less than that is an error. Without it, the body is sent in chunks (to a client that speaks HTTP/1.0, until the connection closes), or with its length if it all fits in one piece.

Until the first piece goes out nothing has been sent, so an error or a panic in the function is answered as a handler's is, by a 500 or an HttpError's status. After that it is logged and ends the connection, so that the client can tell the body isn't whole (a client that speaks HTTP/1.0 can't, without length). When the client goes away, the next write fails, which isn't logged. A HEAD, and a status without a body, don't call the function.

A request's body can be read as it comes too, by a route added with stream_body: true, or, without routes, when the Server has stream_bodies: true:

func save(anon req: Request) -> Response or Error {
    let out = try posix.create("upload.tmp")
    let copied = req.reader().copy_to(out)
    try out.close()                          // whether or not the client went away
    return http.text(f"{try copied} bytes\n", status: 201)
}

routes.put("/upload", save, stream_body: true)

req.reader() is a Reader of the body; without stream_body, of the bytes already read. limits.max_body doesn't hold for a streamed body, nor does body_timeout limit the whole of it: the handler decides how much, and how long, is too much. req.body is empty.

When the client sends something wrong, stops sending for body_timeout, or goes away, a read fails; a handler that passes the error on answers with the 400 or 408 it would have been. A client that asks first (Expect: 100-continue) is told to go on at the first read. What the handler leaves unread is read and dropped when it is short (64 KB); otherwise the connection ends after the response.

items.title: Compressing
items.text:
With Server(compress: true), responses are compressed with gzip for clients that take it (Accept-Encoding), where that is worth it: a Content-Type of text, JSON, JavaScript, XML, SVG or WebAssembly, and a body of 1 KB or more. They then have Content-Encoding: gzip. Such a response has Vary: Accept-Encoding for other clients too, for caches to tell them apart. A streamed body is compressed as it is written, and sent in chunks; flush sends what there is, so events still come at once. compress_level is deflate's.

A response is left as it is when it has a Content-Encoding, an ETag (which names the bytes sent) or a Cache-Control of no-transform, when its status is 206, and when it is streamed to a client that speaks HTTP/1.0.

It is off unless asked for: it takes 10 to 20 µs for each KB, as long as a request or two without it. Don't compress a page that has both a secret (such as a CSRF token) and text the client chose: the length then tells about the secret (the BREACH attack). A Cache-Control of no-transform leaves it out.

items.title: Connections
items.text: A connection carries requests one after another, until the client sends Connection: close (or speaks HTTP/1.0 without keep-alive), a request can't be read, or the client goes away. A request's body is read by its Content-Length or chunked; a client that sends Expect: 100-continue is told to go on. Anything wrong with a request ends the connection, with a 400, or a 413 for a body past the limits, a 431 for headers past them, or a 501 for a Transfer-Encoding other than chunked.

items.title: Server
items.text:
Server(...) has the settings, each with a default. run() listens on host and port and answers requests until stop, or until Ctrl-C or a kill (SIGINT or SIGTERM), which stops it as stop does; a second one ends the program at once. serve(l) answers those that come to a tcp.Listener there is already, and leaves signals alone. Both give none or Error.

func main() -> none or Error {
    let server = Server(handler: hello, max_connections: 500, idle_timeout: Duration(seconds: 15))
    try server.run()
}
Field Default Meaning routes none the Router that answers requests handler answers them all instead, when there are no routes identity none a certificate and key, to speak HTTPS host, port 127.0.0.1, 8080 where run listens; an empty host means every IPv4 interface header_timeout 10 s how long a client may take to send a request's headers, from when it connects or, on a kept-alive connection, from their first byte body_timeout 60 s how long it may take to send the body after them; of a streamed body, how long until the next of it comes write_timeout 60 s how long it may take to read the response; of a streamed one, each 64 KB or less of it idle_timeout 60 s how long a kept-alive connection may wait for its next request stop_timeout 10 s how long requests may go on after stop max_connections 10000 how many connections are open at once stop_on_signals true whether run stops on SIGINT and SIGTERM; when false it leaves signals alone too compress, compress_level false, 4 whether responses are compressed, and how much stream_bodies false whether handler reads the bodies of requests itself limits Limits() caps each request's headers and body, as for a response log stderr a func(str) -> none that gets a line or more for each handler that fails access_log false whether log gets a line for each request too: 127.0.0.1:50123 GET /users/7 200 14 B 0.31 ms, with the length of the body sent and the time until it was

serve(l, handler, limits = Limits()) is Server(:handler, :limits).serve(l).

The timeouts cap the whole of what they name, not each read, so a client that sends a byte at a time is dropped too: with a 408 when it has begun a request (which it may miss if it is still sending), else just closed. A handler has no timeout; use tasks.within for what it waits for.

At max_connections, a kept-alive connection that waits for its next request is closed to make room, the one that would time out first; when there is none, new connections wait to be accepted until one ends. Running out of file descriptors doesn't end the server: it waits a little and tries again.

server.stop(within: d) ends serve: no more connections are accepted, those waiting for a request are closed, and the requests being read or answered get d (stop_timeout when left out) to finish, their responses saying Connection: close. serve then returns, and a later one returns at once; when some hadn't finished, they are cancelled and it returns a TimedOut error. It returns an error when accepting fails or its task is cancelled (task.cancel()) too; then the connections' tasks are cancelled and waited for.

items.title: Building and reading by hand
items.text:
net/http has what client is made of:

Function Meaning parse_url(s) Url or Error with scheme, host, port, target (path and query) resolve(base, location) the Url a Location points to write_request(w, req, keep_alive = false, accept_gzip = false) write an Outgoing (method, url, headers, body) to any Writer, with Connection: close unless keep_alive, and Accept-Encoding: gzip when accept_gzip and there is no Accept-Encoding header already; header names and values with a line break or other control character, and a bad method, are InvalidInput errors read_request(br, limits = Limits()) the next Request from a BufReader, or none when the connection ends before one begins write_response(w, resp, keep_alive = false, head = false) writes resp with a Content-Length and, unless keep_alive, Connection: close; an empty reason is the status's usual one; head leaves out the body, for the answer to a HEAD read_response(br, method, limits = Limits()) read one response from a BufReader; method decides whether there is a body; Response.keep_alive says whether the connection can carry another request

write_request and read_response work on MemWriter and MemReader, which is how they are tested without a network.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• macOS on Apple Silicon (AArch64)
  • Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) — provides as and clang, which compiles the C runtime and links every program

items.title: From source
items.text:
git clone https://codeberg.org/filipsalo/kod
cd kod

items.title: Building the self-hosted compiler
items.text:
The Makefile bootstraps everything from scratch:

make bootstrap   # clean rebuild of stage0 + stage1 (sh_kodc)
make stage1      # incremental rebuild
make test        # rebuild, then run the full test suite

items.title: Running
items.text:
kod is the native tool build/apps/kod/kod. Build it once with make kod, then start it through ./kod, a link to it at the repository root (until it is built, ./kod fails with the shell's no such file or directory):

make kod
./kod build hello.kod   # compile to a native binary
./kod run hello.kod     # build + execute
./kod test hello.kod    # run any `test "..." {}` blocks
./kod check hello.kod   # parse + codegen; report errors but emit nothing

Started through ./kod, it runs make stage1 kod first when something is out of date, so edits to the compiler, the C runtime, the always-linked stdlib modules or the tool itself are picked up automatically (see CLI reference).

items.title: Using kod in other projects
items.text:
The checkout is the installation: put a link to its kod on your PATH.

ln -s ~/src/kod/kod ~/.local/bin/kod

Started through that link, or any other way but its own path build/apps/kod/kod, kod brings the toolchain up to date first, as ./kod does: it finds the checkout by following the links to its own executable. That costs a make -q, some 20 ms, and a rebuild only when something changed. So a git pull in the checkout is all it takes to have the latest: the next kod command anywhere builds it.

Outside the checkout, kod build, run, test and check work on the project in the working directory:

  • Sources are the project's: the file named, and the modules it imports with import "./name", relative to the file that imports them. import "net/http" and the other standard modules come from the checkout's stdlib/.
  • What is built: kod build main.kod writes the program to ./main, as go build does, or wherever -o PATH says. Objects and the programs kod run and kod test make go to the project's hidden .kod-build/, so a .gitignore needs that and the programs. Compiled modules are cached in the checkout's build/cache/, shared by every project.
  • A program that kod run or kod test starts runs in the project's directory, so the paths it opens are the project's.
  • Errors name the project's files by their full paths.

items.title: Linking
items.text:
link.cfg at the repository root says how programs are linked: the clang command and the C files and Kod modules every program contains. Nothing in it is specific to one machine, so most machines never touch it. One that needs something else (a Homebrew LLVM clang first on PATH that does not find the SDK, an unusual SDK) puts the names it changes in link.local.cfg next to it (only names link.cfg sets), for example:

LINK := /usr/bin/clang -target arm64-apple-darwin -Wl,-dead_strip

link.local.cfg is not tracked by git, so each new git worktree needs its own copy (cp ../link.local.cfg .). See Self-hosting for the format.

See CLI reference for the full command surface.

items.title: Streams and I/O errors
items.text:
stdlib/stream.kod defines the error type and the two interfaces that byte streams share, and stdlib/posix.kod implements them over file descriptors: files, standard input and output and, later, sockets. Code that reads or writes takes a Reader or a Writer and doesn't care what is behind it.

import "stream" { Reader }
import "posix" { open_read }

func count_bytes(anon r: Reader) -> int64 or Error {
    let data = try r.read_all()
    return len(data)
}

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let f = try open_read("data.bin")
    print_int(try count_bytes(f))
    try f.close()
    return 0
}

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Every operation that can fail returns T or Error and throws an IoError:

type IoKind = enum {
    NotFound
    PermissionDenied
    AlreadyExists
    InvalidInput
    WouldBlock      // reserved; nothing returns it yet
    TimedOut
    ConnectionRefused
    ConnectionReset
    BrokenPipe
    UnexpectedEof
    Other
    HostNotFound
    Tls
    Protocol
    Cancelled
    StorageFull     // no room left on the disk (ENOSPC)
}

type IoError = struct {
    kind: IoKind
    op: str        // what was attempted: "open data.bin", "read", "write"
    errno: int64   // the OS error number, 0 if the error didn't come from the OS
    detail: str    // the OS's message, or a short explanation
}

to_str gives open data.bin: No such file or directory. Recover the kind with a downcast:

match open_read(path) {
    Ok(f) -> use(f)
    Err(e) ->
        if e is IoError(io) and io.kind == .NotFound {
            print("no such file")
        } else {
            print(e.to_str())
        }
}

kind_of_errno(errno) maps an OS error number to an IoKind; anything it doesn't know is Other. EAGAIN is TimedOut, because a descriptor here is only ever non-blocking through a timeout (see TCP). HostNotFound is for a name that doesn't resolve and has no OS error number (errno is 0). Tls is for a TLS failure that isn't a plain I/O error, such as a certificate that doesn't verify (see TLS). Protocol is for a peer that breaks the rules of the protocol being spoken, such as a malformed HTTP response (see HTTP). Cancelled is for an operation in a task that was cancelled while it waited (ECANCELED). An interrupted system call is retried inside the runtime, so EINTR never reaches a caller.

items.title: Reader and Writer
items.text:
interface Reader {
    func read(self, anon max: int64) -> bytes or Error

    func read_all(self) -> bytes or Error { ... }
    func read_exact(self, anon n: int64) -> bytes or Error { ... }
    func copy_to(self, anon to: Writer) -> int64 or Error { ... }
}

interface Writer {
    func write(self, anon data: bytes) -> int64 or Error

    func write_all(self, anon data: bytes) -> none or Error { ... }
    func write_str(self, anon text: str) -> none or Error { ... }
}

read returns between 1 and max bytes, waiting until there is something to return, and returns an empty bytes at the end of the stream. With max <= 0 it returns an empty bytes without reading, so don't call it that way to test for the end. write returns how many bytes it accepted, which may be fewer than len(data); an empty data writes nothing and returns 0.

A type only has to declare read or write; the rest are provided methods built on them, so every Reader and Writer has them, called on the value itself or through the interface:

Method Meaning r.read_all() read until the end of the stream; bytes or Error r.read_exact(n) exactly n bytes, or an UnexpectedEof error; bytes or Error r.copy_to(w) write everything until the end of the stream to the Writer w, a piece at a time; how many bytes that was; int64 or Error w.write_all(data) write every byte, repeating write as needed; a write that accepts 0 bytes of a non-empty data is an Other error (write returned 0); none or Error w.write_str(s) write_all of a str

items.title: In-memory streams
items.text: MemReader(data: bytes, pos: 0) reads from a bytes value, which is how tests and parsers get a stream without a file. MemWriter(buf: StrBuilder()) collects what is written, and to_bytes() / to_str() return a copy of it. Neither can fail.

items.title: BufReader
items.text:
BufReader wraps any Reader with a buffer, for protocols that mix lines and counted bodies such as HTTP:

let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
let status = try br.read_line()          // str?, none at the end of the stream
let body = try br.read_exact(length)     // takes what is buffered first
Method Meaning read(max) a Reader: the buffered bytes first, else one read of the inner stream read_exact(n) the Reader's, so exactly n bytes, or UnexpectedEof read_until(delim) the bytes up to and excluding the byte delim, which is consumed; bytes?, none at the end of the stream; the last piece comes back even without a delimiter read_line() read_until(10) as a str, minus a trailing \r (str?)

Fields: inner, limit: int64 = 1048576 (a read_until or read_line longer than this fails with an InvalidInput error line too long instead of growing without bound), chunk: int64 = 8192 (the size of each inner read). ended is set when a read_until or read_line returned a last piece that the stream's end cut short, with no delimiter after it; a protocol that needs every line terminated can tell a truncation from a complete line by it. A BufReader doesn't close its inner stream.

items.title: Files and descriptors
items.text:
Fd is a file descriptor and implements both Reader and Writer:

Function Meaning open_read(path) an existing file for reading create(path) a file for writing, created (mode 0644) or truncated append(path) a file for writing, created if missing, written at its end stdin(), stdout(), stderr() descriptors 0, 1 and 2 Fd(fd: n) wrap a descriptor from elsewhere f.close() close it and set f.fd to -1, so closing it again fails; none or Error f.seek(pos) goes on reading or writing pos bytes from the start of a file; none or Error f.is_terminal() whether it is a terminal, rather than a file or a pipe signal(pid, sig) send the signal numbered sig to the process pid, as C's kill; none or Error (for a child of this program, process.Child.kill is the easier way)

items.title: Files that must survive a crash
items.text:
A write is in the operating system's memory when it returns, and reaches the disk some time later. A crash or a power cut in between loses it, or part of it, and so can a rename or a new file whose directory hasn't been written out. A program that must not lose what it has said it kept, such as a database, uses these:

Function Meaning open_rw(path) a file for reading and writing, created (mode 0644) if missing, not truncated, at its start f.sync() waits until what was written to the file, and its length, is on the disk (F_FULLFSYNC, which also empties the drive's own cache); none or Error f.truncate(size) cuts the file to size bytes, or lengthens it with zeros; none or Error f.size() how long the file is; int64 or Error rename(from, to) renames a file or directory, replacing a file at to in one step: a crash leaves the old one or the new, never neither; none or Error remove(path) removes a file; none or Error make_dir(path) makes a directory (mode 0755) in one that exists; none or Error remove_dir(path) removes an empty directory; none or Error list_dir(path) the names in a directory, sorted, without . and ..; [str] or Error sync_dir(path) waits until the directory's changes (files made, renamed or removed in it) are on the disk; none or Error

f.sync() keeps the file's contents, not its name: a new file, or a rename, also needs sync_dir of the directory it is in. The usual way to replace a file whole is to write a new one, sync it, rename it over the old one and sync_dir the directory.

A simulation checks that a program does this: it crashes the disk at a point its seed picks, losing what wasn't synced.

items.title: Waiting on several descriptors
items.text:
poll(read:, write:, timeout:) waits until at least one of the descriptors is ready, and says which, so a program can serve several pipes or connections without blocking on any one of them:

let ready = try posix.poll(read: [out, err], write: [input], timeout: Duration(seconds: 5))
if ready.read[0] {
    let piece = try out.read(65536)         // doesn't wait
}

It returns a posix.Ready or an Error. ready.read and ready.write hold a bool for each descriptor in read and write, in the same order.

  • Ready for reading means a read won't wait: there is data, the stream has ended, or an error is pending.
  • Ready for writing means a write of up to 512 bytes won't wait, or will fail at once because the reader has gone.
  • Ignored descriptors: a descriptor of -1, such as a closed Fd, is never ready.
  • Timeout: without timeout: it waits as long as it takes. When the timeout passes first, every entry is false. With a zero Duration it only looks.
  • Nothing to wait for: if both lists are empty or hold only -1, it fails with an InvalidInput error instead of waiting forever.

stdout() writes straight to descriptor 1, bypassing the buffer that print uses. Call flush_stdout() first when you mix the two. Closing is explicit: an Fd that is dropped stays open until the program exits.

items.title: Colour
items.text:
stdlib/term.kod colours text for a terminal. term.colour(fd) says whether to: fd is a terminal, NO_COLOR is unset or empty, and TERM isn't dumb. The other functions wrap text in the escape codes of a style, whatever the output is, so check first:

import "io"
import "posix"
import "term"

func main() -> int64 {
    mut label = "error:"
    if term.colour(posix.stderr()) {
        label = term.red(term.bold(label))
    }
    io.write_stderr(f"{label} no such file\n")
    return 1
}

The styles are bold, dim, red, green and yellow.

io.read_file gives str or Error: an IoError that says why the file can't be opened or read, such as open data.txt: No such file or directory. Where a missing file means no text, io.read_file(path)? or "" gives the empty string. The older io.write_file keeps its behavior: -1 on failure, with no reason.

items.title: TCP
items.text:
stdlib/net/tcp.kod opens TCP connections. A connection is an Fd, so it is a Reader and a Writer: it works with BufReader and has read_all, write_str and the rest. It is Kod throughout, calling the C library's socket functions through unsafe.

import "net/tcp" { connect, set_timeout }
import "time" { Duration }
import "stream" { BufReader }

func fetch_status_line(host: str) -> str or Error {
    let conn = try connect(host, port: 80)
    try set_timeout(conn, timeout: Duration(seconds: 5))
    try conn.write_str("HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n")
    let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
    let line = try br.read_line()
    try conn.close()
    return line? or ""
}
Function Meaning connect(host, port, timeout = Duration(seconds: 10)) resolve host (a name or an IP literal, IPv4 or IPv6) and connect to the first address that answers; Fd or Error set_timeout(f, timeout) make a read or a write on f fail with TimedOut after a Duration without progress; zero means wait forever; none or Error listen(host, port, backlog = 128) a Listener bound to host:port; an empty host means every IPv4 interface and port 0 picks a free port; Listener or Error l.accept(nonblocking = false) the next connection, waiting for one; Fd or Error. A nonblocking one is written to without waiting first, which is faster when there are other tasks; set_timeout doesn't apply to it l.wait() waits until there is a connection for accept to take; none or Error peer(f) the address at the other end, as 127.0.0.1:50123 or [::1]:50123; "" when there is none shutdown(f, read = false, write = false) ends one direction of the connection, or both: a read of it gives the end of the stream, also one a task waits in, and a write fails is_idle(f) true if nothing is waiting to be read from f; false if it has data, an end of stream (the peer closed it) or an error pending l.port() the port it is bound to l.close() stop listening; none or Error

connect gives up on each address after timeout, so a host with several unreachable addresses can take longer in all. A refused connection is ConnectionRefused, a timeout TimedOut, a name that doesn't resolve HostNotFound, and a port outside 0..65535 or an empty host InvalidInput. Writing to a peer that has closed is a BrokenPipe error and doesn't kill the program with SIGPIPE. A connection has TCP_NODELAY set.

items.title: TLS
items.text:
stdlib/net/tls.kod runs TLS 1.3 over a TCP connection, both sides, with Kod's own implementation (stdlib/net/tls13.kod, on the modules of Cryptography). No system library is involved: a client checks the server's certificates against the system's roots (on macOS, those of its root keychain) itself. A peer that can't speak TLS 1.3 (one that has only TLS 1.2, say) is refused.

import "net/tls" { connect }
import "stream" { BufReader }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let conn = try connect("example.com", port: 443)
    try conn.write_str("GET / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n")
    let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
    print((try br.read_line())? or "")
    try conn.close()
    return 0
}

A TlsStream is a Reader and a Writer, so everything above works on it as on a plain connection.

Function Meaning connect(host, port, trust_file = "", timeout = Duration(seconds: 10)) open a TCP connection with net/tcp and run the TLS handshake; TlsStream or Error s.read(max), s.write(data) as for any stream s.set_timeout(timeout) as net/tcp.set_timeout: a read or write fails with TimedOut after a Duration without progress s.close() send a close notice, then close the connection; none or Error

The server's certificate must be valid for host, chain to a trusted root and be in date; otherwise connect throws an IoError of kind Tls whose detail says why, and the connection is closed. A server that can't do TLS 1.3 as the client does is a Tls error too, such as the server doesn't speak TLS 1.3. timeout limits the TCP connect and, separately, the handshake. What is checked is in Certificates.

trust_file is the path of a PEM file of certificates. When it isn't empty, those certificates are the only trusted roots, in place of the system's: use it for a private CA or a self-signed server. The host name is still checked.

The client offers the x25519 key exchange and the TLS 1.3 cipher suites with AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, and takes ECDSA (P-256 and P-384) and RSA-PSS signatures from the server. It doesn't resume sessions or send early data; a server that asks for a client certificate gets none. s.session is the tls13.Session, whose client holds what the handshake found, such as the server's certificates and the cipher suite. A handshake costs about 0.5 to 7 ms of CPU: 0.3 ms for X25519 and the rest checking signatures, 0.1 to 0.25 ms each for RSA, 0.4 ms on P-256 and 2.5 ms on P-384. The first in a program also reads the system's roots, another 75 ms.

The server's side is accept, on a connection that net/tcp accepted:

import "net/tcp"
import "net/tls"

func main() -> none or Error {
    let identity = try tls.load_identity("cert.pem", "key.pem")
    let l = try tcp.listen("127.0.0.1", port: 8443)
    let conn = try tls.accept(try l.accept(), identity)
    try conn.write_str("hello\n")
    try conn.close()
}
Function Meaning load_identity(cert_file, key_file) a certificate and its private key, from PEM files; Identity or Error. cert_file holds the server's certificate first and then those it was signed by, up to the root (which can be left out); key_file an RSA key, or an EC key on P-256 or P-384, that isn't encrypted (PRIVATE KEY, RSA PRIVATE KEY or EC PRIVATE KEY) identity.close() accept takes it no more; connections made with it go on accept(fd, identity) run the handshake as the server; TlsStream or Error. The connection is the stream's from then on, which closes it; on an error it is closed at once. How long the handshake may take is fd's tcp.set_timeout, which a nonblocking one has not

A key that isn't the certificate's is a Tls error, and so is a key on another curve, or an EC key whose curve the certificate gives by its parameters rather than by name.

The server speaks x25519 (asking a client that sent another key share for an x25519 one), the three TLS 1.3 cipher suites, and the key's signature, ECDSA or RSA-PSS. A client that offers no TLS 1.3, or can't take that key or key exchange, is sent an alert (protocol_version or handshake_failure) and accept fails with a Tls error. Clients have spoken TLS 1.3 since about 2018. s.session.server holds what a handshake found, such as the server_name the client asked for. The client isn't asked for a certificate.

A server handshake costs about 0.5 ms of CPU with a P-256 key (0.18 ms for the signature, 0.3 ms for X25519) and about 3.5 ms with an RSA key of 2048 bits. With an EC key the first handshake in a program also makes a table of multiples of the curve's generator, about 2 ms, which the signatures after it use.

Several tasks can use streams at the same time, and one may read a stream while another writes to it; two writing to one stream at the same time isn't supported.

A server that closes the connection without a close notice reads as an ordinary end of stream, since plain HTTP/1.0 servers do that; a response that carries its own length (Content-Length or chunked) shows a truncation anyway.

items.title: Compiler IR (design)
items.text: Status: steps 1–4 and 8–13 done; steps 5 and 7 measured and not landed. This page is the plan for giving the compiler an intermediate representation; it describes the compiler, not the language.

items.title: Where it starts
items.text:
codegen.kod walks the AST and emits arm64 instructions into a per-function buffer of regalloc.Insn values. Since the structured-instructions work (522f24e … abf4e42) most of them are no longer text:

Variant What it is Slot(store, reg, off) ldr/str to a frame slot Mov(dst, src) register move Mem(op, reg, base, off, has_off) load or store through a register Op(mn, a, b, c, d, flags) any other instruction with one-token operands Call(target) bl Branch(op, reg, target) b, b.cond, cbz, cbnz Label(name) a label Raw(text, info) the rest: about 60 emit sites and the directives

After a function is emitted, passes run over the buffer (peephole, promote_locals, forward_copies, register allocation, long_branches), and the buffer is printed as assembly.

This is already a low-level IR, but an arm64 one: mnemonics are arm64's, physical registers (x0–x7 for arguments, x16/x17 as scratch, fp, sp, xzr) are named in it, and calling, addressing and immediates follow arm64's rules.

items.title: Goal
items.text:
A target-neutral low-level IR (LIR) in place of the arm64 instruction buffer:

  • Operations, not mnemonics: add, load64, store8, compare, branch_if(cond), call, retain, release, … with virtual registers and immediates as operands.
  • Roles, not registers: argument i, the result, scratch, the frame, the stack. Each target maps a role to its register.
  • Lowering per target: one pass turns LIR into a target's instructions. Arm64 first, printing exactly what the compiler prints today; x86-64 later.
  • Passes on LIR: the existing ones, target-neutral where they can be, plus new optimisations.

Not a goal for now: SSA, a mid-level IR between the AST and LIR, or rewriting how codegen.kod walks the AST. Codegen keeps doing what it does; what it emits changes.

items.title: How it gets there
items.text:
Every step until the first optimisation keeps the output byte-identical, checked with make asm-diff over the whole corpus, as the structured-instructions steps were.

  1. Neutral operations (done). Op holds a regalloc.Opcode (Add, Compare, SetIf, AddressPage, …), Mem a direction and a width in bytes, and Branch a BranchKind (Always, If(Cond), IfZero, IfNonzero); the arm64 lowering (arm64_mnemonic, mem_mnemonic, branch_mnemonic) prints their mnemonics. Conditional branches are now always written b.cond, which assembles to the same bytes as bcond (checked with asm_diff --objects). Still strings: the condition operand of SetIf, Select and CompareIf, and the register names.
  2. Register roles (done for the allocator). The register pools come from a regalloc.Target (TARGET, ARM64): the caller- and callee-saved temporaries, the order the prologue saves registers in, and the argument registers. In codegen the registers it names itself stay spelled as arm64 spells them, as role names: x0–x7 for arguments and the result, x16, x17 and x9 as scratch (x17 also passes a value to the reference-counting stubs), fp, sp, xzr, and d0, d1 for floats. Renaming them would decide nothing yet: what a second target needs is to tell argument 0 from the result (both x0 on arm64), and that is for its lowering, which can map x0 to its first argument register and move the result there after each call.
  3. No text left (done). Mem addresses through a MemAt (the base, an offset, an index register, scaled by the access size or not, or a symbol's page offset); register pairs are a Pair (offset, pre- or post-index); a constant too big for one move is a LoadConst, which the line limits count as the four lines arm64 needs; an inlined runtime function is an Intrinsic(label) whose lines come from the arm64 table (arm64_intrinsic); directives and data labels are Data, which no pass reads. Nothing makes instruction text any more: Raw, line_info and the passes' text paths are gone, and an Op operand that isn't one token is a compiler bug. Assembly text exists only at output (format_insn, and print_encodable for an immediate too big to encode). The symbol's page (AddressPage with an @PAGE operand) is still two operations and arm64's way of addressing; one AddressOf(symbol) is left for the second target to need.
  4. The arm64 lowering in its own module (done). stdlib/kod/arm64.kod holds everything that writes arm64: the mnemonics and condition names, each instruction's text (format_insn, given the allocator's vreg-to-register table), the inlined runtime functions, the mov/movk lines for a large constant or an immediate too big to encode, and line_count. regalloc holds the IR and the allocator and doesn't import it. Still in codegen and still arm64's: peephole (its patterns are neutral, but the immediates it folds are arm64's 12-bit ones) and long_branches (arm64's 1 MB branch reach), to move behind the target when a second one exists.
  5. Retain and release cancelling (measured, dropped). The plan was explicit Retain(v) and Release(v) operations and a pass cancelling a retain and a release of the same value with nothing between them that could free it. There are none to cancel: each retain copies a borrowed reference into a place that owns it (a local's slot, 58%, or a field or element, 33%), and its release comes much later, when the slot is overwritten or goes out of scope. Nor would it pay much: compiling codegen.kod runs 46M retains and 50M releases, and with both stubs reduced to a ret the compile is only 5% faster. Most of what reference counting costs is allocating and freeing.

  6. Measured first. Counting how often each basic block runs, on the compiler compiling codegen.kod and on the benchmarks, gives each candidate as a share of the instructions executed (an upper bound on the time saved: a 12% drop in instructions made loop 2% faster):

    Candidate compiler sieve qsort inflate Loads a loop can't change 1.5–3.6% 14% 8.6–16% 1.3–7.4% Register copies 14% 26% 16% 20% Bounds checks run 2.3% 4.7% 7.6% 3.9% Redundant loads within a block 1.8% 1.4% 0.9% 1.0% Dead stores, constant folding <0.5% 0 0 0.2%

Done from it: a frame over 256 bytes is addressed from its bottom in x28, one instruction per slot instead of three (5% of the compiler's instructions), and a large constant skips the movk of a zero part. 7. Loop-invariant loads (tried, not landed; branch ir-hoist-loads). After register allocation, a load in an innermost loop moves to just before the loop's top label when the loop is entered only there, its address doesn't change in the loop (a frame slot it doesn't store to; a heap address whose base it doesn't change, in a loop with no call and no heap store), a heap load's base is one the loop's top already reads through (so it isn't read early past a check for none), and the function leaves a register free for it (callee-saved when the loop makes a call). The load in the loop becomes a copy from that register. Done before allocation instead, the moved loads took registers from promoted locals, which then went back to memory. It made qsort and words about 2% faster and nothing else measurably, while the pass cost 6% of compile time: the safe rules leave most of the loads counted above in place (most hot loops store to the heap), and fewer instructions buy less time than they suggest. Not worth it as it stands. Register copies are the largest category but the least certain win (Apple's cores eliminate most of them when renaming), so they were timed first, on hand-edited output of the hottest loops of sieve and qsort:

| Hand edit | sieve | qsort |
|---|---|---|
| Copies removed (4 of 13 and 2 of 13 instructions) | −0.3% | −0.8% |
| Bounds checks also removed (length load, compare, branch) | −6.1% | −6.2% |

Copies cost next to nothing, so coalescing them isn't worth a pass. Bounds checks cost a few percent where a hot loop indexes an array, but removing one needs a proof that the index is in range, which neither of these loops gives (j <= n against a length built by appends; i/j moved by the comparisons).

Nor do most checks elsewhere. Of the 66M checks run compiling codegen.kod, about a fifth are in a for k in a..len(x) loop that leaves x's length alone, which a simple pass could prove; another fifth follow a test such as i < len(s) and would need the conditions tracked. At the half a cycle a check costs in the timed loops, removing all of them would save about 2.5% of the compile, and the provable fifth about 0.5%; the hot checks of the benchmarks are none of these. Not worth a pass for now. 8. Registers as numbers. An instruction's registers and Op operands are a regalloc.Reg, an int64, instead of text: 4n+1 is vreg n (v12), 4n+2 its 32-bit form (w12), 4n+3 the immediate #n, and 4k the kth name of a table (regalloc.NAMES): 0 is none, x0–x30, fp, lr, sp and xzr come first, and any other operand (a condition, a symbol's page, a negative immediate) is added the first time it's named. Codegen still names registers as text: its emit_ functions turn each into a Reg once (regalloc.reg_of), so the passes compare numbers instead of parsing names, and nothing in an instruction is counted. The output turns them back (regalloc.reg_text, arm64.phys_of). The allocator's pool, the target's registers and each vreg's register are Regs too. Labels, call targets, symbols in an address and directives stay text. What is left of the text is codegen's own: alloc_reg still names a vreg v12, and each emit_ reads the name back. 9. Machine words instead of text (done). Assembling the output costs far more than compiling it: as takes 3.1 s on what the compiler writes for codegen.kod in 0.22 s, and about four fifths of the gates' CPU time. Clang's assembler spends it matching each register operand against every kind of register name (22 µs a line); a line written as the instruction's word, .inst 0xaa0103e0 for mov x0, x1, assembles to the same bytes about 50 times faster. So arm64.encode gives the word of each instruction that names only registers and immediates, and the output writes that; anything with a label or a symbol, and any form encode doesn't know, stays text. With KOD_ASM_TEXT set, each word is followed by its instruction as a comment (.inst 0xaa0103e0 // mov x0, x1), for reading the output; it is left out otherwise, since writing it and skipping it again cost about a twentieth of a compile. asm_diff --objects (tools/asm_diff.kod) checks the result: every object file in the corpus must have the same bytes as when the text is assembled.

Then the object file without as: kod/macho reads the compiler's output (labels, the directives it writes, .inst words, and the instructions that name a label or a symbol) and writes a Mach-O object itself, in the compiler's own process, when link.cfg says AS := kod. What it writes is laid out more plainly than clang's (symbols grouped and sorted, data that points at a temporary label relocated against its section), so the check is by meaning, not bytes: tools/as_diff.kod assembles every file of the corpus both ways and compares each section's bytes with the relocated fields cleared, each relocation's place, kind and target, and the symbols. Every instruction reaches it as a word except those, so the compiler writes the words of large constants and inlined functions too (arm64.encode_text encodes an instruction given as text).

Then no text at all: with AS := kod, sh_kodc _compile (what kod build runs for each module) hands each instruction to macho.Assembler.insn instead of writing it out. A word goes into the section, a call or branch becomes a fixup, a label is defined, and only data and directives are still read as lines. Compiling and assembling codegen.kod went from 348 to 298 ms, and the object has the same bytes as through the text. The Makefile keeps clang's assembler, since it runs before any compiler of this tree exists. 10. Copy-on-write checks out of loops (done). Arrays are values: before an element store, emit_unique checks that the array's count is 1 and copies it otherwise. In an innermost loop entered only at its top that calls nothing but panics, releases and the copy, no array can gain a holder (that takes a retain, a call) or be replaced where it's kept (the same), so hoist_unique_checks drops the loop's checks on an array in a local's slot the loop doesn't store to, or in a field of a struct in a register the loop doesn't write or a slot it doesn't store to, and checks once before the loop instead. Dropping a check that repeats one in straight-line code (qsort's swap) was tried and gained nothing measurable.

The same reasoning moves loads: in such a loop (with the copy's check gone too), a field and an array's header change only through a call, so hoist_loop_loads loads them once before the loop when the base doesn't change in it (or is reloaded before it from a slot the loop doesn't store to), nothing in the loop stores at that offset, the loop writes the loaded register only there, and the loop's first block reads through the base. The values then live across the loop, which only the strict allocation of promoted locals keeps apart, so the moved body is used only when that succeeds. qsort is 6% faster, compiling 1% slower; unlike step 7 it moves nothing in loops that call, and a store to the heap doesn't stop it. 11. Bounds checks out of the way (done). An index in range falls through its check (cmp; b.hs), so the common case takes no branch; the slow path (wrapping a negative index, or the panic) is a cold block laid out after the next unconditional jump, a loop's after its back edge (blocks from before a loop wait until after it). The allocator counts a cold block's lines as its check's line, and its jump back as no loop, so it keeps nothing live longer; the hoisting passes count a loop's cold blocks as part of it. qsort and sieve are 6% and 9% faster, the others about 3%. 12. Instructions without a heap object each (branch compact-insns; done). An Insn is an enum value, so each instruction is a heap cell, and branches, calls and labels hold a str. Profiled on codegen.kod, the instruction passes take about 42% of compiling; within them, counting, allocating, freeing and copying arrays of instructions take about 13% of the whole (7% promoting locals and allocating, 2% freeing the list after each function, 3.4% making the instructions). InsnBuf keeps a function's instructions as parallel arrays of numbers (a variant tag and the fields) and its labels, targets and data lines in a string table, so an instruction is a few array slots and a pass reads its fields in place. In steps, each keeping the output byte-identical (the self-hosting check compares every file) and measured: 1. InsnBuf with push of an Insn and at(i) back; codegen's buffer is one, and the passes get today's [Insn] from it at one boundary. Done: compiling codegen.kod went from 3.25 G instructions (main) to 3.68 G, 244 to 270 ms. 2. The emitting functions write the fields straight into it. Done: a push_ method per variant, settle_borrows and the loop sp fixup copy within InsnBufs (push_from), and each function goes out as soon as it is finished (the module buffer held them all, and doubling six arrays was 2.5% of a compile); its body goes from the passes' [Insn] straight to the output. 3.38 G instructions, 249 ms against main's 244 ms in the same run. 3. The passes read and rewrite InsnBufs, and the boundary goes. Done, one pass at a time in the order compile_func runs them: the peephole, the two hoists, promoting locals with forward_copies and the liveness of regalloc.run (cold_positions, extend_over_loops, vreg_counts), the frame base and long branches, and last the output (Assembler.insn, arm64.write_insn, insn_word and the word encoders read instruction i of a buffer). A pass reads the arrays directly (a kind/text method call and the string it retains cost 0.7% of a compile in the label maps alone) and compares labels as strings, as before. Converting alone didn't pay: a pass building a new InsnBuf with a put per instruction costs more than an [Insn] append, and with the boundary gone the compile was 3.41 G instructions. What made it pay: derived buffers share their input's strings, so a copy is six numbers; the peephole and forward_copies only drop and fold, so they compact the buffer they get in place; and each try of promote_locals rewrites a clone (the arrays shared until the first write copies them whole). Still Insn: codegen's cold blocks and the tail-call label fix (before the passes), the text of the rare far immediate, pair and constant lines, encode of text lines, and the tests' to_insns.

  | commit | what | G instructions |
  |---|---|---|
  | main | | 3.25 |
  | 19248e7 | step 2 | 3.38 |
  | bbd37bf | peephole | 3.45 |
  | dc754b5 | hoists | 3.49 |
  | 3b29ea5 | promote, liveness | 3.50 |
  | 24013e2 | frame base, long branches | 3.50 |
  | 7ec2470 | output: no boundary | 3.41 |
  | 43ea430 | compact in place | 3.32 |
  | 51746d1 | no accessor calls | 3.27 |
  | 9979bb8 | promote in a clone | 3.21 |

  Compiling `codegen.kod` (self-built compiler, `hyperfine -N -w 3 -r
  30`): main 239.4 ms, step 2 246.6 ms, step 3 225.4 ms, 6% faster than
  main and 1.5–2% fewer instructions; less than the 8–10% the plan
  expected, because copying a buffer's fields in Kod code costs about what
  the heap objects did. What's left is copying where a pass inserts
  (`settle_borrows`, the hoists, the frame base) and compacting
  (`move_from`, about 2%), and the emitters' `put`.
  1. Loads made once (branch load-reuse; done). qsort's swap (let t = self.xs[i]; self.xs[i] = self.xs[j]; self.xs[j] = t) loaded self.xs, its length and its buffer again for each access, and checked twice that the array was its field's own. Hand-edited, the swap ran 2.6% faster with those loads made once within it, 5.3% with the second check gone too, and 8.4% reusing the header, length and buffer the scan loop before it had loaded.

regalloc.reuse_loads walks a function's body once, in layout order, while it is still in vregs (after the hoists, before promoting locals, so a value reused is only a vreg that lives longer), numbering values: a vreg gets a value number where it is written and keeps it while nothing writes it; a copy and an add of 0 keep their source's; an add of a constant is its base plus an offset; a slot's load is the value last stored to or loaded from the slot, so self loaded twice is one base. A load is known by its address (the base's number and offset, or for an element [buf, idx, lsl #k] the base's and the index's numbers) and width. One whose value a vreg still holds becomes a mov from it.

What may change memory forgets what it may have changed: - a store through an index (an element of an array, str or bytes: codegen writes those only that way, into buffers apart from any header or field) forgets the elements; - any other store forgets every load but the frame slots'; - a store to a slot forgets that slot; a slot's own facts stay across everything else, unless the function takes an address in its frame (other than a copy-on-write check's place), when every store and call forgets the slots too; - a call forgets every load but the slots', except the retain stub, which writes only a count word (it forgets loads at negative offsets and of 4 bytes), and a panic, which doesn't come back. A release can free anything, and the copy-on-write stubs replace the array in its place, so both forget every load.

Where ways meet, what is known is what all of them know, and a vreg written on any of them since the first branched (looked back over at most 512 writes) gets a new number. A label no branch goes to (Lline$) is no join. Branches back to a label are of two kinds: - from a block laid out further on that only branches before the label reach and nothing falls into (a bounds check's cold block, which only wraps the index): the state its branch had, less what the block writes, meets the rest; - a loop's: when nothing outside the stretch from the label to its last backward branch (and the blocks after it that only it reaches and that end in a panic) branches into it, what the stretch writes, stores or calls is forgotten at the label, and the rest goes into the loop. Anything else (a label whose address is taken, a directive amid the code) forgets everything.

The copy-on-write check (ldr h, [p], the count's load, cmp #1, b.eq L, the stub, mov h, x17, L:) is a join of its own: after L, either way, [p] holds h, and an array's count is 1. A later check of the same array, with nothing between that could give it a holder (a call, a retain) or put another array in the place (a store), goes, so the stores after it reuse the header and buffer the first one left. (A value struct's check doesn't learn the count: its stub leaves a constant struct as it is.)

It runs only on functions that change an array in place (that have such a check). On every function, it found a load to reuse in about one line of 300 of the compiler's own code, made the compiler no faster, and cost 9% of compiling codegen.kod; 32 of its 889 functions have a check. The rewritten body is used only when promoting locals succeeds with it: the strict allocation keeps the longer-lived vregs apart, and the loose one, which counts on the emitter's own register discipline, can't.

t in the swap stayed in its frame slot: promoted, it is a callee-saved vreg no call crosses, so the allocator gave it the caller-saved class, and with those all taken dropped it. Now such a vreg takes a free callee-saved register first.

qsort, CPU cycles (least of 20 runs, the machine being busy; 911 M cycles is about 227 ms):

M cycles main 911 the allocator's fallback alone 906 −0.6% reusing loads alone 859 −5.7% both 837 −8.2% hand-edited (above) 838 C -O2 644 −29%

words, trees, sieve, loop and fib compile to the same code. Compiling codegen.kod (self-built compiler): 3.18 G instructions on main, 3.20 G (+0.8%); 831 M cycles, 837 M (+0.75%); 226.2 ms, 227.4 ms. 14. Then, as needed: an x86-64 lowering (see the parked assessment: register pools, calling convention, runtime stubs, symbol names).

items.title: Open questions
items.text:
• Calls: today codegen moves arguments into x0–x7 itself. Roles cover that while a target has at least as many argument registers as a call needs; x86-64 has six. A Call(target, args) with the arguments as operands would let lowering place them, at the price of touching every call site.
  • Data: string literals, vtables, line tables and the symbol table are emitted as directives through the same buffer. They need their own representation once text goes.

items.title: JSON
items.text: stdlib/json.kod parses and emits JSON, strictly as RFC 8259 defines it.

items.title: Quick example
items.text:
import "json"

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let v = try json.parse("{\"name\": \"kod\", \"tags\": [1, 2.5, \"\\u00e9\"]}")
    let name = v.get("name").as_str()
    print(name? or "?")                       // kod
    print(v.emit())                           // {"name":"kod","tags":[1,2.5,"é"]}
    print(v.emit_pretty())
    return 0
}

items.title: Parsing
items.text:
func parse(anon src: str, max_depth: int64 = 512) -> Value or Error

Malformed input is an error you can handle, never a panic. The error is a JsonError, which carries where it went wrong:

type JsonError = struct {
    message: str     // "unexpected character", "unterminated string", ...
    offset: int64    // byte offset in the input
    line: int64      // 1-based
    column: int64    // 1-based, in bytes
}

Its to_str reads json: unexpected character at line 2, column 7. Recover it with a downcast (e is JsonError(je), see Types).

What the parser accepts is exactly JSON text: one value, with optional whitespace (space, tab, newline, carriage return) around it. It rejects, with an error saying what and where:

  • an empty input, text after the value, and a missing or doubled comma, colon or bracket;
  • trailing commas, comments, single quotes, unquoted keys, NaN, Infinity and a leading +;
  • numbers like 01, -, 1., .5, 1e and 0x10;
  • a raw control character (below U+0020) inside a string;
  • an escape other than \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \uXXXX;
  • a \u escape that isn't four hex digits, and an unpaired surrogate (\ud800 not followed by \udc00..\udfff, or a lone low surrogate);
  • nesting deeper than max_depth, which stops [[[[... from exhausting the stack. Depth counts the arrays and objects around a value, so max_depth: 1 allows [1] and not [[1]].

A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start is skipped. Bytes of 0x80 and up inside strings are taken as they are: the parser doesn't check that they are valid UTF-8.

items.title: The Value type
items.text:
type Value = enum {
    Null
    Bool(value: bool)
    Number(value: int64)
    Str(value: str)
    Array(items: [Value])
    Object(keys: [str], values: [Value])
    Decimal(text: str)
}

An integer that fits in int64 is a Number (-0 is Number(0)). Any other number is a Decimal: one with a fraction or an exponent (2.5, 1e3, -0.0), or an integer too large for int64. A Decimal keeps the number's text exactly as it was written, so nothing is rounded and it is written back unchanged. Read it as a float64 with parse_float on as_number_text(), and build one with to_str. \uXXXX escapes are decoded into UTF-8, with a surrogate pair giving one four-byte character, and \u0000 gives a NUL byte inside the str.

Object entries are stored as parallel arrays (keys[i] is the key of values[i]), in the order they were written. A repeated key is kept, and get finds the first. Objects parsed one after another with the same keys share one keys array.

items.title: Accessors
items.text:
Methods on Value. None of them can fail: they return Null or none when the value isn't what you asked for, so v.get("a").get("b") is safe on any input.

Method Returns v.get(key) the first value of that key in an object; Null if the key is missing or v isn't an object v.at(index) the element of an array; Null if out of range or v isn't an array v.as_str() str?, for a Str v.as_int() int64?, for a Number (a Decimal is none, even 3.0) v.as_bool() bool?, for a Bool v.as_array() [Value]?, for an Array v.as_number_text() str?, the text of a Number or a Decimal v.is_null() bool

items.title: Building values
items.text:
Constructing a Value by hand means .Object(keys: [...], values: [...]) with two arrays that must stay in step. Two builders do the bookkeeping:

let body = json.ObjectBuilder()
body.put_str("title", "a bug")
body.put_int("priority", 2)
body.put_bool("urgent", false)
body.put("labels", json.array_of([.Str(value: "bug"), .Str(value: "ui")]))
let text = body.build().emit()
// {"title":"a bug","priority":2,"urgent":false,"labels":["bug","ui"]}
Method Meaning put(key, value) add an entry with any Value; entries keep the order they were added in, and a repeated key is added again put_str(key, s), put_int(key, n), put_bool(key, b), put_null(key) the same for the common cases build() -> Value the Object; the builder can go on being used

array_of(items: Items) -> Value makes an Array from a [Value]; str_value(s), int_value(n) and bool_value(b) make the scalar Values, for building those arrays.

items.title: Emitting
items.text:
func emit(self) -> str
func emit_pretty(self, indent: int64 = 2) -> str

Both are methods on Value: v.emit(), v.emit_pretty(indent: 4).

emit writes compact JSON with no spaces. emit_pretty puts each array element and object entry on its own line, indented by indent spaces per level, with ": " after a key; an empty array or object is [] or {}, and there is no newline at the end. Both write strings with \", \\, \b, \f, \n, \r, \t and \u00XX for any other control character, and leave everything else, UTF-8 included, as it is. The text of a Decimal is written verbatim; a Decimal built by hand whose text isn't a JSON number is written as null, so the output is always valid JSON.

Emitting what parse(s) returns gives the same JSON as s, except for the whitespace, the choice of escapes in strings, and -0 written as 0.

items.title: Key-value store
items.text:
stdlib/kv.kod keeps a map from str keys to bytes values in a directory, so that it survives the program, and a crash or a power cut: once put or remove has returned, the change is on the disk.

import "kv"

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let db = try kv.open("settings")
    try db.put("colour", kod_str_to_bytes("blue"))
    if db.get("colour") is bytes(value) {
        print(str(value))
    }
    try db.remove("colour")
    try db.close()
    return 0
}
Call Does kv.open(dir) opens the store in dir, making the directory if it isn't there (its parent must be); kv.Store or Error db.get(key) the value, or none; bytes? db.put(key, value) sets key to value, and returns once that is on the disk; none or Error db.remove(key) removes key, if it is there, and returns once that is on the disk; none or Error db.keys() the keys, sorted; [str] db.len() how many keys there are db.compact() writes what the store holds afresh, dropping the changes that led to it; none or Error db.close() closes its files; none or Error db.syncs how many times the store has synced its log, for measuring

Everything the store holds is in memory as well: get doesn't read the disk. It is for what fits in memory many times over, such as settings, sessions or an index, not for a large data set.

items.title: What is kept
items.text:
• What returned is kept. put and remove write the change to the end of a log and sync it before they return. A crash after that, the machine's included, leaves it there.
  • What didn't return may be kept or not. A change that was being written when the crash came is there after it, or isn't: never half of it.
  • A disk that fails stops the store. When a write or a sync fails, the change may or may not reach the disk, and after a failed sync the system may have given up on what it was to write (Disk faults). So the store doesn't try again: that call, and every later one that changes it, fails with the error, while get and keys go on answering from memory. Opening the store again reads what is on the disk. A full disk (StorageFull) is the exception: the change is undone, nothing else is lost, and the store goes on, so that a program can make room and try again.

Tasks can share a store: changes go to the log in the order they were asked for, and get sees each once its put has returned (not before: until then it may not be on the disk).

items.title: Many writers
items.text:
A sync takes milliseconds (on a Mac's SSD, about 4), and the program waits for it, every task included, so one sync for each change would hold a store to a few hundred changes a second however many tasks make them. Instead, changes that tasks make at the same time share a sync: a task whose change needs one lets the others that are ready write theirs to the log first, then syncs once for them all, and each of them returns once the sync has covered its own change. One task alone syncs once for each change, as before.

512 puts to a store in build/, on a Mac's SSD:

Tasks putting One sync per change Shared syncs 1 248 a second 245 a second 8 236 1,706 64 249 10,039

items.title: On the disk
items.text:
The directory holds two files:

  • log: the changes since the last compact, one record each: its length and a CRC-32 of the rest (4 bytes each, little-endian), then a byte for the kind (1 put, 2 remove), the key's length (4 bytes), the key and the value.
  • snapshot: what the store held at the last compact, as a record for each key, written the same way.

open reads the snapshot and then the log, each record changing what the one before left. It stops at the first record that is cut short or whose CRC is wrong, which only a crash in the middle of writing it leaves, at the end; that tail is cut off, and new records go right after the last good one.

compact writes the snapshot to snapshot.new, syncs it, renames it over snapshot, syncs the directory, and empties the log. A crash before the rename leaves the old snapshot and the log; after it, the new one and a log whose changes it already holds, or the end of such a log after a new record: either way the old records change nothing when read again, since each key's last record among them is what the snapshot holds. compact runs by itself when the log has grown to four times the size of what the store holds, and to at least a megabyte.

items.title: Tested by crashing it
items.text: stdlib/kv_test.kod runs a store under a simulation with crashes and disk faults: four tasks make changes the seed picks, noting each that returned, while compaction runs now and then; after the crash, the store has to hold every change that returned, and at most the one that hadn't (each task's one in the middle). Over 500 seeds, none fails; with the log's sync left out, 150 do; with the directory's sync after the snapshot's rename left out, 109; and with a failed sync tried again instead of stopping the store, 8. Of the mistakes shared syncs invite, 26 seeds find a task that returns once any sync has run, even one that began before its change was written, and 23 a compact that empties the log before syncing what is in it.

items.title: A service
items.text:
examples/kv_service/ serves a store over HTTP: service.kod has the routes, kv_service.kod the program.

kod run examples/kv_service/kv_service.kod data 8080
curl -X PUT --data blue http://127.0.0.1:8080/keys/colour
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/keys/colour
Request Answer GET /keys the keys, one a line GET /keys/{key} the value, or 404 PUT /keys/{key} sets it to the body: 200 once it is on the disk DELETE /keys/{key} removes it: 200 once that is on the disk

A full disk is a 507, and a store stopped by a failing disk a 503; a change answered either may or may not have been kept.

service_test.kod runs it under a simulation: the service and three clients over the simulated network, a crash and disk faults as the seed picks, then a restart that checks every change a client was answered 200 for. None of 200 seeds fails. A service that answered 200 whatever the store said fails under 60 of them, and one that answered before the change was synced (doing the put in a task of its own) under 64.

items.title: Memory Layout
items.text: This document describes how Kod values are represented in memory at runtime.

items.title: Primitive types
items.text:
Primitive values are stored directly — on the stack in local variables, or passed by value in registers.

Type Width Representation int64 8 Two's-complement 64-bit int float64 8 IEEE 754 binary64 bit pattern, in an integer slot str 8 Pointer to { buf, len }: buf points at the bytes (NUL after them), len counts them bool 1 0 (false) or 1 (true) none 8 Always 0 (null sentinel)

items.title: Struct values
items.text:
Struct variables are reference types: the variable holds an 8-byte pointer to the struct's data, which lives on the heap.

stack slot (8 bytes)          heap memory
┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐
│   pointer ───┼─────────────▶│   field 0    │  offset 0
└──────────────┘              │   field 1    │  offset 8
                              │   ...        │
                              └──────────────┘

Fields are laid out sequentially in declaration order, each at its natural alignment. The total allocation size (data_width) is the sum of all field widths.

items.title: Example: Point
items.text:
type Point = struct {
    x: int64    // offset 0, width 8
    y: int64    // offset 8, width 8
}
  • data_width = 16 (allocated on the heap)
  • width = 8 (size of the pointer stored in a stack slot)

items.title: Reference semantics
items.text:
Assigning a struct variable copies the pointer, not the data:

let p = Point(x: 3, y: 4)
let q: Point = p        // q and p point to the same object
q.x = 10               // also modifies p.x

The same holds for any expression that yields a struct, such as a call, a match expression, x? or fallback or try f(): the binding stores the pointer the expression produced.

items.title: Arrays of small structs
items.text:
An array whose elements are a plain struct or a tuple of two to four fields, each an int64, a float64, a bool or an enum whose variants carry nothing, keeps each element's fields in its own buffer, one after another, instead of a pointer to a cell per element. A [(int64, int64)] element is 16 bytes in the array and nothing else; a Map or Set keeps its keys in an array, so finding a key reads the fields where they are instead of following a pointer.

[(1, 2), (3, 4)]     buffer:  1 | 2 | 3 | 4        (8 bytes each)

Reading a field (xs[i].x), comparing or hashing an element, storing one, and appending one from another such array (ys += [xs[i]]) work on the fields in place, and xs += [Cell(x: 1, y: 2)] or ts += [(a, b)] builds the new element's fields in the function's frame and copies them onto the end. Reading an element whole, to pass it to a function or keep it, makes a cell holding a copy of it. Inside a loop each such read and each for x in xs keeps one cell, used again on the next pass unless something kept the last one, so a loop over the elements allocates nothing in the usual case. A struct with a mut self method still has it: the method changes a copy, which goes back into the array when it returns.

A struct with a field of another kind, a shared struct, or one with an op_index_set method is kept as a pointer, as before.

items.title: Enum values
items.text:
Enums are heap-allocated, like structs. A stack slot holds an 8-byte pointer; the cell at the pointer is:

[offset 0]  discriminant : int64  (variant index starting from 1)
[offset 8]  payload      : max(variant payload sizes) bytes

Because enum variables are pointers, they fit in a single register and pass through the ARM64 calling convention without any multi-word ABI gymnastics.

A variant without a payload has one cell per module, in the module's data, with its discriminant and zeroes for the payload: .Up or TokenKind.EOF is the address of that cell, so making one allocates nothing. The cell is outside the counted heap, so counting it does nothing either, and it is never freed. An enum none of whose variants has a payload has no other values, so the compiler doesn't count them at all.

See docs/enums.md for details.

items.title: Union values
items.text: A union is an enum the compiler writes, with one variant per member, so its value is a pointer to a cell of the same shape: the discriminant says which member it holds, and the payload is that member's 8-byte value. Members are numbered in a fixed order worked out from the types themselves, so a union is laid out the same in every module however it's spelled. A struct, enum or other reference held in a union is a pointer to its own cell, so it costs a second allocation. A T | none is a T? with an optional's layout; the optional of a larger union is an optional cell holding a pointer to a union cell.

items.title: Reclaiming memory
items.text:
Kod counts references. Every struct, enum value, optional cell, interface cell, array and computed string has a count, and it is freed when the count reaches 0, as are the references it held. A program does nothing to make this happen: there is no free, no scope to declare and no collector that pauses it, and a server that handles requests for days stays the size its live data needs.

A cycle is never freed. Two values that refer to each other keep each other alive after the last outside reference is gone:

A value can't refer to itself, so only shared structs (see Structs) make one:

type Node = shared struct {
    name: str
    other: Node?
}

let a = Node(name: "a", other: none)
let b = Node(name: "b", other: a)
a.other = b  // a and b now live until the program exits

A closure makes a cycle easy to write without seeing it: a closure stored in a struct it captures keeps that struct alive, as in req.on_done = func() { req.count += 1 }. That costs nothing for something that lives as long as the program, and leaks once per req for something made per request.

Make the back reference a weak field and the cycle doesn't form: a weak field doesn't keep its value alive, and reads as none once the value is freed.

type Node = shared struct {
    name: str
    weak other: Node?
}

Otherwise break the cycle when you are done with it (a.other = none), or keep the back reference as an index or a key instead of a struct. A closure's captures can't be weak. Most data, including all of the compiler's, has no cycles.

A weak field holds a small counted box with the value's address, made the first time anything refers to that value weakly and shared by every weak field that does; freeing the value empties the box. A value nothing refers to weakly costs nothing extra.
