Memory that has been freed is used again for new values but isn't returned to the OS, so a program stays as big as it has ever been. There are no threads, so counts aren't atomic.

items.title: The heap
items.text:
Counted objects live in one reserved address range of 64 GB (stdlib/rc.c), so whether a pointer is counted is a check on its address, and string literals and vtables need no count. A program that fills the range stops with rc: the counted heap is full.

The 8 bytes before an object hold its header:

[offset -8]  count      : 32 bits
[offset -4]  size class :  8 bits
[offset -3]  slot mask  : 24 bits
[offset  0]  the object

Bits 0 to 20 of the mask say which 8-byte slots of the object hold references, which is what freeing follows. Bit 21 marks an array whose elements are references, bit 22 an array, and bit 23 an object with references past slot 20, whose block ends in a pointer to a descriptor of them in the data section.

A block comes from the free list of its size class, or else from the end of the used part of the range. Classes go up in steps of 16 bytes to 1 KB and in powers of two after that.

items.title: What generated code does
items.text:
• A call returns a reference its caller owns. A value a statement computes and doesn't keep is released when the statement ends.
  • A store into a variable, field or element retains the new value and releases the old one. When the value is fresh the store takes the reference over instead.
  • A function borrows its parameters: a parameter costs nothing unless the body assigns to it. So that what it borrows can't go away, a caller holds a value it read from a field or element for the length of the statement.
  • A pattern borrows what it binds from an enum's payload when the subject is a variable the function never assigns to: the subject keeps the payload alive for as long as the binding can be used. A binding that shares its slot with one the function owns (the same name bound another way, or assigned to) is owned too.
  • for x in xs borrows each element: the loop holds the array, so x costs nothing unless the function assigns to it, or its slot is owned for the same reasons as a pattern's binding.
  • A function releases its variables when it returns, except that a let or mut local holding an array or a struct that isn't shared (a map or set too) is released after the last statement of its block that uses it; a use inside a loop or a nested block counts for the whole statement. What it shared is then the other holder's alone, and changing it doesn't copy it. A local that a function literal captures, or that a let-else binding borrows from, lives as long as that does.

retain and release are calls with the object in x17, to _rc_retain_stub and _rc_release_stub. They change only x16, x17 and lr, and no flags, until an object is freed, and freeing saves the rest, so they can sit anywhere in an expression.

Every reference a function owns is in a slot of its frame, 0 while it holds nothing, whenever the function calls anything that may panic. So when a catch takes a panic, each function between is let go of by releasing its slots, which a row of the __DATA,__kod_unwind section lists (emit_unwind_row in codegen.kod, kod_unwind in runtime.c). A mut parameter's slot is put back into the caller's instead, and a map entry that was being changed back into its map.

items.title: Function values
items.text:
A function value is a reference to a cell whose first word is the address of the code. A named function or a literal that captures nothing has one such cell in the data section, written only if the function is used as a value, and using it never allocates. A literal that captures allocates a counted cell each time it's evaluated, with the captured values after the code address:

closure cell:  [code, capture 0, capture 1, ...]

A call through a function value is ldr x16, [f]; mov x17, f; blr x16, so a function reached that way finds its cell in x17. One that captures copies the values into its frame on entry and borrows them, like parameters, since its caller keeps the cell alive for the call. A local function also keeps x17 itself as the value of its own name, so a call to itself passes the same cell on. Other functions ignore x17.

A mut that a literal captures is kept in a counted one-word struct from its declaration on (_MutCell[T] in builtins.kod). The function's slot and each closure that captures it hold a reference to the struct, and a read or an assignment loads or stores its word. The parser makes the change, so codegen sees an ordinary let of a struct and n.value for each use of n.

items.title: Testing for mistakes
items.text:
To test the rules themselves, build the runtime so that freed memory is overwritten and never used again, by putting this in link.local.cfg and running the tests:

CFLAGS := -target arm64-apple-darwin -I stdlib -O2 -DRC_POISON

A use after free then shows as wrong output or a crash. -DRC_STATS adds counts of allocations and frees, printed at exit when KOD_RC_STATS is set. A program can declare extern func rc_live_bytes() -> int64 to ask how much of the heap is in use.

items.title: Calling convention (ARM64, macOS)
items.text:
• Arguments: passed in x0–x7
  • Return value: in x0
  • Caller-saved: x0–x15
  • Callee-saved: x19–x28
  • Frame pointer: fp (x29)
  • Link register: lr (x30)

Since struct variables are 8-byte pointers, they fit in a single register and can be passed to and returned from functions normally.

items.title: Stack frame
items.text: A function pushes fp and lr, points fp at them and keeps each local in an 8-byte slot below fp, including the compiler's own temporaries. Values that must survive a call in the middle of an expression are pushed below those slots. The epilogue restores sp from fp, so a try that returns from inside an expression, such as an array literal element or a call argument, leaves the stack as the function found it.

items.title: Modules
items.text: Each .kod file is a module. Imports name either a file relative to the importing module or a stdlib module.

items.title: Importing
items.text:
Two forms:

import "./utils"        // relative — utils.kod next to the importing file
import "./math/vec"     // relative — math/vec.kod below the importing file's directory
import "kod/ast"        // stdlib — stdlib/kod/ast.kod
import "io"             // stdlib — stdlib/io.kod

Paths beginning with ./ resolve against the directory of the importing file, not the project root or the current directory. Anything else resolves under stdlib/.

The imported module's public names are accessible via the import alias, which is the last path component:

import "./math/vec"

func origin() -> vec.Vec2 {
    return vec.Vec2(x: 0, y: 0)
}

Qualified constructors have the imported type, so let v = vec.Vec2(x: 1, y: 2) needs no annotation before v.x. Calling a function the module doesn't declare, such as vec.lenght(v), is an error with a did-you-mean hint. No local can be named like an import alias: a let, mut, parameter, for variable or pattern binding named vec is an error, `vec` is the name of an import; give the local another name, so vec. always means the module. A function named like an import alias doesn't hide it: with func vec() declared too, vec() calls the function and vec.make(1) the module's.

To use some names unqualified instead, list them after the path:

import "./math/vec" { Vec2, dot }

func norm2(anon v: Vec2) -> int64 {
    return dot(v, v)
}

An import that lists names binds only those names, not its alias, so vec.dot is an error there (unknown name `vec`; an import that lists names binds no `vec`, so add a plain import of it to write `vec.`) and a local may be named vec. That keeps the usual way of naming a value after its module working:

import "net/http" { Client }

let client = Client()      // `client` is a local, and `http` names nothing

To have both, import the module twice: import "./math/vec" binds vec and import "./math/vec" { Vec2 } adds Vec2, and then no local can be named vec.

Each listed name must be a function, extern, constant, variable or type the module declares; otherwise it's an error with a did-you-mean hint: module `vec` has no function, constant or type `dto`; did you mean `dot`?.

items.title: Where names resolve
items.text:
Parameter defaults, struct field defaults and the method bodies of a generic type resolve function names, type names and import aliases in the module that wrote them, even though they run as part of the caller's code. A default in util.kod that calls helper() calls util's own helper, a function util imports with { helper }, or the builtin of that name, never one that belongs to the caller. Likewise rng.seed() in that default means util's own import "./rng", whether or not the caller imports a module named rng:

// util.kod
func helper() -> int64 {
    return 1
}

func f(x: int64 = helper()) -> int64 {
    return x
}

// main.kod
import "./util"

func helper() -> int64 {
    return 2
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let helper = 3          // not visible to util's default either
    print(f"{util.f()}")    // 1
    return 0
}

The same holds for a function literal or a function value used as a default (cb: func() -> int64 = helper). A name the defining module doesn't have is an error, reported at the default when a call leaves the parameter out, even when the caller happens to declare it.

A bare type name T means, in this order: a type parameter of the generic declaration around it, a primitive (int64, bool, str, bytes, none), a type the module declares (its own aliases included), a type it lists in an import (import "./pa" { Pt }), then a builtin type. A type of a module imported without listing it, or loaded only because another module imports it, is written through the module: pa.Pt. Otherwise it's an error with a hint naming the file that declares it: unknown type `Pt`; lib/pa.kod declares `Pt`: write `pa.Pt` or list it in the import (`{ Pt }`), or unknown type `Pt`; lib/pa.kod declares `Pt`: import it to use it here when the module doesn't import that file. kod finds the file anywhere in the program being built, so the hint also names a module that imports this one or that only another module imports. sh_kodc run on one file knows only that file's imports.

m.T means a type that the module imported as m declares, its own aliases included. This holds in a type, a constructor m.T(...), a type argument, m.E.V and a pattern b: m.T. Types that m only imports aren't reachable through it. Otherwise it's an error: module `m` has no type `T`, with a did-you-mean over m's types (module `m` has no function or type `T` for a call m.T(...)). When m isn't a module this one imports, the error spells what was written: unknown type `m.T`. A generic type takes its arguments the same way, as in m.Box[m.Pt](v: p), also where it is itself a type argument: Stack[m.Box[str]].

A module exports only what it declares, never what it imports. When m lists T in one of its own imports, m.T, m.f(), m.f and import "./m" { T } say where T comes from: `T` is imported by `m`, not declared there; import it from lib/b.kod. A value of such a type can still be used without naming it, as in let t = m.make(). To pass a type on deliberately, m declares an alias of it, type T = b.T (which needs a plain import "./b"), and for a function a wrapper.

A module declares each of its names once. A function, extern, struct, enum, interface or type alias with the name of an earlier one in the same module is an error at the second declaration (`f` is already declared on line 1), and so is a method, field or variant with the name of an earlier one of the same struct, interface or enum (`Kind.A` is already declared on line 2). A method can't take the name of a field of its struct either; the error is at the method (`Bag.len` is already declared on line 3).

A name an import lists counts the same way. A module can't both declare a name and list it in an import, and two imports can't list the same name, whether it names a type or a function. The later one is the error: `Pt` is already imported on line 1, or `Pt` is already declared on line 3 when the declaration comes first. Two imports can't share a name either, unless they load the same file: after import "./a/util", import "./b/util" is `util` is already imported on line 1, while a second import "./a/util" { Vec2 } only adds to the first import's list.

Each module's structs, enums, interfaces and type aliases are its own. Two modules may declare a type of the same name, and they are different types: pa.Pt and pb.Pt don't convert to each other, is pa.Pt doesn't hold for a pb.Pt, and Box[pa.Pt] and Box[pb.Pt] are different instances. Aliases of different types may share a name across modules, and an alias may take its target's name (type Pt = pb.Pt), so a module that imports only this one reaches the type as its Pt. Only the builtins may declare Map, Option, Result, Error, Stringable or ExitCode; anywhere else it's an error: `Option` is the name of a builtin type; give this type another name. A module is one module however its path is spelled: import "./lib/../lib/pa" and import "./lib/pa" load the same file once.

A message writes a type by its bare name, unless another module of the program declares a struct, enum or interface of that name too (an alias doesn't count, as a message writes the type it stands for). Then it's written the way the module being compiled would write it (pa.Pt, or Pt when the module has it under that name: declared, aliased or listed in an import), or with its file when that module can't name it (Pt (lib/pb.kod)).

items.title: Standard library
items.text:
The stdlib lives under stdlib/ in the repository.

Module Contents builtins Always imported. print, print_int, len, fail, Map[K, V], the Error / Stringable / ExitCode interfaces. primitives/int64, primitives/float64, primitives/str, primitives/bool (and int64_float, str_float, which hold to_float64 and parse_float, and float_text, which both float methods use) Methods on the primitive types (to_str, hash, parse_float). Auto-loaded; not imported directly. io read_file, write_file, and stdin/stdout/stderr helpers. fs FileSystem interface with DiskFs (real disk) and MemFs (in-memory, for tests). process process.run(argv) — spawn a subprocess and capture stdout/stderr/exit code. process.exec(argv) — replace the calling process (compiled programs only). env get, set and unset for environment variables. See Built-ins. time monotonic_ns(), unix_ns(), Duration, sleep(d), and Time with now(), parse(s) and parse_date(s). See Time. sets Set[T], a hash set built on Map: Set[str](), with add, contains, remove(x) -> bool, values() and len; for x in s goes over the elements in the order they were first added. sort sorted(xs) and sorted_by(xs, less:), stable, returning a new array. See Arrays. arrays contains(xs, x) and equal(a, b). See Arrays. json Strict JSON parse/emit, with builders. See JSON. strbuilder, bytebuffer, stream, posix StrBuilder; ByteBuffer; Reader / Writer and IoError; file descriptors. See Strings and Streams. net/tcp, net/tls, net/http TCP, TLS, and HTTP/1.1 messages with a client and a server. See Streams and HTTP. jsonrpc Content-Length framed messages on stdin/stdout, as used by LSP. encoding/base64 Base64, standard and URL-safe, strict decoding. See Encodings. hash/crc32 CRC-32 (gzip polynomial), streaming or one-shot. compress/deflate, compress/inflate Compress to and decompress from gzip, zlib and raw deflate. See Encodings. kod/ast AST node types (for the self-hosted compiler). kod/lexing Tokenizer (self-hosted). kod/parsing Parser (self-hosted). kod/codegen ARM64 code generator.

items.title: Circular imports
items.text: Circular imports work: a struct, enum or interface declared in a module of the cycle is the same type on either side, so a value of it can be passed both ways, also inside an array, an optional, a Map or another generic type's instance such as Box[Pt], and is recovers a struct from an interface value whichever side boxed it.

items.title: Visibility
items.text:
Top-level functions, externs, constants and types are visible to importing modules, except those whose name starts with _. Those are private to the module that declares them, which uses them like any other name:

// lib.kod
let _LIMIT: int64 = 3

type _Slot = struct {
    n: int64
}

func _clamp(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n > _LIMIT {
        return _LIMIT
    }
    return n
}

func slots(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    return _Slot(n: _clamp(n)).n
}

// main.kod
import "./lib"

func main() -> int64 {
    print_int(lib.slots(5))     // 3
    lib._clamp(5)               // error: `_clamp` is private to module `lib`
    return 0
}

The same error is reported for lib._LIMIT, lib._Slot(...), lib._Slot in a type, and _clamp in an import list (import "./lib" { _clamp }). Did-you-mean hints never suggest another module's private names.

A private name keeps a helper out of the module's interface, so the module can change or remove it without breaking its importers. A public function may still take or return a private type: callers can use such a value, its fields and its methods, but can't write the type's name. Fields and methods whose names start with _ are private to their struct; see Structs.

A module's top level holds declarations (func, type, interface, import, extern and test) constants (let NAME: T = value, see Module-level constants) and variables (mut NAME: T = value, see Module-level variables). Any statement there is an error. Constants and variables are visible to importing modules like functions, and only the declaring module assigns a variable.

items.title: Symbol and object names
items.text:
A module is identified by its normalized path: ./x and ./a/../x are one module, while x (the file under stdlib/) and ./x (the project's own) are two. Everything a module emits (functions, types, tests) is labelled $<prefix>$<name>. The prefix is computed from the path and from whether stdlib/<path>.kod exists (step 5):

  1. Drop the .kod extension, and the leading / of an absolute path.
  2. A path under stdlib/ drops that directory: stdlib/io.kod is io, stdlib/kod/ast.kod is kod$ast.
  3. Each remaining byte becomes symbol characters. / becomes $. Letters, digits and _ stay. . stays, except as the first byte. Every other byte (space, -, +, @, $, each byte of a non-ASCII character) becomes $$ followed by its two lowercase hex digits: my-app is my$$2dapp.
  4. The label is $<prefix>$<name>, and the assembler reads $ followed by a digit as a number, and takes no $$name at all, so a prefix is never empty and never starts with $ or a digit. If it would, a . is put in front: -x is .$$2dx, 01_hello is .01_hello, 2024/report is .2024$report, and a file named .kod is .. (A digit after an inner $ is fine: tests/3d is tests$3d.) The assembler also reads . and digits followed by e or E as a number (.1e5), so then that letter is written $$65 or $$45 as well: 1e5 is .1$$655, 2East/lib is .2$$45ast$lib.
  5. A module outside stdlib/ whose path also exists under stdlib/ is in the namespace .user$: a project's io.kod is .user$io and does not clash with the stdlib io. The check is a file test, so on a case-insensitive volume a project's Io.kod also gets the marker; that is harmless, because every project module is recompiled for each program.

Two different normalized paths never get the same prefix: a prefix's own leading . is always escaped by step 3, so a raw leading . comes only from step 4, the marker .user$ starts .u, which step 4 never produces, and $$65 and $$45 are escapes that step 3 never writes (it keeps letters). (An absolute path and the relative path with the same components still collide, as before.)

A vtable and a type's identity word are shared between objects by label, so their labels have to differ for different types as well: the parts of those labels are joined with $$for$, $$of$ and the like, which step 3 never writes (a $$ it writes has two hex digits after it). is and interface calls therefore can't mix up two types, whatever their paths are called. A method's label joins its type and name the same way, $<prefix>$<Type>$$m$<name>, so T.m in x.kod and a function m in x/T.kod are two symbols, not one defined twice.

kod build writes a program's objects under build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/, mirroring the source tree: stdlib/json.kod becomes <stem>.obj/stdlib/json.kod.o, a project's lib/json.kod becomes <stem>.obj/lib/json.kod.o. The compiler writes the object itself; its assembly, .s, sits beside the .o only when asked for (KOD_ASM_TEXT, see self-hosting). A .. directory is written %2e%2e (a . one %2e), the root of an absolute path %2f, and a literal % in a name %25. The _main shim is <stem>.obj/<entry>.main.{s,o} (<stem>.obj/<first entry>.testmain.{s,o} for tests). The executable is build/apps/<stem>/<stem>, or <stem>_test for kod test; <stem>.obj can equal neither. <stem> is the entry's file name without .kod; for kod test <dir> it is the directory with every byte outside letters, digits, _ and - replaced by _ (its last 200 bytes, when it is longer), then _tests. A file whose name without .kod is empty, . or .. (.kod, ..kod, ...kod) has no program name and is refused. An entry named kod or lsp (other than tools/kod.kod and tools/lsp.kod, however they are spelled) is refused, because its executable would replace the tool. So is one whose directory the volume takes for the tool's, such as KOD on a case-insensitive volume.

The object path has to fit the file system as well: a file name of more than about 240 bytes (the shim adds .kod.main.s), or an absolute entry path of more than about 950 bytes (build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/%2f/ goes in front of it), is too long, and the build stops with a message that a file could not be opened or a directory made.

kod test <dir> builds every *_test.kod below <dir> into one program, except a file with a path component below <dir> that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files, the scratch .kod_compile_test.kod) and a build directory directly below <dir>. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.

items.title: Link inputs
items.text:
A module that needs C code or a system library says so in the comment lines at the top of its file, before its first declaration:

// kod:require ${OPENSSL}/include/openssl/ssl.h  brew install openssl@3
// kod:cc tls.c -I${OPENSSL}/include
// kod:link -L${OPENSSL}/lib -lssl -lcrypto

import "io"
  • kod:cc <file.c> [flags...]: a C file beside the module. kod build compiles it with CC and CFLAGS of link.cfg followed by the flags given, and links the object. Flags are passed as written; a relative -I is relative to the repository root, where kod runs. The file is compiled on every build, like the modules, so an edit to it, to a header it includes or to CC and CFLAGS is picked up by the next one. A C file that several modules of a program name (or several test files of one kod test <dir>) is compiled and linked once; naming it with different flags is an error.
  • kod:link <args...>: arguments for the final link, after all objects: -lz, -L..., -framework Security, a path to a .a. They are passed in the order the modules appear in the program, and a -lname that comes up again is passed once.
  • kod:require <file> [hint...]: the file (a path from the repository root, or an absolute one) must exist before anything is compiled; otherwise the build stops with path:line:1: error: needs <file> (<hint>) (needs <file> when there is no hint), for each such file, naming the line of the directive. Use it for a file outside the repository that the other lines rely on, so that a machine without it gets the hint instead of 'openssl/err.h' file not found.

${NAME} in a word is replaced by the value of NAME in link.cfg, or in link.local.cfg when that overrides it (the example assumes link.cfg has an OPENSSL line). A name that neither file sets, or one whose value is not exactly one word, is an error, and so is a $ that does not start ${NAME}. Words are separated by spaces; there is no quoting, and a tab or another control character in a directive line is an error.

Only the leading block counts: the lines from the top of the file that are blank or start with //, up to the first other line. In it a line that starts with // kod: (after any indent) is a directive, and any other comment line is just a comment; a // kod: line further down is a comment too and does nothing. A line in the block that is spelled like a directive but not so (//kod:cc x.c, // kod:cc x.c, // Kod:cc x.c, // kod :cc x.c) is an error, so that a slip is not taken for a comment. A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the file is skipped, as the compiler skips it. Put a blank line after the block, or the first declaration takes it as its doc comment (shown on hover).

These are errors, path:line:1: error: ..., from kod build, kod run, kod test and kod check: an unknown directive (unknown directive kod:linkk), a directive spelled almost right, a tab in a directive line, a directive without its argument, a kod:cc that does not name a .c file beside the module (a bare file name ending in .c, which has to exist), and a ${NAME} that cannot be replaced. kod check validates the lines, and that the C file is there, but it does not test kod:require and compiles no C.

Only a program that imports the module compiles its C file or passes its arguments, and that includes a module that only a test file imports: kod test reads the lines of every module of its program, and kod test <dir> builds all its files into one program, so one test file's missing kod:require file stops them all. A program that imports no such module compiles no C file. A C file's object is <stem>.obj/<path>.c.o in the tree of Symbol and object names, next to the module's own <path>.kod.o. If the C compiler fails, kod shows its output and kod: compiling <file> failed, exits 1 and links nothing.

A module that declares link inputs cannot be one that the Makefile builds: it does not read their lines. That is a module listed in STAGE0_KOD of link.cfg, one of the compiler's own modules (COMPILER_KOD in the Makefile) and kodc.kod and tools/kod.kod. For a STAGE0_KOD module the driver says so (path:line:1: error: ...) and stops, rather than leave the lines unread; for the others a test of the repository checks that there are none.

C files export bare symbols into one namespace shared with libc and runtime.c: name them kod_<module>_.... #include "kod_rt.h" (CFLAGS has -I stdlib) declares what they need of the runtime:

  • KodStr: what a Kod str is when it crosses into C. buf points at len bytes followed by a NUL byte, and a str parameter or result is a KodStr *.
  • KodArray: a Kod [T]: ptr points at len elements of 8 bytes each (one byte each for a [bool]), with room for cap.
  • arena_alloc(size): memory that is never freed.
  • rc_alloc(size, mask): a counted object, zeroed, with a count of 1 that the caller owns. mask says which of its 8-byte slots hold references, bit 0 for the first; it must not use bits past 20. rc_alloc_raw is the same but leaves filling it to the caller. rc_retain_c(p) and rc_release_c(p) count a reference up and down, and do nothing for memory outside the counted heap.
  • kod_str_new(len): a new str of len bytes for the caller to fill in. kod_str_from_bytes(p, n): a str that is a copy of n bytes at p, which may contain NUL bytes.
  • panic(msg): print panic: and the message with a backtrace, and exit 1, or go to the catch that takes it; either way it doesn't come back.

A function value isn't a C function pointer, so an extern can't take or return one: an `extern` can't take or return a function value. To give C a function to call back, pass the address unsafe.c_function(f) gives as an int64.

Kod values are reference counted, and C code follows the same rules as generated code. A parameter is borrowed: it stays alive during the call, and C code that keeps it after returning calls rc_retain_c. A result is owned by the caller, which releases it, so returning anything other than a new object, such as a parameter or something kept in a static, takes an rc_retain_c first. The same goes for references written into an object: each one needs its own count.

items.title: Panics
items.text:
A panic is how a program stops at a bug: an index out of range, a division by zero, a failed must or assert, a key that isn't in a map, a call of panic(msg). It prints the message and a backtrace to stderr and the program exits with status 1.

Errors a program expects (a file that isn't there, input that doesn't parse) are values of type T or Error, not panics: see Error handling.

items.title: Catching a panic
items.text:
A program that does many independent pieces of work, such as a server answering requests, can keep one piece's bug from ending the others. The panics module runs a function and catches a panic in it:

let p = panics.run(func() {
    let xs = [1, 2, 3]
    print(xs[5])
})
if p is panics.Panic(caught) {
    print(caught.message)      // index 5 out of bounds for array of length 3
    kod_eprint(caught.backtrace)
}
panics.run(body) -> Panic? calls body, a func() -> none: the panic that stopped it, or none panics.catch(body) -> T or Error calls body, a func() -> T or Error: what it gave back, or the Panic that stopped it, as the error panics.again(p) panics with p's message; its backtrace is p's

A Panic is an error with these fields:

message: str what would have followed panic: backtrace: str the lines that would have followed it, backtrace: first, down to the catch

Nothing is printed for a panic that is caught: the code that caught it decides.

match panics.catch(func() -> str or Error { return try answer(0) }) {
    Err(panics.Panic(p)) -> kod_eprint(f"answer panicked: {p.message}\n{p.backtrace}")
    Ok(text) -> print(text)
    Err(e) -> print(e.to_str())
}

A run or catch can be inside another: the innermost one running takes the panic.

items.title: What is undone
items.text:
The functions between the panic and the catch don't go on. What they held is let go of, as when they return: their variables and the values they were working on are freed, and the tasks they spawned are cancelled and waited for. A mut parameter keeps what it was last changed to, and a module-level variable whose initializer panicked is worked out again at its next use.

Nothing else is undone:

  • What they had already changed in values that outlive them (a shared struct's fields, module variables, variables the body captured) stays changed, so a change made in several steps may be half made.
  • A file, socket or child process one of them had open stays open, and a tasks.Mutex one held stays locked. Open what must be closed outside the catch.

items.title: Tasks
items.text:
A task belongs to the function that spawned it, and so does its panic. When that function runs under a catch, a panic in its task doesn't end the program: it panics the function, with the task's message and backtrace, at its next wait (the one it is in, if it's waiting), or when it returns, waiting for its tasks. The function's other tasks are cancelled, and the catch around the function takes the panic. task.wait() on a task that panicked panics too.

func sum_parts() -> int64 {
    let a = spawn part(5)
    let b = spawn part(0)          // panics
    return a.wait() + b.wait()
}

let p = panics.run(func() { print(sum_parts()) })
assert p is panics.Panic(_caught)

A generator's panic comes out where its values are received. A detached task belongs to nothing that could take its panic, so it ends the program even when the code that spawned it runs under a catch: a detached task catches its own. So does a panic in a task, or a generator, started under no catch at all.

items.title: What can't be caught
items.text:
• all tasks are asleep: deadlock.
  • A crash: a stack overflow, a full heap, or anything a wrong unsafe call or C code does.

A call from Kod through C back into Kod (a callback) is abandoned like the rest, but C's part of it holds on to whatever it held.

items.title: Cost
items.text: Code pays nothing for this while it runs: each function that can hold a reference has a list of the places in its frame that do (a program is about 2% bigger for them), read only when a panic is caught. run costs about 0.1 µs more than calling body, and a caught panic a few microseconds: the backtrace and each function given up is looked up in tables that grow with the program.

items.title: Pattern matching
items.text: Kod's match statement dispatches on a value and binds sub-parts.

items.title: Syntax
items.text:
match <expression> {
    <pattern> -> <arm-body>
    <pattern> -> {
        // multi-statement arm
    }
}

Arms are tested top-to-bottom. The first matching arm executes.

items.title: Catch-all (else)
items.text:
else matches any value the other arms didn't cover. It must be the last arm. The arrow is optional after else:

match x {
    1    -> print("one")
    2    -> print("two")
    else -> print("other")    // arrow form
}

match x {
    1 -> print("one")
    else { print("other") }   // block form
}

items.title: Integer literal
items.text:
match n {
    0    -> print("zero")
    1    -> print("one")
    -1   -> print("minus one")
    else -> print("other")
}

A - directly before the digits makes the literal negative. As in an expression, the smallest int64 is written -9223372036854775808. Only a literal can be a pattern, so -n is not one.

items.title: String literal
items.text:
match s {
    "hello" -> print("greeting")
    "bye"   -> print("farewell")
    else    -> print("unknown")
}

items.title: Bool
items.text:
match b {
    true  -> print("yes")
    false -> print("no")
}

A literal pattern needs a value of its own type, so matching a str against 3 is an error. On an optional it tests the value inside (see Optional): 3 on an int64? matches a 3 and not none.

items.title: Enum variant (explicit)
items.text:
type Color = enum {
    Red
    Green
    Blue
}

match c {
    Color.Red   -> print("red")
    Color.Green -> print("green")
    Color.Blue  -> print("blue")
}

items.title: Enum variant (implicit shorthand)
items.text:
When the type is clear from context, the enum name can be omitted:

match c {
    .Red   -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
    .Blue  -> print("blue")
}

items.title: Payload variant
items.text:
Bind the payload fields:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

match shape {
    Shape.Circle(radius) -> print_int(radius)
    Shape.Rect(w, h)     -> print_int(w * h)
}

Bindings are by position — the names in the pattern don't have to match the field names. A pattern may bind fewer names than the variant has fields, but not more, and it can't bind one name twice, though _ and _name can repeat. Naming an enum or variant that doesn't exist is an error, as is an implicit .Variant that no enum declares.

Each binding takes the type of the field it binds, so different arms can reuse a name for payloads of different types:

type Value = enum {
    I(value: int64)
    S(value: str)
}

match v {
    .I(value) -> print(f"int {value}")
    .S(value) -> print(f"str {value}")
}

items.title: Optional
items.text:
match maybe_n {
    Some(n) -> print_int(n)
    none    -> print("nothing")
}

A pattern that can't match none (a literal, a variant or a type pattern) tests the value inside, so it needs no Some. _, and a name in a payload position, match the optional itself, none included, so Some(n) is how to bind what's inside:

let color: Color? = .Red
match color {
    .Red    -> print("red")
    .Rgb(v) -> print_int(v)
    none    -> print("no color")
}

let count: int64? = 0
match count {
    0    -> print("zero")
    none -> print("unknown")
    else -> print("some")
}

The same holds inside another pattern and after is: color is .Red is false for none.

items.title: Type patterns
items.text:
A union is an enum whose variants are named by their types. T(name) matches when the value holds a T, and binds it as a T; a bare T only tests. none is the member that holds nothing, so it takes no payload:

let id: int64 | str | none = "abc"

match id {
    int64(n) if n < 0 -> print("negative")
    int64(n) -> print_int(n)
    str -> print("text")
    none -> print("nothing")
}

if id is str(s) {
    print(s)
}

On a value whose type is exactly T, T(name) always matches and binds the value, so it covers every case on its own: int64(n) on an int64, Shape(s) on a Shape, or T(x) in a generic function whatever T turns out to be. On a union, T has to be a member otherwise, or a union or optional whose members all are: on an int64 | str | bool, Id(i) with type Id = int64 | str matches an int64 or a str and binds it as an Id, and with type MaybeInt = int64?, MaybeInt(n) on an int64 | str | none matches an int64 or none. That is also what T(t) does in a generic function when T is a union or an optional. When two arms cover the same member, the first one wins. A member's type is written as it is declared, pa.Pt(p) for a type of another module; a member with no name of its own, such as [str], needs a type alias to be matched by type.

On a T or Error, a type pattern tests the value of an Ok, and Error(e) is Err(e) (see Fallible types).

On an interface, T is a struct or enum that implements it, and the pattern is a downcast, so a match still needs an else:

func describe(anon s: Shape) -> str {
    match s {
        Circle(c) if c.r > 10 -> return "big circle"
        Circle(c) -> return f"circle {c.r}"
        Square -> return "a square"
        else -> return "something else"
    }
}

An optional takes these patterns directly, like any pattern that can't match none (see Optional), whether it holds the type itself, a union or an interface. int64(n) on an int64? is Some(n), and on an int64 | str | none it is Some(int64(n)), which is also valid:

let maybe: int64 | str | none = "here"

match maybe {
    int64(n) -> print_int(n)
    str(s) -> print(s)
    none -> print("nothing")
}

The same holds inside another pattern. In a payload position a name that names a type is that type's pattern, not a binding: on a field of type int64 | str | none, .Full(str) tests and .Full(str(s)) binds, next to .Full(none). That's why a local can't take a type's name (see Bindings and mutability). An error for a missing arm spells it the same way, as doesn't cover `str`. A let-else takes it too: let str(s) = id else { return }.

items.title: Struct patterns
items.text:
A type pattern with labels matches a struct field by field: each label names a field, and what follows it is the pattern that field must match, or the name to bind it to:

type Rect = struct {
    w: int64
    h: int64
}

match shape {
    Rect(w: 0) -> print("flat")                 // tests a field
    Rect(:w, :h) -> print_int(w * h)            // `:w` binds field `w` as `w`
    Circle(radius: r) if r > 10 -> print("big") // binds field `radius` as `r`
    Circle(c) -> print_int(c.radius)            // no label: the whole value
}

if node is Node(name: "root", parent: none) {
    print("the root")
}
  • A struct pattern matches where a type pattern of its type would (on the struct's own type, or a union, interface or optional that may hold it) and then only when every field it names matches. The fields come in any order, and the ones it doesn't name are ignored.
  • What follows a label is any pattern: a name to bind, _, a literal, none, an enum variant with its payload, or another struct pattern, so Node(parent: Node(name: "root")) tests the parent's name.
  • :name is short for name: name, as in a call. A field bound to a name gives the field's value with the field's type; a weak field gives its S? as reading it would.
  • Every argument has a label: Rect(r) keeps its meaning, the whole value, and Rect(r, w: 0) is an error.
  • Naming a field the struct doesn't have, or one twice, is an error.
  • A struct pattern with a field that can fail to match doesn't cover its type for exhaustiveness, any more than an arm with a guard does; one whose fields only bind names covers it.

items.title: is test
items.text:
A lightweight check without destructuring:

if x is none {
    print("empty")
}
if x is not none {
    print("has value")
}

items.title: Narrowing
items.text:
After an if tests a name, the name has the type the test proves inside the block that runs, with no new name to bind:

func describe(anon shape: Shape, anon id: int64 | str | none) -> none {
    if shape is Circle {
        print_int(shape.r)          // a Circle here
    }
    if id is not none {
        print(f"{id is str}")       // an int64 | str here
    }
    if id is none {
        print("no id")
    } else if id is int64 {
        print_int(id + 1)           // an int64 here
    }
}

x is T, x is Some, x is Ok, x is Err and x is not none narrow the block, and the later operands of an and chain, as in if x is not none and x > 3. x is none and x is not T narrow the else block. Narrowing is a binding of the same name, as x is T(x) would make, so it applies only when:

  • x is a plain name, such as a local or a parameter, not a field or a call;
  • the type is written by its own name, not through a module: m.T doesn't narrow, so bind it, as in if e is errs.NotFound(nf);
  • the block doesn't assign to x, which then keeps its declared type there.

After the block, x has its declared type again. A for condition doesn't narrow.

An early exit narrows the rest of its block too. After an if with no else whose block ends in return, throw, break, continue or panic(...), the statements that follow in the same block run only when the test failed:

func total(anon xs: [int64?], limit: int64 or Error) -> int64 {
    if limit is Err(e) {
        print(e.to_str())
        return 0
    }
    mut sum = 0                     // limit is an int64 from here on
    for x in xs {
        if x is none {
            continue
        }
        sum += x                    // x is an int64 from here on
    }
    if sum > limit {
        return limit
    }
    return sum
}

x is none, x is Err and x is not T narrow this way, under the rules above, with the rest of the block in place of the else block. The block has to end in the exit: a return, throw, break or continue, or a call that never returns, which is panic(...) or a function or method that can't finish by the rules in return (a -> none function with no return that ends in such a call, or in a for true loop without a break):

func fail(anon msg: str) -> none {
    panic(f"config: {msg}")
}

func port(anon raw: str?) -> int64 {
    if raw is none {
        fail("no port")
    }
    return raw.parse_int()? or 80   // raw is a str from here on
}

A call through a function value or an interface value is taken to return, so it doesn't narrow, and neither does a block that ends in an if whose branches all return. When the call can return, the rest of the block sees the name as it was.

try x or must x on its own line narrows the rest of the block the same way, under the same rules: see T or Error.

items.title: Nested patterns
items.text:
A payload position can hold a pattern instead of a name. The arm matches only when every nested pattern does, and a failed test moves on to the next arm:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

match shape {
    .Rect(w, 0)     -> print(f"flat {w}")   // h must be 0, w is bound
    .Rect(_, _)     -> print("rect")
    .Circle(radius) -> print_int(radius)
}

let best: Shape? = find_best()
match best {
    Some(.Circle(r))  -> print_int(r)
    Some(.Rect(w, h)) -> print_int(w * h)
    none              -> print("nothing")
}

Patterns nest to any depth, and each kind above can appear inside another: literals, none, Some(...), Ok(...), Err(...), enum variants, and a type pattern such as .Wrap(Sq(s)) or .Wrap(Sq). In a payload position a bare name binds, unless it names a type. A nested literal needs a field of its own type.

Tests run left to right and from the outside in, and each nested pattern sees the field's type, so .Pair(Some(0), "x") needs an optional int64 and a str.

Nested patterns work wherever a pattern can bind: in a match, in an if or for condition (if best is Some(.Circle(r)) { ... }), and in a let-else (let .Some(.Circle(r)) = best else { return }). Elsewhere is is only a test, and a nested pattern is an error: use a match, or an if of its own.

items.title: Guards
items.text:
An arm's pattern can be followed by if and a condition. The arm runs only when the pattern matches and the condition is true; otherwise the next arm is tried. The pattern's bindings are in scope in the guard:

match shape {
    .Circle(r) if r > 100 -> print("big circle")
    .Circle(r)            -> print_int(r)
    .Rect(w, h) if w == h -> print("square")
    .Rect(_, _)           -> print("rect")
}

The guard must be a bool. It runs at most once for each arm, after that arm's pattern has matched, and can call functions. On an arm with alternatives it applies to each of them: .Plus | .Minus if ready -> .... Guards work in match statements and match expressions, but not on else, which has no pattern to guard. A guard can't bind names itself; put the pattern in the arm instead: Some(.Circle(r)) -> ... rather than Some(s) if s is .Circle(r) -> ....

items.title: Alternatives (|)
items.text:
Patterns joined with | share an arm, in a match statement or expression:

match token {
    .Plus | .Minus -> print("additive")
    .Star | .Slash -> print("multiplicative")
    else print("other")
}
match n {
    1 | 2 | 3 -> print("small")
    else print("big")
}

The arm counts as one arm for each alternative when the compiler checks that a match is exhaustive. Alternatives can't bind names, because each would have to bind the same ones; _ and nested literals are fine, as in .Circle(_) | .Dot and .Rect(0, _) | .Rect(_, 0). Give an arm that binds a line of its own.

items.title: Match as expression
items.text:
A match produces a value when every arm has a value, in the simplest case a single expression:

let label: str = match direction {
    .North -> "north"
    .South -> "south"
    .East  -> "east"
    .West  -> "west"
}

Payload, Some(x), and Ok(v) / Err(e) bindings are in scope in the arm's expression, just as in the statement form. They may hide a local of the same name, which is back after the arm (see Blocks and bindings):

let area: int64 = match shape {
    Shape.Circle(r)  -> 3 * r * r
    Shape.Rect(w, h) -> w * h
}

Without an annotation, the match takes the type of its first arm that isn't none, and each arm's bindings have that arm's payload types:

let name = match w {
    .S(value) -> value          // value: str
    .I(value) -> f"#{value}"    // value: int64
}
print(name + "!")               // name: str

A none arm, or an arm of type T? next to arms of type T, makes the match a T?, and the plain arms are wrapped: let found = match k { 1 -> "one" else -> none } is a str?. Every other arm must have the match's type, so 1 -> "a" next to else -> 2 is an error. With an annotation each arm is converted to the annotated type, which is how arms of different structs become one interface value: let s: Shape = match k { 1 -> Sq(s: 2) else -> Circle(r: 1) }.

When the match's value is used, every arm needs a value: an arm that calls a function returning none is an error, unless the call never returns, like panic(...) or a helper that ends in one, an imported module's function (log.die(...)) included (see Return values). In a -> none or -> none or Error function, return match k { 1 -> a() else -> b() } doesn't use the value, so its arms may return none. Without an annotation, a match whose arms are all none is an error too, as let x = none is, since its type can't be inferred.

items.title: Arms with several statements
items.text:
An arm of a match expression may be a block. Its last statement must be an expression, and that expression is the arm's value; the statements before it run first, and what they bind is gone after the arm:

let size: int64 = match shape {
    Shape.Circle(r) -> {
        let d = 2 * r
        d * 3
    }
    Shape.Rect(w, h) -> w * h
}

The block is an ordinary block, so it may return, throw or try (they leave the function, not just the arm), and an arm without braces is still one expression. else { ... } takes a block too. A block that is empty, or whose last statement is not an expression (let, an if without an else, an assignment), is an error: the arm would have no value. A match statement needs none of this, since its arms are blocks already.

items.title: if X is .Variant(bindings) { ... }
items.text:
When you want a one-arm match with bindings in scope for the body, the if/is sugar is shorter than a full match:

if module.decls[i] is .Func(decl_id) {
    // decl_id is in scope here
}

An optional else { ... } runs when the pattern doesn't match, and else if chains on as it does after any if; that if can bind names of its own: if r is Ok(v) { … } else if r is Err(e) and e.code > 0 { … }. Pattern bindings stay scoped to the matching arm — they aren't in scope in the else block. There and after the if, a name the pattern binds means what it meant before the if, such as an outer local it hid in the arm: in if o is Some(o) { … } else { … } the else block's o is the optional. As in a match arm, the pattern can name the enum, if s is Shape.Rect(w, h), or an imported one, if s is geo.Shape.Rect(w, h).

On a T? value, .Some(v) and .None are the same patterns as Some(v) and none, here, in a match and with a bare is. On a T or Error value, .Ok(v) and .Err(e) are the same as Ok(v) and Err(e). Naming the enum works too, as in Result.Ok(v). A generic enum is named without type arguments, and the bindings take the value's payload types: on a Maybe[int64], Maybe.Just(n) binds an int64.

Any other variant pattern needs an enum value, or an optional of one, where it tests the value inside: on a Color?, .Red matches a .Red and not none. Likewise .Some and .None need an optional, and .Ok and .Err a T or Error.

A bare is also tests an enum value's variant without binding its payload: if c is .Red and ready { ... }, s is .Circle(_).

A pattern with bindings can also be one of the operands an if condition joins with and. Its names are in scope in the operands after it and in the body, as if each is were its own if nested inside the one before:

if decl is .Import(_path, alias, _items) and not alias.starts_with("#") {
    aliases += [alias]
}
if a is .Some(x) and b is .Some(y) and x == y {
    print_int(x)
} else {
    print("no match")
}

The else block runs when any operand fails, and sees none of the bindings. A for condition can bind the same way (see for).

An and chain anywhere else, as a let value, an argument or what a function returns, binds the same way for the operands after the is: it is false when the pattern doesn't match, and the rest when it does.

let small = tok is .Num(n) and n < 10       // true

Elsewhere a pattern can't bind: not under or or not, not with is not inside an and chain, and not in an is on its own outside a condition. There the is is only a test, and .Circle(r) is an error.

if v is .Some(x) {
    print_int(x)
} else {
    print("missing")
}

items.title: let .Pattern(bindings) = expr else { ... }
items.text:
Destructure with an early-exit on the non-matching case. The else block must exit the enclosing scope (return / throw / panic, or break / continue in a loop) so the bindings are guaranteed-in-scope below. A block that can reach its end is an error, decided by the same rules as the end of a function (see Return values): it may end in an if/else or a match whose every branch exits, in a for true loop it can't break out of, or in a call that never returns, as for match arms above:

let .Some(v) = m.get(key) else { return -1 }
// v is in scope here

The bindings start after the else block, so inside it a name the pattern binds still has the binding it had before the let-else, if any.

The pattern is a variant with its payload, as in .Some(v), Some(v), Ok(v) or Shape.Circle(r), or a type pattern such as str(s) (see Type patterns). On a T? value (like m.get(key) above), .Some(v) binds the unwrapped payload and .None matches none. On a T or Error value, .Ok(v) binds the value and .Err(e) the error. On an enum value, the variant is looked up in that value's enum, even when another enum declares a variant of the same name:

let .Ok(text) = read_text(path) else { return 1 }
print(f"{text}!")    // text is a str

items.title: Exhaustiveness
items.text:
A match on an enum (or on T?, a union or bool) must cover every variant. The compiler reports an error if any variant is missing and no wildcard arm is present. An arm naming a variant the enum doesn't declare is reported instead, since it's usually a misspelling of the missing one, and its bindings don't cause further errors in the arm.

type Color = enum {
    Red
    Green
    Blue
}

let c: Color = .Red
// error: match on `Color` doesn't cover variant `Blue`
match c {
    .Red -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
}

An arm with a guard doesn't cover anything, since its condition can be false: some other arm has to handle that variant too.

Nested patterns are checked all the way down. These arms cover every Shape?, so no else is needed:

match best {
    Some(.Circle(_))  -> print("circle")
    Some(.Rect(_, _)) -> print("rect")
    none              -> print("nothing")
}

Drop the .Rect arm and the error names what is left: match onShape?doesn't coverSome(.Rect(_, _))`. A nested literal never completes a field of typeint64orstr, so.Rect(w, 0)` needs another arm for the same variant.

Add the missing arm or an else catch-all:

match c {
    .Red -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
    else -> print("other")
}

The single-arm sugar (if X is .V(b) { ... } and let .V(b) = X else { ... }) is not subject to exhaustiveness — they're explicitly one-variant checks.

A match on int64 or str must include an else arm — the compiler reports an error otherwise. (int64 and str have too many possible values to enumerate; the else makes the fall-through explicit.)

items.title: Profiling
items.text:
stdlib/kod/profiling.kod is a sampling profiler for finding where a program spends its time. It stops the program at a fixed interval of CPU time, notes where it was, and at the end prints which functions it was caught in most:

import "kod/profiling"

func main() -> int64 {
    profiling.start(interval_us: 1000)      // a sample every 1 ms of CPU time
    run_the_slow_part()
    profiling.stop()
    profiling.report()
    return 0
}

profile: 412 samples
  64%  264 samples  parse_line (app.kod:52)
  20%  84 samples  checksum (app.kod:107)
  8%  35 samples  <unresolved>
  7%  29 samples  parse_line (app.kod:49)

Each row is a place the program was caught: the function, the line in it, and the share of samples taken there. A function busy on several lines has a row for each. <unresolved> gathers the samples taken outside Kod code, in the C runtime or the system's libraries.

Function Meaning start(interval_us:) empty the samples and take one every interval_us microseconds of the program's CPU time; time spent waiting, sleeping or reading doesn't count stop() take no more; the samples stay report() print the summary above n_samples() how many samples there are depth(sample) how many addresses sample sample has, 0 for one there isn't frame(sample, at:) address at of the sample: 0 is where the program was, then the return addresses up the stack, its callers; 0 past the end

items.title: Reading it
items.text:
• Self time only. A sample counts toward the function the program was in, not the ones that called it. A function that only calls slow ones shows little; to find its callers, look at the sample's other frames with frame and resolve them with kod/inspect, which gives none for an address outside Kod code, such as main's caller:
import "kod/inspect"

for i in 0..profiling.n_samples() {
    if inspect.resolve(addr: profiling.frame(i, at: 1)) is Some(f) {
        print(f.name)                     // who called the function sampled
    }
}
  • Inlined functions. A small function the compiler compiles into its caller shows as the caller.
  • The interval. 1 ms suits a run of a few seconds. A shorter one finds more in a short run, and costs a little more while the program runs.
  • Up to 4096 samples, each of up to 32 addresses. Past that, start's timer keeps running but no more samples are kept, so the summary covers the beginning of a long run: start it just before the part to measure.

For a whole program, macOS's own sample command (sample <pid> 5) needs no change to it, and reports call trees as well.

The handler that takes the samples is a Kod function the system calls on SIGPROF (see Callbacks); it only reads registers and memory and stores addresses, so it is safe to run at any point in the program.

items.title: Hello, world
items.text:
Work in the repository root, and build the tool once with make kod (see Install): ./kod is a link there to it.

Create hello.kod:

func main() -> int64 {
    print("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

Build and run:

$ ./kod build hello.kod
$ ./build/apps/hello/hello
Hello, world!

./kod run hello.kod does both in one step.

items.title: A real program
items.text:
func greet(anon name: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let names: [str] = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
    for name in names {
        greet(name)
    }
    return 0
}

items.title: Variables
items.text:
Bindings are declared with let and are immutable — the name can't be reassigned. A type annotation is usually required:

let x: int64 = 42
let s: str = "hello"
let flag: bool = true

For a binding you intend to reassign, use mut:

mut count: int64 = 0
count = count + 1   // ok

let limit: int64 = 10
limit = 20          // error: cannot reassign immutable binding `limit`

items.title: A test file
items.text:
// arithmetic_test.kod
test "addition" {
    assert 2 + 2 == 4
}

test "subtraction" {
    assert 10 - 3 == 7
}

$ ./kod test arithmetic_test.kod
ok   addition
ok   subtraction

2/2 passed

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Types — the full type system
  • Functions — declaration, parameters, return types
  • Control flow — if, for, match
  • Testing — the test and assert syntax

items.title: Regular expressions
items.text:
stdlib/regex.kod finds text by pattern. Its syntax is RE2's, which Go's regexp and Rust's regex share, and it runs in time linear in the text whatever the pattern: there is no backtracking, so no pattern and input make it slow, and so no backreferences or lookaround, which need backtracking.

import "regex"

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let date = try regex.compile(r"(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})")
    let Some(m) = date.find("due 2026-11-27, paid later") else { return 1 }
    print(m.text())                     // 2026-11-27
    print(m.named("month")? or "")      // 11
    print(date.replace_all("2026-11-27", with: "$day/$month/$year"))   // 27/11/2026
    return 0
}

Write a pattern as a raw string, r"\d+", whose backslashes are its own (see Raw strings); in an ordinary string each is doubled, "\\d+", and "\d+" is an error, as \d isn't a string escape.

items.title: Compiling
items.text:
regex.compile(pattern) gives a Regex, or a RegexError for a pattern that isn't one:

type RegexError = struct {
    message: str
    offset: int64    // byte offset in the pattern
}

Its to_str() is regex: <message> at offset <offset>, such as regex: missing closing ) at offset 0. Compile a pattern once and use it many times; a Regex doesn't change as it is used, so tasks can share one.

items.title: Finding
items.text:
Method Gives r.matches(s) whether the pattern matches anywhere in s r.find(s, from = 0) the first match at or after byte from, as a Match? r.find_all(s) every match, left to right, none overlapping, as [Match] r.full_match(s) a match of all of s, as a Match? r.replace_all(s, with: t) s with each match replaced by t, in which $1 or ${1} is group 1's text, $name or ${name} a named group's, $0 the whole match and $$ a $; a name runs as far as letters, digits and _ go, so $1x is the group named 1x (none: empty) and ${1}x is group 1 then x r.replace_with(s, f) s with each match m replaced by f(m), a func(Match) -> str r.split(s) the text between matches, as [str] r.group_count() how many capturing groups the pattern has r.group_names() the name of each group, "" for one without; [0] is the whole match's

When several matches start at the same place, the one taken is the one a backtracking engine would find first: alternatives are tried left to right, *, +, ? and {n,m} take as much as they can and their lazy forms (*?, ...) as little. find_all, replace_all and split go on after each match; an empty match right after the previous one is skipped, so a* in "baa" matches at 0 (empty), then aa.

A Match holds where it is in the text it came from:

Field or method Gives m.start, m.end the byte offsets of the whole match m.text() the matched text m.group(i) group i's text, str?: none when the group took no part in the match m.named(name) the named group's text, str? m.span(i) group i's byte offsets, (int64, int64)?

Offsets are bytes, as Kod's string indexes are, and always at the start of a character.

items.title: Syntax
items.text:
The pattern and the text are UTF-8; . and a class each match one character (a code point), and a byte that isn't valid UTF-8 counts as a character of its own that only . and negated classes match.

Pattern Matches x the character x . any character but ; any with the s flag [abc], [a-z], [^a-z] one of the characters, one in the range, one not in it; \d, \w, \s and the escapes below work inside \d, \w, \s an ASCII digit; letter, digit or _; whitespace (, , , \v, , ) \D, \W, \S any character the lower-case one doesn't match , , , , \v, \0 newline, tab, return, form feed, vertical tab, NUL \x41, \x{263a} the character with that code point \., \, \( ... the punctuation character itself xy x then y x|y x or y, x first x*, x+, x? zero or more, one or more, zero or one x, as many as can be x{n}, x{n,}, x{n,m} exactly n, at least n, n to m xs; n and m at most 1000 x*?, x+?, x??, x{n,m}? ... the same, as few as can be (x) a group, which captures what it matches, numbered from 1 by its ( (?P<name>x), (?<name>x) a group named name (?:x) a group that doesn't capture ^, $ the start and end of the text; of a line with the m flag \A, \z the start and end of the text, always , \B an ASCII word boundary, and anywhere else (?flags), (?flags:x) flags from here to the end of the group, or for x only: i case-insensitive, m multi-line, s . matches , and - before those to turn off

The i flag folds ASCII letters only ((?i)é doesn't match É). There are no Unicode classes (\p{L}), backreferences or lookaround.

items.title: Speed
items.text:
Matching keeps every way the pattern could still match as it reads the text, each step at most once per character (a Pike VM), so the time is linear in the text times the pattern's size: (a|aa)*b on 40 as, which a backtracking engine would take hours over, takes a millisecond. A pattern that starts with a literal string skips ahead with a search for it.

Finding \w+@\w+\.com 13,000 times in a megabyte takes about 75 ms, and (a|b)*c 26,000 times about 100 ms; Go's regexp takes 32 and 35.

stdlib/regex_test.kod checks the matches, groups, replacements and splits of some 1,200 cases against what Go's regexp gives (stdlib/testdata/regex_cases.go writes them).

items.title: Self-hosting
items.text: Kod's compiler is written in Kod and compiles itself. A checked-in binary of it, the snapshot, is what builds it from source.

items.title: Status
items.text:
The self-hosted compiler sh_kodc exists and is the production path. make stage1 builds it, and every kod build / kod run / kod test invocation uses it for codegen when available.

Sources in Kod:

File Role stdlib/kod/lexing.kod Tokenizer stdlib/kod/parsing.kod Parser (AST built into a pool of int64 ids) stdlib/kod/ast.kod AST node types stdlib/kod/regalloc.kod Register allocation over the emitted instructions stdlib/kod/codegen.kod ARM64 assembly emitter stdlib/kod/build.kod Import resolution and whole-program registration kodc.kod sh_kodc entry point: compile a module, emit the _main shim tools/kod.kod The native kod driver: build / run / test / check

sh_kodc reads a .kod file and emits ARM64 assembly to stdout, plus a few internal subcommands (_compile, _emit-runtime-main, _emit-test-runtime-main).

items.title: Build chain
items.text:
bootstrap/sh_kodc   checked-in sh_kodc snapshot
build/stage0/       C runtime objects, the always-linked stdlib modules, and the
                    compiler library shared by sh_kodc and the kod driver
build/stage1/       sh_kodc + its .s/.o, plus runtime_main.{s,o}
build/apps/kod/     the native kod driver
build/apps/<stem>/  the final executable; its objects are in <stem>.obj/, a tree that
                    mirrors the source tree (see Modules, "Symbol and object names")
link.cfg            how everything is linked, read by the Makefile and by kod

Driven by the Makefile:

  1. stage0: the checked-in snapshot bootstrap/sh_kodc compiles the always-linked stdlib modules and the compiler library to assembly; as assembles them and clang builds arena.c, rc.c and runtime.c.
  2. stage1: the snapshot compiles kodc.kod and writes the _main shim; clang links everything into build/stage1/sh_kodc. So sh_kodc is the current compiler sources, compiled by the snapshot.
  3. apps: kod build foo.kod compiles each of the program's modules with build/stage1/sh_kodc to build/apps/foo/foo.obj/<path>.o and links them against build/stage0/.

Two consequences: a codegen change reaches user programs right away, but the stage0 stdlib modules keep the snapshot's codegen until make bootstrap-snapshot refreshes it. And the compiler sources themselves may only use features the snapshot can compile.

There is no other way in: without the snapshot, make stops and says how to restore it. See Refreshing the snapshot and Recovering from a bad snapshot.

items.title: The link configuration
items.text:
link.cfg at the repository root describes the link once. The Makefile includes it and tools/kod.kod reads it, so both link the same way. One NAME := word word ... per line, and nothing else:

  • A name is capital letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, and is set once per file.
  • Words are separated by one space. A word is letters, digits and the characters _ . / , = + @ -; there is no quoting, no $(...), no continuation line, no tab, no trailing space.
  • A line that starts with # is a comment, and an empty line is skipped. A # anywhere else in a line is an error, and so is a comment that ends in \.

kod rejects a line that does not fit, naming the file and line; for a line that fits, Make and kod read the same words. link.local.cfg (untracked) is read after link.cfg and overrides single names on one machine; a new git worktree needs its own copy. It overrides and does not add: a name there that link.cfg does not set (a typo, or a name of Make's own such as STAGE0 or SHELL) is an error in both. Neither accepts a LINK, AS, RUNTIME_C or STAGE0_KOD that ends up empty.

Name Meaning LINK command that links an executable: clang -target arm64-apple-darwin -Wl,-dead_strip. clang finds the SDK and the macOS version. AS what assembles a .s file. kod (the default) writes the object in the compiler's own process, with stdlib/kod/macho.kod: no assembler is started, and a module compiled by kod build goes from the compiler's instructions to its object without being written as text at all. Any other value is a command run as AS -o file.o file.s, such as clang -target arm64-apple-darwin -c -x assembler, clang's own assembler (what as runs, minus an xcrun shim and a script). The Makefile's own rules read kod as the compiler that wrote the .s (the snapshot, or the stage being checked), run as sh_kodc _assemble file.s file.o. tools/as_diff.kod (./kod run tools/as_diff.kod) checks that the two agree, by meaning, over every file of the corpus. CC, CFLAGS compile a C file: clang, -target arm64-apple-darwin -I stdlib -O2. The target is pinned as in LINK (and as), so a clang that follows the architecture of the shell it runs in (one under Rosetta) does not produce x86_64 objects that the arm64 link rejects. RUNTIME_C C files linked into every program; built to build/stage0/<name>.o STAGE0_KOD Kod modules linked into every program, in link order; prebuilt by the snapshot compiler to build/stage0/_<basename>.o, so their basenames must be unique

A program links, in order: LINK, -o <exe>, the RUNTIME_C objects, the STAGE0_KOD objects, the program's module objects, the objects of the C files its modules name, its _main shim, and last the arguments its modules give with kod:link (see Modules). A module that declares such lines cannot be in STAGE0_KOD, nor be one of the compiler's own modules: the Makefile does not read them. kod says so for STAGE0_KOD, and a test checks the others. Adding an always-linked module is one more word in STAGE0_KOD; the Makefile derives its rule. make rebuilds the C runtime objects and relinks sh_kodc and kod when link.cfg or link.local.cfg changes (the objects also when a header in stdlib/ does, such as kod_rt.h), and also when the configuration in force is not the one they were built with (it keeps that in build/.link-config), so removing link.local.cfg, or a name from it, rebuilds too. A program gets the deployment target of the machine that builds it, as clang chooses it (MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET in the environment overrides that).

Requirements: clang (Xcode Command Line Tools). kod is run from the repository root; from another directory it says link.cfg not found. Calling build/apps/kod/kod directly does not rebuild build/stage0/, so after a change to runtime.c or link.cfg run make kod (or ./kod, which does); when the configuration names an always-linked object that is not there yet, kod says build/stage0/_name.o not found; run make.

items.title: Refreshing the snapshot
items.text:
make bootstrap-snapshot

Runs make selfhost-check, checks that the stage2 and stage3 binaries are byte-identical, and only then copies the stage2 sh_kodc over bootstrap/sh_kodc. It takes seconds. Commit the new binary on its own.

A feature takes two steps to reach the compiler's own sources: commit the feature, refresh the snapshot, and only then use it there. The compiler sources may use only what the snapshot can compile.

Don't rewrite the history of bootstrap/sh_kodc: each old version can build the sources of its time, which makes them the way back.

The snapshot is arm64-darwin only. Bringing the compiler to another platform means adding the target and cross-compiling from a Mac.

items.title: Recovering from a bad snapshot
items.text:
The fixed-point check shows that a compiler reproduces itself, not that it is right: a snapshot with a bug that reproduces itself passes. If bootstrap/sh_kodc is lost or bad:

  1. Restore a good version from git, the newest one before the problem: git log -- bootstrap/sh_kodc, then git checkout <rev> -- bootstrap/sh_kodc. If it can't compile the current sources, check out the sources of that commit as well and work forward one snapshot at a time.
  2. As a last resort, the tag python-bootstrap is the last commit with the Python interpreter, which builds the compiler with no binary at all: check it out and run make bootstrap-snapshot (about 11 minutes). From that compiler, work forward through later commits the same way.

items.title: What's still Python
items.text: Nothing. ./kod, the link at the repository root, starts the native tool, which refreshes the toolchain with make itself. Tests call build/apps/kod/kod and build/stage1/sh_kodc directly, and the stand-in servers some of them start (tests/support/github_api.kod, tests/support/http_fixture.kod) are Kod programs they build.

items.title: Codegen design
items.text:
codegen.kod is a single-pass emitter built around a few key data structures:

  • Expression / statement / type-expr pools on the parser: AST nodes are stored in flat arrays and referenced by int64 ids.
  • Struct / enum / interface tables on the codegen: registration happens before compilation; field/method lookups index these tables. Each module also keeps a table of the type names it declares, so a type name resolves in the module that wrote it: through that module's own table, the tables of the modules its import lists name, then the builtins', and m.T through the table of the module imported as m.
  • Register pool: x8–x15 used as expression temporaries; saved/restored across calls via stack spills as needed. Code nested too deeply for the pool saves every live register to frame slots and compiles with all of them free, so nesting has no fixed limit.
  • Instructions: each function is emitted into a buffer of regalloc.Insn values, a low-level IR of operations on virtual registers (see Compiler IR); regalloc allocates registers over it and arm64.kod writes it out as assembly.
  • Generic monomorphisation: each unique Map[str, int64] instantiation gets its own struct entry; methods compile once per instantiation.
  • Interface dispatch: {data_ptr, vtable_ptr} cells on the heap, one vtable per (struct, interface) pair; primitives box implicitly.

items.title: Verifying self-hosting
items.text:
make selfhost-check

Fixed-point check. build/stage1/sh_kodc compiles the compiler into build/selfhost/stage2/, that compiler compiles it again into build/selfhost/stage3/, and the two sets of assembly must be byte-identical. A miscompile in the compiler that changes its own behavior shows up as a difference. Takes a few seconds; make test runs it (tests/selfhost_test.kod).

It then compiles every .kod file in the repo (the make asm-diff corpus) with both build/stage1/sh_kodc and the stage2 compiler, and fails if any file's assembly, diagnostics or exit status differ, writing both outputs under build/selfhost/corpus-diff/. Stage1 is the current sources compiled by the snapshot and stage2 the same sources compiled by themselves, so a difference means the snapshot miscompiles some of the new compiler code, typically a construct it handles differently than the current compiler does. Compiler sources must then avoid that construct until the snapshot is refreshed.

items.title: Checking that a compiler refactor changes nothing
items.text:
make asm-diff            # compare against HEAD
make asm-diff BASE=main  # or any other revision

Builds sh_kodc at BASE (cached under build/asm-diff/), compiles every .kod file in the repo with both that compiler and the working tree's, and reports each file whose assembly, diagnostics or exit status differ. A pure refactor should report no differences. Both compilers read the working tree's stdlib/, so the comparison isolates changes to the compiler itself. The comparison is tools/asm_diff.kod, built to build/apps/asm_diff/asm_diff, which make asm-diff runs from the repository root. With --objects (build/apps/asm_diff/asm_diff --objects [BASE]), a file whose assembly is only written differently, the same diagnostics and status and the same object bytes once assembled (bne against b.ne), counts as unchanged.

items.title: Reading the assembly
items.text:
kod build doesn't write a module's assembly: the instructions go straight into its object. With KOD_ASM_TEXT set it does, as <module>.kod.s beside the .o, and each instruction written as its machine word (.inst 0xaa0103e0) has its text as a comment after the word. sh_kodc file.kod prints the assembly, with the comments only when KOD_ASM_TEXT is set:

KOD_ASM_TEXT=1 build/stage1/sh_kodc file.kod > file.s

The object file is the same either way.

items.title: Checking that types are worked out consistently
items.text:
KOD_SHADOW_TYPES=1 build/stage1/sh_kodc file.kod > /dev/null

With KOD_SHADOW_TYPES set, the compiler reports on stderr two things that would make a recorded type per expression unsafe:

  • SHADOW <phases> file:line <first> -> <later>: an expression whose inferred type changed within one function. The phases are C (reserving the function's slots, which types only function literals and, for the inliner, a callee's locals), W (the walk that checks whether a function returns) and E (compiling). Narrowing (x is T(y), x? or d) and a generic instance's default fields are the expected EE cases.
  • UNTYPED-STORE file <function number> <name>: a store into a binding before it has a type, which counts the value as a reference whatever it is. A program that compiles should have none.

tests/shadow_types_test.kod runs this over every .kod file in the repo and fails on anything but an EE change in a file that compiles. The language server relies on it: it compiles the buffer with record_kinds, which keeps the type each local, field, call and element had where it was compiled, and shows those types on hover and uses them to complete after x., a.b., f(). or xs[i]..

items.title: Simulation
items.text:
A bug between tasks often shows up once in a hundred runs, and only when the machine is busy. stdlib/sim.kod runs a test's body many times, each under a simulation decided by a seed: which ready task runs next, how much of a write goes at once, and what the clock says. A run that fails says its seed, and the same seed gives the same run again, every time, so the bug can be looked at until it is understood.

import "net/tcp"
import "sim"

func echo(anon l: tcp.Listener) -> none {
    let conn = must l.accept()
    let got = must conn.read(100)
    must conn.write_all(got)
    must conn.close()
}

test "an echo server, simulated" {
    sim.run(count: 100, body: func() {
        let l = must tcp.listen("127.0.0.1", port: 7000)
        spawn echo(l)
        let c = must tcp.connect("127.0.0.1", port: 7000)
        must c.write_str("hi")
        assert kod_bytes_to_str(must c.read(100)) == "hi"
        must c.close()
        must l.close()
    })
}
Function Does sim.run(count: 100, from: 0, start: none, body: f, restart: none, disk_faults: false) runs f, a func() -> none, under the seeds from to from + count - 1, one after another; when one fails it panics, saying the seed and the panic it had. With restart:, a second func() -> none, each run crashes and restart runs after; with disk_faults: true, the disk fails under some seeds sim.replay(seed, start: none, body: f, restart: none, disk_faults: false) runs f under seed alone, letting its panic through as it is: for looking at a failure run found sim.crashed() in restart: whether the crash stopped the body before it ended sim.faulted() whether the disk has failed a call in this run sim.simulating() whether code runs under a simulation sim.seed() the seed of the run under way sim.digest() a number standing for every choice the last run made; two runs with one seed give the same

KOD_SIM_SEEDS=n in the environment makes every sim.run take n seeds, for a longer hunt now and then.

items.title: What is simulated
items.text:
• Which task runs. When several tasks are ready, the seed picks one; a task that reads or writes a connection may give way to another first. Under half the seeds the pick goes by priority instead, as in PCT (probabilistic concurrency testing): each task has one the seed draws, the highest ready one runs, and a task that is preempted drops below all the others. So one task can run on while another, ready, waits its turn, as on a busy machine.
  • Where a task is preempted.
