As outside a simulation, a task that runs without waiting gives way at the top of a loop iteration or a function call (Preemption), but after a number of those that the seed draws each time, as likely a handful as thousands, rather than every 10 ms. A check that comes right after a store to what other tasks can reach preempts sooner: under some seeds the first such check, under others one of the next hundred. What counts is a module-level variable, and a field of a shared struct that was handed to another task: passed to a function spawn runs, or captured by one, or sent on a channel, or reachable from such a value. A struct a task made and kept to itself doesn't count, and only the last store before a check is looked at (with eight marks, one per store site in turn, instead of one, the seeds that find the TLS bug below were the same 52 when measured). So a race between two tasks that read and write the same data without waiting in between shows up under some seed too, and that seed preempts at the same places again. The store itself is never cut in two, and nothing is preempted where it couldn't be outside a simulation.
  • Time. time.monotonic_ns(), time.unix_ns() and time.now() read a clock that stands still while tasks run, its calendar starting at start (a time.Time), or 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. A test that checks a certificate made today passes start: time.now(), taken before the run, so that the certificate is in date; the run is then the same for that start. When every task waits and one of them waits for a time (time.sleep, a timeout), the clock jumps to the earliest such time. A test of a 30-second timeout takes no time at all.
  • The network. tcp.listen and tcp.connect to 127.0.0.1 or localhost make connections within the program, on any port, whatever is running on the machine. Each connection is a pair of Unix-domain sockets, with small buffers, so a write of a few kilobytes waits for the other end to read; a write goes in pieces of a size the seed picks. Connecting to a port nothing listens on is ConnectionRefused; to another host, an error.
  • The disk. Files and directories a run makes, writes, renames or removes are the simulation's, in memory, and gone when the run ends; a path the run hasn't changed is read from the real disk, so a test can read its certificates and data files. What posix and io do with files is simulated: opening, reading, writing, syncing, renaming, listing, stat. Without restart: nothing is lost; with it, see Crashes.
  • Randomness. crypto/random gives bytes that come from the seed, so the keys and nonces a run makes, and the work done with them, are the same each time.
  • Deadlock. When every task waits and nothing it waits for can come, the run fails with simulation: every task waits, and nothing can wake one, where outside a simulation the program would hang.

items.title: Crashes
items.text:
With restart:, the seed picks a point where the machine loses its power: before one of the body's changes to the disk (a write, a sync, a new file, a rename, a removal), under some seeds one of the first few, under others one of the first thousands, and under a quarter of them none, so that the body ends first. Every task stops there, never to run again, and the disk loses what wasn't on it yet:

  • Data. What was written to a file since its last sync is lost, or kept, in pieces of 512 bytes: under some seeds all of it is lost, under others none of it (the program crashed, not the machine), and under the rest some pieces and not others, whatever order they were written in. A piece kept past the file's synced end leaves zeros before it where a piece was lost. A truncate since the sync is kept or lost as a piece is.
  • Names. Files and directories made, renamed and removed since the last sync_dir are kept in the order they were made: all of those up to a point the seed picks, and none after. A sync_dir keeps every change made before it, in any directory, as a journaling file system does. f.sync() keeps a new file's contents but not its name.

Then restart runs, as the program would when the machine came back: what the crash left on the disk, a new network with no connection open, and the clock where it was. Values in memory, such as one the body and restart both capture, are kept, which is how a test says what the body was told was kept; what a module-level variable holds, the program's own included, is too, which a real restart wouldn't keep.

import "posix"
import "posix" { Fd }
import "sim"

// Appends `line`, and is done once it is on the disk.
func log(anon f: Fd, anon line: str) -> none or Error {
    try f.write_all(kod_str_to_bytes(line + "\n"))
    try f.sync()
}

type Kept = shared struct {
    lines: [str] = []
}

test "a log keeps what it said it kept" {
    let kept = Kept()
    sim.run(count: 100, body: func() {
        kept.lines = []
        must posix.make_dir("db")
        must posix.sync_dir(".")
        let f = must posix.open_rw("db/log")
        must posix.sync_dir("db")
        for i in 0..20 {
            must log(f, f"line {i}")
            kept.lines += [f"line {i}"]
        }
    }, restart: func() {
        // Before its first line, the log may not be there at all.
        if len(kept.lines) == 0 {
            return
        }
        let text = kod_bytes_to_str(must (must posix.open_rw("db/log")).read_all())
        for line in kept.lines {
            assert text.contains(line + "\n")
        }
    })
}

Without the f.sync(), or without either sync_dir, some seeds lose a line the body was told was kept, and the run fails, naming its seed. Of 200 seeds, 115 find a missing f.sync() there and 72 the missing sync_dirs; replacing a file by a rename, 77 find a missing sync of the new file and 98 a missing sync_dir after the rename.

The tasks a crash stops never let go of what they held: a few kilobytes a run stay allocated until the program ends. A body the crash stops may have failed for it, so how it ended doesn't matter: restart runs either way. Under a simulation, renaming a directory that is on the real disk fails with InvalidInput.

items.title: Disk faults
items.text:
With disk_faults: true, under three seeds in four the disk fails once, or fills up, at a point the seed picks:

  • A full disk. From one of the body's writes on, the disk has no more room than its files then take: a write that would make them longer writes what fits and fails with StorageFull once nothing does, and so does a truncate that lengthens a file. Removing or cutting short a file makes room again.
  • A write that fails. One write fails with an I/O error (EIO, kind Other), having written nothing.
  • A sync that fails. One f.sync() fails with an I/O error, and what was written to the file since its last sync never reaches the disk: the program still reads it back, but the next sync doesn't write it and a crash loses it, as on Linux, where a sync that failed has given up on the pages it was to write. A program that tries the sync again and takes its success as the data's is wrong; one that stops, or writes it all again, is right.
  • A read that fails. One read fails with an I/O error.

Which call fails is counted among those of its kind: one of the first few under some seeds, one of the first hundreds under others, in the body; a fault the body doesn't come to doesn't come in restart, though a disk the body filled is still full there.

A program may well stop when its disk fails, as a database should when a sync fails. With restart:, a body that ends with a panic after a fault isn't a failure: the power is cut there, as if it had crashed, and restart checks what is left. Without restart: it is, and the body has to cope with the error itself.

import "posix"
import "posix" { Fd }
import "sim"

type Kept = shared struct {
    lines: [str] = []
}

// Appends `line`, and is done once it is on the disk; a sync that fails
// stops the program, since what it was to write may be gone.
func log(anon f: Fd, anon line: str) -> none or Error {
    try f.write_all(kod_str_to_bytes(line + "\n"))
    if f.sync() is Err(e) {
        panic(f"the log can't be kept: {e.to_str()}")
    }
}

test "a log keeps what it said it kept, whatever the disk does" {
    let kept = Kept()
    sim.run(count: 100, body: func() {
        kept.lines = []
        let f = must posix.create("log")
        must f.sync()
        must posix.sync_dir(".")
        for i in 0..20 {
            // A full disk or a write that fails: the line isn't kept.
            if log(f, f"line {i}") is Ok(_) {
                kept.lines += [f"line {i}"]
            }
        }
    }, restart: func() {
        if len(kept.lines) == 0 {
            return
        }
        let text = kod_bytes_to_str(must (must posix.open_read("log")).read_all())
        for line in kept.lines {
            assert text.contains(line + "\n")
        }
    }, disk_faults: true)
}

Had log tried the sync again, a seed whose sync fails would find a line missing that the body was told was kept: 13 seeds of 200 do (a quarter of the faults are syncs, and the failing one has to be among the log's 21).

items.title: What isn't
items.text:
Child processes, posix.poll and the standard streams are the real ones, and so is a file opened only for reading that the run hasn't changed; a body that waits for those, or for another program, isn't repeatable. The simulated disk fails a call only as Disk faults says: one fault a run, and never a slow disk or a sync that silently does nothing. Tasks must not outlive the body: those it spawned are waited for when it ends, as at any function's end.

With a bug fixed on 2026-11-27 put back (a TLS reader that sent records a writer had queued but not yet sent, while the writer had been preempted between the two), 55 of 200 seeds of a connection writing and reading at once deadlock. The window is a few checks among hundreds of thousands: none of 200 seeds found it without the preemption after stores, nor without priorities, and 32 did while stores to every shared struct counted.

A seed gives the same run whether run comes to it after other seeds or replay runs it alone, as long as the body doesn't depend on what earlier runs left behind: a cache the program fills, say, makes the run that fills it do more work, so it is preempted at other places. A module-level variable is the exception: the work its initializer does isn't counted, so it doesn't matter which run worked it out.

items.title: Strings
items.text: Strings in Kod are UTF-8 byte sequences. The type is str.

items.title: Literals
items.text:
let s: str = "hello, world"

Supported escape sequences:

Escape Meaning \n newline \t tab \r carriage return \0 NUL byte \\ backslash \" double quote \' single quote \{, \} a brace: in an f-string, one that doesn't start or end an interpolation, as in f"\{\"n\": {n}\}" \xHH the byte HH, two hex digits (00 to FF) \u{H...} a Unicode character, 1 to 6 hex digits, written as UTF-8

\x gives a single byte, so "\xC3\xA9" and "\u{e9}" are both é (two bytes), while "\xE9" is one byte that isn't valid UTF-8 by itself. A string may hold any bytes. A \u{...} must be a Unicode scalar value: at most 10FFFF, and not a surrogate (D800 to DFFF).

A malformed \x or \u is an error: a \x without two hex digits, a \u without braces, an empty or unterminated \u{}, more than six digits, or a value that isn't a scalar value. So is any other escape, such as "\d": a backslash that stands for itself is written \\, or the string is written raw (below). Non-ASCII UTF-8 can also be written directly in the source. Character literals ('a') take the simple escapes only.

items.title: Raw strings
items.text:
r"..." is a string whose text is taken as it is written: a backslash is a backslash, and nothing is an escape. It ends at the next ", so it can't hold one; r"""...""" can, and is dedented as a """ string is. Raw strings suit text full of backslashes, such as regular expressions and Windows paths:

let digits = r"\d+(\.\d+)?"            // the same as "\\d+(\\.\\d+)?"
let path = r"C:\Users\kod"
let quoted = r"""
    say "\n" for a newline
    """                                  // say "\n" for a newline, and a newline

Byte literals (b"...") and f-strings take the same escapes. In an f-string, the braces of \u{...} are part of the escape, not an interpolation: f"\u{e9}{n}" is é followed by the value of n.

items.title: F-strings
items.text:
Interpolate expressions into strings with f"...":

let name: str = "world"
print(f"hello, {name}!")          // hello, world!

let n: int64 = 42
print(f"the answer is {n}")       // the answer is 42

Anything inside { } is a Kod expression, string literals and nested f-strings included (f"[{f"<{n}>"}]", f"{"}" + s}"). Non-str values are auto-converted via their to_str method:

print(f"{a} + {b} = {a + b}")
print(f"flag={true}")             // flag=true
print(f"items: {len(items)}")    // any type with to_str works

Interpolations are evaluated left to right, as are the operands of an operator or a comparison chain, the parts of xs[i] and xs[lo..hi], and the receiver, index and value of a store such as xs[i] = v, so in f"{bump(:c)} then {c.n}" the second part sees what bump did.

What can be interpolated:

  • str, and bytes as-is
  • int64 and bool
  • a struct, by its func to_str(self) -> str if it declares one; otherwise a plain struct as its name and fields, Point(x: 1, y: 2) (see Structs are values)
  • an array, as its elements in brackets (see As text)
  • a value of an interface that declares the same to_str, such as Stringable or Error; the call goes to the concrete type's to_str
  • an enum, by its func to_str(self) -> str if it declares one, and otherwise as the name of its variant: f"{c}" is Red, and an Op.Lit(n: 4) is Lit, without its payload. A T or Error isn't one of these: test it first

print(x) takes the same values as {x} does.

Anything else is a compile error: an optional (T?), a function value, and a shared struct or interface without a func to_str(self) -> str, including one whose to_str takes arguments or returns something else. Unwrap an optional first, e.g. f"{n? or 0}".

The braces hold one expression, which may be followed by a format spec.

items.title: Format specs
items.text:
After a :, a format spec says how wide the text is and how a number is written, as in Python:

let n = 42
let x = 3.14159
let name = "kod"
print(f"[{n:5}] [{n:<5}] [{n:^5}] [{n:05}] [{n:+}]")  // [   42] [42   ] [ 42  ] [00042] [+42]
print(f"{x:.2} {x:8.3} {x:e} {0.25:.1%}")            // 3.14    3.142 3.141590e+00 25.0%
print(f"{255:x} {255:#X} {5:08b} {1234567:,}")        // ff 0XFF 00000101 1,234,567
print(f"[{name:>6}] [{name:*^7}] [{"truncated":.5}]")  // [   kod] [**kod**] [trunc]

The parts, in this order, each optional:

Part Meaning fill and align < left, > right, ^ centred, after an optional fill character (a space if none). Numbers align right and everything else left unless told otherwise. sign + writes a + before a positive number, and a space writes a space there; a negative number always has its -. # Puts 0x, 0X, 0o or 0b before a number written in that base. 0 Pads a number with zeros after its sign and base prefix, to the width. width The least number of characters (code points); a longer value isn't cut. , or _ Groups the digits of a decimal number in threes, or with _ those of a hex, octal or binary number in fours. .precision For a float, the digits after the point; for a string, the most characters to keep. type For an int64: d decimal (the default), x and X hex, o octal, b binary. For a float64: f fixed point (six digits after the point unless a precision says), e exponent form (3.141590e+00), % the value times 100 with a %. For a string: s.

A float without a type or precision is written as {x} writes it, then padded; with a precision and no type, it has that many digits after the point. Digits are rounded correctly from the float's exact value, ties to even. A bool, an enum or a struct is formatted as the text {x} gives it, so only the fill, align, width and precision apply.

A spec that doesn't fit the value is a compile error: {n:.2} on an int64, {x:x} on a float64, {name:05} on a str. The spec is written out, so {n:{w}} with a width taken from a variable is an error too.

The same specs are also methods: n.format("05"), x.format(".2") and s.format(">10") give what f"{n:05}" and the others do.

items.title: Concatenation
items.text:
Use + to concatenate strings, or += to append in place:

let greeting: str = "hello" + ", " + name + "!"

mut buf: str = "lines:\n"
buf += "  one\n"
buf += "  two\n"

+= works on struct fields too: obj.message += " (cont.)".

Both operands of + must be str; nothing else is converted, so "n = " + 5 is an error. Convert with str(...) or use an f-string: "n = " + str(n) or f"n = {n}". bytes concatenate only with bytes.

items.title: Multi-line strings
items.text:
Triple-quoted strings span multiple lines:

let preamble: str = """
    .text
    .globl _main
    _main:
    """

The closing """ must sit on its own line. Its indent anchors the dedent — every content line has at least that many leading spaces (or tabs) stripped. The newline immediately after the opening """ is not part of the value; the newline before the closing """ is. So the example above produces:

.text
.globl _main
_main:

(four-space indent gone; trailing newline kept).

Combine with f for interpolation:

let asm: str = f"""
    bl ${mangled}$main
    ret
    """

Escape sequences work the same as in regular strings. Each content line must be indented at least as far as the closing """; a content line with less indent is a lex error.

items.title: Length
items.text: let n: int64 = len(s)

items.title: Character access
items.text:
Index into a string to get the ASCII value of a character (as int64):

let c: int64 = s[0]   // 'h' → 104

Negative indices count from the end:

let last: int64 = s[-1]

The index must be an int64, so s["a"] is an error.

Strings are immutable, so assigning to an element (s[0] = 'H') is an error. for … in over a str gives its bytes, as s[i] does; for text, iterate over s.code_points() instead.

items.title: Slicing
items.text:
let sub: str = s[2..5]   // bytes at positions 2, 3, 4

Either endpoint may be omitted: s[..k] is s[0..k] and s[k..] is s[k..len(s)]. s[..] returns a copy.

A negative bound counts from the end, as an index does: "hello"[..-1] is "hell" and "hello"[-3..] is "llo". Then both endpoints clamp to [0, len(s)], so "hello"[3..40] is "lo" and "hello"[-9..2] is "he". An end before the start yields "". Both bounds must be int64. bytes slices follow the same rules.

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
if s == "hello" {
    print("match")
}
if s != "bye" {
    print("not bye")
}

String equality compares contents, not identity. <, <=, > and >= order two strings byte by byte, a prefix before the longer string: "apple" < "apples" < "zebra". The same holds for two bytes values.

items.title: Searching and comparing
items.text:
All of these work on bytes. For text that must be split at code points, use code_points() or char_slice.

"GET /index".starts_with("GET")        // true
"a.kod".ends_with(".kod")              // true
"hello".contains("ell")                // true
"hello".find("l")                      // 2, an int64?
"hello".find("l", from: 3)             // 3
"hello".find("z")                      // none
"abc".strip_prefix("a")                // "bc", a str?
"abc".strip_suffix("x")                // none

find returns the byte offset of the first match at or after from (default 0; a from outside the string is clamped into it). The empty string is found at from. strip_prefix and strip_suffix return none when the string doesn't start or end that way. "" is a prefix and a suffix of every string.

items.title: Splitting, trimming and joining
items.text:
"a,b,,c".split(",")                    // ["a", "b", "", "c"]
"3-5".split_once("-")                  // ("3", "5"), as a (str, str)?
"".split(",")                          // [""]
"abc".split("")                        // ["abc"]
"a\r\nb\n".lines()                      // ["a", "b"]
" 1  2\t3\n".split_whitespace()          // ["1", "2", "3"]
"  hi\r\n".trim()                     // "hi"
"  hi ".trim_start()                   // "hi "
"  hi ".trim_end()                     // "  hi"
", ".join(["a", "b", "c"])             // "a, b, c"
"ab".repeat(3)                         // "ababab"
"a-b-c".replace("-", to: "+")        // "a+b+c"

split always returns at least one element and keeps empty pieces, so sep.join(s.split(sep)) == s for a non-empty sep. An empty separator doesn't split. split_once gives what is before the first sep and what is after it, or none when sep isn't there, so let (k, v) = must line.split_once(": ") takes a line apart. lines splits at each \n and drops a \r before it; a newline at the end makes no empty line after it, so "".lines() is []. split_whitespace gives the pieces between runs of space, tab, \n and \r, with no empty ones. trim removes space, tab, \n, \r from the ends. replace replaces every non-overlapping match from the left; an empty old replaces nothing. repeat with a count of 0 or less gives "".

items.title: Case and numbers
items.text:
"Content-Length".lower()               // "content-length"
"abc".upper()                          // "ABC"
"-42".parse_int()                      // -42, an int64?
"4x".parse_int()                       // none
"".parse_int()                         // none

lower and upper change only ASCII letters and leave other bytes alone. parse_int accepts an optional - or + followed by one or more decimal digits and nothing else (no spaces); it returns none for anything else and for a value outside the int64 range.

items.title: Building strings
items.text:
+= copies the whole string every time, so a loop that appends thousands of pieces does quadratic work. Use a StrBuilder for that:

import "strbuilder" { StrBuilder }

let out = StrBuilder()
out.append("HTTP/1.1 200 OK")
out.append("\r\n")
out.append_byte(10)
out.append_bytes(body)
print(out.to_str())
Method Meaning append(s: str) add a string append_bytes(b: bytes) add raw bytes append_byte(b: int64) add one byte; only the low 8 bits are used append_int(n: int64) add n in decimal, as n.to_str() writes it, without making that string len() -> int64 bytes so far clear() drop the content, keep the capacity to_str() -> str a copy of the content; the builder stays usable to_bytes() -> bytes the same as bytes

The buffer doubles when it is full, so appending n bytes costs O(n) overall. to_str makes a StrBuilder usable in an f-string. Embedded NUL bytes are kept. A StrBuilder is a handle: copies of it (let b = a) share one buffer.

items.title: Building bytes
items.text:
A ByteBuffer is a growable buffer of bytes that, unlike a StrBuilder, can read back what it holds and copy from itself. Decompressors are what it is for: compress/inflate writes its output into one, and the compiler builds its object files in them.

import "bytebuffer" { ByteBuffer }

let out = ByteBuffer()
out.push_bytes(b"ab")
out.push(0x63)
out.copy_back(distance: 3, length: 7)
assert out.to_bytes() == b"abcabcabca"
assert out.at(2) == 0x63
Method Meaning push(b: int64) add one byte; only the low 8 bits are used push_bytes(b: bytes) add bytes push_le(value: int64, size: int64) add the low size bytes of value, lowest first (little-endian); size from 0 to 8 push_buffer(other: ByteBuffer) add the bytes of other copy_back(distance: int64, length: int64) add length bytes, each a copy of the one distance before it, so a distance shorter than length repeats the last distance bytes drop_front(n: int64) drop the first n bytes slice(from: int64, to: int64) -> bytes a copy of the bytes from from up to to at(i: int64) -> int64 the byte at i, 0 to 255 set(i: int64, b: int64) replace the byte at i; only the low 8 bits of b are used len() -> int64 bytes so far to_bytes() -> bytes a copy of the content; the buffer stays usable

at and set panic for an index outside 0..len(), push_le for a size outside 0..8, and copy_back for a distance outside 1..len() or a negative length, the way indexing an array out of range does. The buffer doubles when it is full. Like a StrBuilder, a ByteBuffer is a handle: copies of it share one buffer.

items.title: Conversion
items.text:
Primitives have a to_str method:

let s: str = 42.to_str()           // "42"
let t: str = true.to_str()         // "true"
let u: str = "hi".to_str()         // identity

A struct can have its own by declaring func to_str(self) -> str. F-string interpolation calls to_str automatically. str(x) converts the same values an f-string interpolates, and rejects the same ones.

See Built-ins for the full list of string-related functions.

items.title: Structs
items.text:
Structs are named product types — a fixed set of named fields. They come in two kinds:

  • A struct is a value, like an int64 or an array: assigning it, passing it or storing it gives the other place the struct as it is, and changing a field later changes only the struct where it was changed (see Field mutation).
  • A shared struct is one object that everything holding it shares: a field assigned through any of them shows through all of them. It is for things with state of their own, such as a parser, a log or a node in a graph.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64
}

Comments are allowed inside the body:

type Rect = struct {
    // top-left corner
    x: int64
    y: int64
    // dimensions
    width: int64
    height: int64
}

A shared struct is declared the same way, with shared before struct:

type Parser = shared struct {
    pos: int64
}

shared is a word only before struct; it can still name a variable or a field.

A field's type can name the struct itself:

type Node = struct {
    kids: [Node]
    parent: Node?
    name: str
}

items.title: Construction
items.text:
Pass fields by name using labeled arguments, in any order:

let p: Point = Point(x: 10, y: 20)
let q: Point = Point(y: 20, x: 10)   // the same point

The values are computed in the order they're written. Every value needs its label, so Point(10, 20) is an error at each value:

let p: Point = Point(10, 20)   // error: argument 1 of `Point` needs a field label (`x:`)
                               // error: argument 2 of `Point` needs a field label (`y:`)

Each unlabelled value is offered the next field, in declaration order, that no label names.

Every field must be supplied unless it has a default. Omitting a field with no default is a compile error — there's no implicit zero/null value:

let p: Point = Point(x: 10)   // error: struct `Point` requires field `y`

Each field value must have the field's type, with the same implicit conversions as a function argument: Point(x: "a", y: 1) is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), while 3 is fine for an int64? field and a struct for an interface field. A field can be given only once: Point(x: 1, x: 2, y: 3) is an error (field `x` is given twice).

items.title: Field defaults
items.text:
A field may declare a default with = expr. When a construction omits that field, the default expression is evaluated and stored:

type Counter = struct {
    label: str
    count: int64 = 0
    history: [int64] = []
}

let c: Counter = Counter(label: "hits")   // count = 0, history = []
let d: Counter = Counter(label: "x", count: 5)

The default is evaluated fresh at each construction (so a [] default yields a new empty array per instance, not a shared one). Defaults are ordinary expressions evaluated in the struct's defining module, and they can't see the local variables of the function doing the construction. A default must have its field's type, which is checked where it is declared, so count: int64 = "x" is an error even if no construction omits count. Anything else wrong in it, such as an unknown name or variant, is reported where a construction omits the field, and a generic struct's default is checked only at each construction that omits it. A default that builds its own struct without giving the field needs itself, and is an error.

This is what lets the built-in Map[K, V] be created with no arguments — all three of its fields default to []:

let m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()

items.title: Custom constructors
items.text:
A struct may declare its own constructor, a function named init inside the body with no self:

type Port = struct {
    number: int64

    func init(number: int64) -> Port or Error {
        if number < 1 or number > 65535 {
            throw BadPort(number: number)
        }
        return Port(number: number)
    }
}

let p = try Port(number: 8080)     // calls init

From then on Port(...) anywhere outside the struct's own functions calls init, with the usual rules for a function call: labels, defaults and skipped labels. The field constructor is not available there, so a label init doesn't declare is an error. init is the only way to make a Port, and whatever it checks holds for every Port at the moment it is made.

Inside the struct's own functions, init and the other methods, Port(...) is the field constructor as before. That is how init builds the value, and how methods such as op_add make a new one without going through the checks again. A method can't call init itself.

init must return the struct (-> Port) or a result of it (-> Port or Error), which makes try Port(...) and must Port(...) work as for any fallible call. A struct without init is built from its fields as described above.

A generic struct may declare init too. It returns the struct with its own type parameters, Range[T] or Range[T] or Error, and is called with the type arguments spelled out as for any construction of one:

type Range[T] = struct {
    lo: T
    hi: T

    func init(lo: T, hi: T) -> Range[T] or Error {
        if hi < lo {
            throw Backwards()
        }
        return Range[T](:lo, :hi)
    }
}

let r = try Range[int64](lo: 2, hi: 9)

Inside its own functions, any instance of the struct is built from its fields, so a method of Pair[A, B] can make a Pair[B, A] directly.

Public fields stay assignable, so p.number = 0 is still possible after a checked construction. To keep what init checks true for the value's whole life, make the field private.

items.title: Private fields
items.text:
A field whose name starts with _ is private: only the struct's own functions (init, its methods and its operator methods) can read or assign it, or name it in the field constructor.

type Duration = struct {
    _ns: int64

    func init(seconds: int64 = 0, ms: int64 = 0) -> Duration {
        return Duration(_ns: seconds * 1 000 000 000 + ms * 1 000 000)
    }

    func as_ms(self) -> int64 {
        return self._ns / 1 000 000
    }
}

let d = Duration(seconds: 5)
print_int(d.as_ms())    // 5000
d._ns                   // error: field `_ns` is private to `Duration`
d._ns = 0               // error: field `_ns` is private to `Duration`

Only Duration's own functions can set _ns, so whatever init checks about it holds for as long as the value lives. Callers depend only on the methods, so the representation can change without breaking them: Duration could store microseconds instead and no caller would notice.

Outside the struct, a private field can't be named in the field constructor either. A private field with a default is filled in from it; a private field without one means the struct can only be built through init or its own functions. Public and private fields mix freely.

Privacy covers the field, not what it points to. A method that returns a private array returns the array itself, which the caller can then change by indexing it; return a copy when that matters.

items.title: Private methods
items.text:
A method whose name starts with _ is private in the same way: only the struct's own functions can call it, as self._name(...) or on another value of the struct.

type Duration = struct {
    _ns: int64

    func _whole(self, unit: int64) -> int64 {
        return self._ns / unit
    }

    func as_ms(self) -> int64 {
        return self._whole(unit: 1 000 000)
    }
}

d.as_ms()               // fine
d._whole(unit: 1)       // error: method `_whole` is private to `Duration`

That keeps helpers that assume the struct's invariants, or that would break them, out of the struct's interface. A method of a primitive type such as str or int64 is private to the module that declares it.

An interface can't declare a private method: calling it through the interface would reach the struct's method from outside.

items.title: Weak fields
items.text:
A field declared weak refers to a struct without keeping it alive, for a reference back up a tree or across a graph, which would otherwise make a cycle that is never freed:

type Node = shared struct {
    name: str
    children: [Node] = []
    weak parent: Node?           // starts as none
}

let root = Node(name: "root")
let leaf = Node(name: "leaf", parent: root)
root.children += [leaf]

if leaf.parent is Node(p) {
    print(p.name)                // root
}
  • Only a shared struct has weak fields, and a weak field's type is an optional shared struct, S?: a value has no identity to refer back to. It starts as none unless it has a default or the construction gives it a value.
  • Assigning to it, or giving it a value in a construction, doesn't count as a reference: when nothing else refers to the struct, it is freed, and from then on the field reads as none.
  • Reading it gives a S? of its own, which keeps the struct alive for as long as it is used, as any other value does: p above can't be freed out from under the code that reads it.
  • Each read checks whether the struct is still there and makes a new optional, so a weak field costs a little more to read than a plain one.

weak is only special before a field's name; elsewhere it is an ordinary name.

items.title: Field access
items.text:
print_int(p.x)
print_int(p.y)

items.title: Field mutation
items.text:
p.x = p.x + 1

A field of a struct is assigned only through a name that could be assigned: a mut binding or a mut parameter, or a field or element of something that may itself be changed. On a let struct, a parameter not declared mut or a for variable, p.x = 1 is an error (cannot change `p`, an immutable binding; declare it with `mut`), and so is changing an array in one of its fields. Each place has a struct of its own, so a change shows only there:

mut a = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
let b = a
a.x = 10                     // a.x is 10, b.x is still 1

mut line = Line(from: a, to: b)
line.from.y = 5              // line.from.y is 5, a.y is still 2

As with arrays, nothing is copied until it has to be: assigning or passing a struct shares it, and its fields are copied the first time one holder changes it while another still has it.

A shared struct's fields are assigned through any name that holds it, mut or not, and every holder sees the change.

Reading or assigning a field the struct doesn't declare is an error, with a did-you-mean hint when the name is close to a real field. So is .field on a value that isn't a struct, such as an interface or an optional; for a T?, use p?.x.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Define methods inside the struct body. The first parameter must be self:

type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64

    func distance_sq(self) -> int64 {
        return self.x * self.x + self.y * self.y
    }

    func translate(mut self, dx: int64, dy: int64) -> none {
        self.x = self.x + dx
        self.y = self.y + dy
    }
}

Call methods with dot notation:

mut p: Point = Point(x: 3, y: 4)
print_int(p.distance_sq())   // 25
p.translate(dx: 1, dy: 0)
print_int(p.x)               // 4

A method that changes its struct declares mut self, like a mut parameter: the receiver is the caller's struct, which must be one the caller could change (p is mut above), and has the method's changes when it returns. The call needs no mut. Other methods can't assign to self's fields (cannot change `self`; declare the method with `mut self`). A mut self method isn't one an interface can call, so it doesn't make the struct satisfy an interface. A shared struct's methods change it through any self, and can't declare mut self.

Methods can also be invoked on non-Ident receivers — 0.to_str(), p.field.method(), f().bar(), etc.

A method's parameter and return types can name the struct itself or a type declared later in the module, so func scaled(self, by: int64) -> Point inside Point chains as p.scaled(by: 2).distance_sq().

items.title: Generic structs
items.text:
Type parameters in square brackets after the name; each unique instantiation is monomorphised:

type Pair[A, B] = struct {
    first: A
    second: B

    func swap(self) -> Pair[B, A] {
        return Pair[B, A](first: self.second, second: self.first)
    }
}

let p: Pair[str, int64] = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42)
let q = p.swap()    // Pair[int64, str]

Construction always spells the type arguments; a bare Pair(...) is an error.

A method of an instance is compiled for its type arguments when something uses it: a call, an operator or other syntax that calls it, or the instance becoming a value of an interface, which uses all of that interface's methods. So a Box[T] whose contains uses == can hold a struct that has no ==, as long as nothing calls contains on that Box. Only a method's signature is checked otherwise, so a mistake in the body of a method nothing uses isn't reported, as with a generic function nothing calls. An error in a body names the instance, as in `<` doesn't take `Color` operands; declare `op_lt` on `Color` to use it (in `Box[Color]`), and a line of the template is reported for one instance only.

A generic struct or enum may name itself, with any type arguments, in its fields, payloads and method signatures, as in kids: [Tree[T]] or the Pair[B, A] above. The instances have to end, though: one that keeps naming a bigger type, like next: W[[T]]? in W[T] or a called method of W[T] that makes a W[[T]], is an error once it is 64 instances deep (generic type `W` is 64 instances deep; each one names another with a new type). Methods that branch into new types are stopped earlier, when a module passes 4096 instances.

The built-in Map[K, V] is the canonical example.

items.title: Structs are values
items.text:
A plain struct compares, prints and hashes by its fields, with nothing declared:

type Place = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64
    name: str? = none
}

let a = Place(x: 1, y: 2)
assert a == Place(x: 1, y: 2) and a != Place(x: 1, y: 2, name: "home")
print(a)                                // Place(x: 1, y: 2, name: none)

mut steps = Map[Place, int64]()         // a key of a Map, an element of a Set
steps[a, default: 0] += 1
assert (steps[Place(x: 1, y: 2)]? or 0) == 1
  • == and != compare two values of the same struct: they are equal when each field of one is == to the other's. Two optional fields are equal when both are none or what they hold is. A struct with a field that has no == (a function, an interface value, a Map) has none either, which the error names.
  • As text, in an f-string, str(x) or print(x), it is its name and its fields, each as an f-string shows it, with none for an optional that holds nothing. Every field must have a text.
  • hash(x), and so a place as a Map's key or a Set's element, needs fields that can all be hashed, or optionals of such. A float64 can't.

All fields count, private ones too. A method of the struct's own comes first: op_eq for == (see Operators), func to_str(self) -> str for its text, and func hash(self) -> int64 for its hash. A struct that declares op_eq must declare hash to be hashed, as equal values must have the same hash.

A shared struct is one object rather than a value, so it has none of these but by such methods, nor do Map and Set have == or a hash.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
A struct gives the arithmetic and comparison operators a meaning by declaring methods with reserved names. The operator on the left operand's struct calls the method with the right operand as its one argument:

Operator Method Returns a + b op_add(self, other) any type a - b op_sub(self, other) any type a * b op_mul(self, other) any type a / b op_div(self, other) any type a % b op_mod(self, other) any type a == b, a != b op_eq(self, other) bool a < b, a > b, a <= b, a >= b op_lt(self, other) bool 
type Money = struct {
    cents: int64

    func op_add(self, other: Money) -> Money {
        return Money(cents: self.cents + other.cents)
    }

    func op_mul(self, times: int64) -> Money {
        return Money(cents: self.cents * times)
    }

    func op_eq(self, other: Money) -> bool {
        return self.cents == other.cents
    }

    func op_lt(self, other: Money) -> bool {
        return self.cents < other.cents
    }
}

let total = Money(cents: 250) + Money(cents: 100) * 3     // 550
if total > Money(cents: 500) { ... }

!= is not op_eq. The four orderings come from op_lt alone: a > b is b < a, a <= b is not (b < a) and a >= b is not (a < b). a += b is a = a + b, and so on for the other compound assignments, and a < b < c chains as it does for numbers. The operators keep their usual precedence, and the operands are evaluated left to right whichever one the method belongs to.

When the left operand has no method for the operator, the right operand's reflected method is called instead, with the left operand as its argument: 3 * price calls op_rmul on price with 3. The left operand can be of any type, such as an int64, a float64 or a struct without op_mul:

type Vec = struct {
    x: float64
    y: float64

    func op_rmul(self, k: float64) -> Vec {
        return Vec(x: self.x * k, y: self.y * k)
    }
}

let v = 2.0 * Vec(x: 1.0, y: 2.0)     // Vec(x: 2.0, y: 4.0)

The reflected methods are op_radd, op_rsub, op_rmul, op_rdiv and op_rmod. The left operand's own method, when it has one, always wins, even if it doesn't take the right operand's type; and there is no reflected comparison.

A method that implements an operator takes self and one more parameter, and the comparison methods return bool; otherwise it is an error where the operator is used. A struct that doesn't declare the method still can't use the operator, so a + b on one without op_add is an error; only == and != need no method, on a plain struct (see above). A prefix minus is 0 - x, so -price calls op_rsub with 0. not, and, or and is are never overloaded.

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
Struct fields are laid out sequentially, each taking 8 bytes, allocated on the heap:

[ offset 0  ] field_0 : 8 bytes
[ offset 8  ] field_1 : 8 bytes
...

Struct variables hold a pointer to the allocation. The allocation is counted like any other object; before a struct (not a shared one) is changed, generated code checks that the count is 1, and otherwise _kod_obj_unique copies it, retaining what its fields refer to, stores the copy where the struct was, and lets go of the original.

items.title: Tasks
items.text: A task is a call that runs on a stack of its own, taking turns with the others on the program's one thread: one runs until it waits or gives way, then the next ready one runs. Nothing is shared between threads, so there are no data races. Concurrency (design) is the plan this is the start of; what is below is what is built.

items.title: spawn
items.text:
let user = spawn fetch_user(7)        // tasks.Task[str]
let orders = spawn fetch_orders(7)    // tasks.Task[int64]
print(user.wait())                    // user 7
print(orders.wait())                  // 14

spawn takes a call. The arguments are evaluated where spawn is, and the call then runs as a new task, which starts the next time the spawning one waits or gives way. For a call that gives back a value, spawn gives a tasks.Task[T], and task.wait() gives that value once the task has ended; until then the waiting task waits. A result can be waited for any number of times, by any task. A call that gives back nothing is spawned as a statement: spawn log(line).

The function, method or function value called is any a call can name: spawn fetch(url), spawn conn.serve(req), spawn handler(event), with labels and defaults as in the call. A receiver or function value is the one the name holds where spawn is. A mut argument can't be passed: the task runs after the spawning function has gone on.

spawn needs no import; a module that uses it imports tasks on its own, and naming the type in an annotation (tasks.Task[int64]) needs import "tasks".

items.title: Tasks belong to the function that spawns them
items.text:
A function doesn't return while a task it spawned is running: where it returns, by return, by throw or through a try, it first waits for each of its tasks that hasn't ended. So no task is left running by mistake, and main waits for its tasks before the program ends.

func fetch_all(anon urls: [str]) -> none {
    for url in urls {
        spawn fetch(url)
    }
}   // returns once every fetch has ended

items.title: Cancellation
items.text:
A function that returns an error, by throw or through a try, cancels the tasks it spawned that haven't ended before it waits for them; one that returns anything else just waits. A cancelled task goes on until it next waits, and that wait gives up:

  • reading, writing, accepting, connecting and waiting for a child fail with an IoError of kind .Cancelled, which try passes up, so the task's own tasks are cancelled in turn;
  • a sleep ends at once, a receive gives none and a send isn't made;
  • task.wait() and tasks.give_way() go on as usual: they can't fail.

A loop whose only waits are such ends by asking: tasks.cancelled() is whether the running task is cancelled.

task.cancel() cancels a task directly, unless it has ended; task.wait() then gives what the task gave back after giving up, an error from its wait for a fallible one. A task that never waits can't be cancelled, and nothing cancels a detached task.

tasks.within(d, body) runs body as a task for at most d: it gives what body gives back, or an IoError of kind .TimedOut once d has passed, when the task is cancelled and waited for.

let page = tasks.within(Duration(seconds: 5), func() -> str { return fetch_page() })

A task that should outlive its function is started with spawn detached: it gives no Task, nothing waits for it, and it runs until its call returns or the program ends.

spawn detached serve(n)

items.title: Channels
items.text:
A tasks.Channel[T] carries values from tasks that send them to tasks that receive them, in the order they were sent:

let numbers = tasks.Channel[int64]()             // unbuffered
spawn produce(numbers)
for n in numbers {                                // until it is closed
    print(n)
}
tasks.Channel[T](capacity: n) a channel that holds up to n values no task has received yet; n is 0 when left out ch.send(value) adds value; waits while capacity values sent before it haven't been received, so with 0 until a task receives this one ch.send_now(value) -> bool adds value if the channel is open and fewer than capacity values are waiting to be received, without waiting; whether it did ch.receive() -> T? the next value; waits while there is none, and gives none once the channel is closed and every value has been received ch.close() no more values will come: those waiting to receive get none once the rest are received for v in ch receives each value until the channel is closed and empty

Sending on a closed channel, or closing one twice, panics, as in Go; so does a send still waiting when its channel is closed. A channel can carry any value, shared structs too: every task is on the one thread. A channel of an optional type can't tell none sent from closed, as T? of an optional is that optional.

items.title: select
items.text:
select waits for whichever of several channel operations can go first:

select {
    receive(results) is r -> total += r? or 0
    send(jobs, next) -> sent += 1
    after(Duration(seconds: 5)) -> print("nothing for 5 s")
    else -> print("nothing ready")
}

Each channel and each value to send is evaluated first, in order. Then the arm whose operation can go at once runs, picked at random among those that can, so that none is passed over for good:

  • receive(ch) is v when ch has a value or is closed: v is what ch.receive() gives, a T? that is none once the channel is closed and empty; receive(ch) drops it;
  • send(ch, value) when ch can take the value without the sender waiting for long (it has room, or a task is waiting to receive), or is closed, when the send panics;
  • after(d) once d has passed and nothing else has gone;
  • else at once, when nothing else can go.

Without else, select waits until an arm can go. A cancelled task's select takes its first receive arm (with none if nothing is there), or its first after, or else.

items.title: Generators
items.text:
A function with yield in it is a generator: it gives back a tasks.Channel[T] at once and runs its body as a task, which each yield value sends on:

func countdown(anon n: int64) -> tasks.Channel[int64] {
    for i in 0..n {
        yield n - i
    }
}

for k in countdown(3) {
    print(k)                 // 3, 2, 1
}

The channel is unbuffered, so the body runs only as far ahead as the reader reads, and it is closed when the body ends, by its last line or a return, which takes no value. yield goes in a named function or method that gives back a tasks.Channel[T], not in a function literal.

The body runs while something holds the channel. Once nothing does, say a for over it stopped early and the channel was let go, the body ends at its yield, as at a return there: the channel isn't closed, nothing being left to read it. A body already waiting in a yield when that happens ends when the next generator starts. A cancelled body's yield ends it too. Like a spawn detached task, the body belongs to no function, so nothing waits for it.

for k in countdown(1000000) {
    if k < 999998 {
        break                // countdown's body ends at its next `yield`
    }
}

items.title: Helpers
items.text:
tasks.all(fs: [func() -> T or Error]) -> [T] or Error runs each call as a task and gives back their results in order, or the first error to come, after cancelling the others tasks.first(fs: [func() -> T or Error]) -> T or Error runs each as a task and gives back the first result that isn't an error, cancelling the others, or the last error when all fail tasks.map_concurrently(xs: [T], f: func(T) -> U, limit: int64) -> [U] f of each of xs, in order, with at most limit calls running at a time tasks.Mutex() lock() waits until no other task holds it, unlock() lets the next one have it

A Mutex is for a value that must not change between being read and written back: across a wait, or across a loop iteration or a call, where a task may be preempted.

items.title: Waiting for I/O
items.text:
A task that would wait for the outside world lets the others run meanwhile:

  • time.sleep(d);
  • reading and writing a posix.Fd, and so a socket, a pipe to a child or anything streams are built on, including TLS and HTTP;
  • tcp accepting and connecting;
  • waiting for a child process (process.Child.wait).

While the others have nothing to do either, the program waits for the first of those events (kevent). A program with one task just blocks there, as without tasks.

Still holding up every task: posix.poll, io.read_stdin_line and the rest of io's standard input (read through C's buffered FILE), looking up a host name (getaddrinfo has no form that doesn't block), and reading a regular file, which is ready at once. Two tasks waiting to read one descriptor at the same time aren't supported.

Closing a descriptor, a listener or a TLS stream that another task waits for ends that wait with an error (Bad file descriptor; for TLS, connection is closed).

Timeouts hold in a task as without tasks: tcp.connect's, and a socket's own (tcp.set_timeout, and so the HTTP client's), which ends a read or write that waits too long with .TimedOut. HTTP has requests made at the same time, and a server that serves each connection in a task.

items.title: Signals
items.text:
signals.listen gives the signals that come to the program on a channel, instead of what they would do by themselves, such as end it:

import "process" { Signal }
import "signals"

func reload_on_hup() -> none or Error {
    let sigs = try signals.listen([.Hup])
    for _sig in sigs.channel {
        reload()
    }
}
Name Meaning signals.listen(sigs) a Signals or Error for a list of process.Signal; .Kill is an InvalidInput error s.channel a Channel[Signal] of those that have come s.stop() ends it: closes the channel, and the signals do again what they did before

When several listen for a signal, each gets it, and it does what it did before again once the last has stopped. A signal that comes while 16 wait to be received is dropped. A signal the program was started to ignore, as by nohup, is given too. While something listens, waiting isn't a deadlock: a signal may come.

A task doesn't have to wait for one to come: a busy loop is preempted for it, but a call that holds up every task (as above) delays it. Programs started with process don't inherit any of it.

items.title: Giving way
items.text: tasks.give_way() lets the tasks that are ready run, then goes on. Tasks run in the order they became ready: a new one after those already waiting to run, and one that gives way after the others. A task gives way where it waits, and where it is preempted.

items.title: Preemption
items.text:
A task that runs for a while without waiting is made to give way, so one busy loop doesn't keep the others waiting: about every 10 ms, the running task gives way at the top of its next loop iteration or function call, as if it called tasks.give_way() there.

func crunch() -> int64 {
    mut sum: int64 = 0
    for i in 0..1000000000 {     // runs for seconds
        sum += i % 7
    }
    return sum
}

let busy = spawn crunch()
let quick = spawn work(1)
print(quick.wait())              // doesn't wait for crunch to end

So between two iterations of a loop, and as a function is called, other tasks may have run, as across a wait: a value read from a shared struct before may have changed since. Nothing else is interrupted: only those two are places where a task is preempted, so no reference count or array is left half changed.

Every loop and function has the check, a load of a flag the program sets when it is time, and a branch, not taken until then, to a call (Concurrency (design)); it costs a percent or two in the tightest loops, and a program that never starts a task pays that too. Under a simulation the same checks are counted, and the seed says at which one a task gives way. A child process made by fork (as testing.run does) isn't preempted.

Waiting that can't end, because every task is waiting (for a task, a channel or a send to be received; a task waiting for itself, say), stops the program: panic: all tasks are asleep: deadlock. A panic in a task stops the program, as anywhere, unless the function it belongs to runs under a catch. Its backtrace is the task's own calls, from the call spawn made (spawn fetch), then under spawned at: the calls the spawning task was in when it spawned it, and so on up to the program's first task.

A module-level variable is worked out at its first use, as without tasks (see Module-level variables). When its initializer waits and another task uses the variable meanwhile, that task waits for the value rather than work it out again.

Each task has 8 MB of stack, as the program's first thread has, reserved as address space and used only as far as the task goes, with a guard page below it: a recursion too deep for it stops the program, as on the first thread. A switch from one task to another costs about 50 ns, and starting a task about 1 µs: the stacks of tasks that have ended are kept for new ones.

items.title: What isn't built yet
items.text: Tasks run on one thread; using several cores is step 2.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Kod has built-in syntax for unit tests: test "description" { ... } blocks and an assert <expr> statement. kod test runs them.

items.title: A first test
items.text:
// arithmetic_test.kod
test "addition works" {
    assert 2 + 2 == 4
}

test "negative arithmetic" {
    assert -1 + 1 == 0
    assert -5 - 5 == -10
}

$ ./kod test arithmetic_test.kod
ok   addition works
ok   negative arithmetic

2/2 passed

items.title: assert <expr>
items.text:
If the expression evaluates to false, the current test is marked failed and the source text of the expression is captured in the failure message — no need to type f"got {x}, want {y}":

test "this one will fail" {
    let n: int64 = 7
    assert n == 4
}

    foo_test.kod:3:5: assertion failed: n == 4
FAIL this one will fail

Multiple asserts per test continue running — they accumulate failure messages but don't short-circuit, so a single test surfaces every failing condition at once.

Outside a test block, assert panics with the same message (exit 1). Same syntax, intent matches the surrounding context — like Rust's always-on assert!.

items.title: fail(msg)
items.text:
For failures that aren't a boolean check, call the builtin fail:

test "map lookup hits" {
    mut m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()
    m.set("a", 1)
    match m.get("a") {
        Some(v) -> assert v == 1
        none -> fail("missing key after set")
    }
}

fail is a builtin — no import needed. It works from any function a test calls, not only inside the test block. Outside kod test there is no test to fail, so fail panics with its message, as assert does outside a test.

items.title: Discovery
items.text:
• kod test <file> builds the file and every transitively imported module that contains test blocks, then runs them all in one binary.
  • kod test <dir> walks the directory for *_test.kod and builds them all into one binary, with no temporary module. Each file keeps its own type names (see Modules), so two test files may both declare a helper type Pt, and two test files may share a file name (a/dup_test.kod and b/dup_test.kod).
  • kod test . walks the entire project.
  • The walk skips a file with a path component below the directory that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files, scratch files such as .kod_compile_test.kod) and a build directory directly below it. (The test suite's own finder skips the dot-directories and a top-level build/, but not dot-files.) Only files count: a directory named x_test.kod is walked, not run. A match that is not a readable file (a link to nothing) stops the run with kod test: cannot read <path>, since a test skipped without a word reads as one that passed. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.

The aggregate exit code is 0 if every test passed, non-zero otherwise.

items.title: Each test in a process of its own
items.text:
Each test runs in a child process of the test binary, made with fork just before it, so a test that panics or crashes fails alone: its panic message (and backtrace) or the signal that killed it is printed under it, it reports FAIL, and the tests after it run as usual. A test starts from the state the program had before the first test, not where the test before it left it: what one test stores in a module-level variable, the next one doesn't see.

stdlib/foo_test.kod
  ok   one (1.20 ms)
panic: index 5 out of bounds for array of length 1
backtrace:
  #0  test "boom" (stdlib/foo_test.kod:7)
  FAIL boom (1.35 ms)
      killed by SIGSEGV
  FAIL bad pointer (985 μs)
  ok   three (1.30 ms)

A backtrace names a test's frame test "<its name>" and ends there. Starting the process costs about a millisecond, which the time shown includes.

items.title: Running code in a process of its own
items.text:
testing.run(body) runs the function body in a child process and gives back what that process did, so a test can check what a program prints, reads or exits with, and that something panics:

import "io"
import "testing"

test "indexing past the end panics" {
    let r = testing.run(func() {
        let xs = [1]
        print_int(xs[5])
    })
    assert r.status == 1
    assert r.stderr.contains("panic: index 5 out of bounds for array of length 1")
}

test "print ends the line" {
    let r = testing.run(func() { print("hi") })
    assert r.stdout == "hi\n"
}

test "read_stdin_line reads one line" {
    let r = testing.run(func() { print(io.read_stdin_line()) }, stdin: "a\nb\n")
    assert r.stdout == "a\n"
}

The result is a testing.Ran:

Field Meaning status the exit status: 0 when body returned, 1 when it panicked, 2 when it called fail; -1 when a signal ended it. body is a function, not a test block, so an assert in it panics when it fails signal the number of the signal that ended it (SIGSEGV is 11), else 0 stdout, stderr everything it wrote to them, through print or C's putchar alike

stdin: is what the child reads from standard input (nothing by default). The child starts from the state of the test at the call, and what it changes (variables it captured, module variables) stays in the child. Its output goes to files rather than pipes, so it can write any amount.

items.title: Output
items.text:
kod test replaces itself with the test binary, so the output appears as the tests run, and the exit code is the binary's. The reporter flushes stdout around every ok/FAIL line and the file header, and before a failure's detail goes to stderr, so the lines stay in order when stdout and stderr are the same pipe or log. What a test prints with print is flushed with them, so it comes out before that test's result line. A panic (an index out of bounds, a failed must) flushes stdout before its message too.

When stdout is a terminal, ok is green, FAIL red, and the time each test took dim; the summary line is green when all passed and red when any failed. The same NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb turn this off as for errors.

items.title: Hermetic tests
items.text: A test needs nothing the repository does not have, and no network: a test of code that talks to a server starts a server of its own on the loopback interface. A test that needs the internet does not belong among the *_test.kod files that kod test <dir> and the test suite run. A module under test may declare C files and libraries (see Link inputs); kod test compiles and links them like kod build does, and a kod:require file that is missing stops the build, naming the line that asks for it.

items.title: Layout convention
items.text:
Test files live next to the code they test, Go-style:

stdlib/
  builtins.kod
  map_test.kod
  primitives/
    int64.kod
    int64_test.kod
    str.kod
    str_test.kod

The naming convention *_test.kod makes them auto-discoverable by kod test <dir> without showing up as importable modules.

items.title: How it works (briefly)
items.text:
• The parser turns test "..." { ... } into a Decl.Test carrying a synthesized FuncDecl.
  • The codegen emits each test as a regular function (<prefix>$__test_N) and, per module, a <prefix>$__run_tests dispatcher. <prefix> is described in Modules.
  • The runner is a Kod module, stdlib/testing.kod, which kod test links into every test program (and kod build into any program with a test block, since the block's code is linked even though nothing runs it). Its counters are module-level variables.
  • kod test builds a runtime _main that calls every test-bearing module's __run_tests in turn, then the runner's summary once at the end.
  • fail/assert set a per-test "failed" flag the dispatcher reads after each test returns; that flag drives the ok / FAIL line and the aggregate count.

items.title: Testing the compiler itself
items.text:
make test rebuilds the toolchain, then builds and runs the test runner, tools/run_tests.kod, which runs every *_test.kod in the repository that contains test blocks through kod test <file> (skipping dot-directories and the top-level build/); the files of tests/unit run together, as one kod test tests/unit. A file passes when kod test exits 0, its summary line says all passed, and it ran at least as many tests as the file has test blocks. Among them:

  • Example programs (tests/examples_test.kod): every other tests/**/*.kod. Trailing // expected output:, // expected errors:, // expected stderr:, // expected status: and // expected mode: comments say what should happen. Each one is compiled and run; mode: skip opts out, for a module other fixtures import.
  • Self-hosting (tests/selfhost_test.kod): the fixed-point check described in Self-hosting.

The tests run programs through the native tools, build/apps/kod/kod and build/stage1/sh_kodc.

The runner runs as many files at once as the machine has cores (-j N for another number), the slow ones first. Files that build the same program, into the same build/apps/<name>, share a group, and two of a group never run at the same time; the lists of groups, slow files and serial files are at the top of tools/run_tests.kod. The serial files (those that rebuild or replace the kod driver, write into the project root, or run make on the real tree) run afterwards, one at a time. Each file has 120 seconds: one still running then is killed with everything it started, and fails. The runner prints a line per file as it ends, then the whole output of each file that failed and a summary, and exits 1 if any failed. Given files or directories, it runs only those:

$ make -s stage1 kod && build/apps/kod/kod build tools/run_tests.kod
$ build/apps/run_tests/run_tests -j 4 stdlib/ tests/lsp_test.kod

make gates is what to run before a commit: make fmt-check, which runs kod fmt --check (see CLI) on every .kod file git tracks except the few in the Makefile's FMT_SKIP, whose spacing is what they test or which don't parse on purpose; then make test, then make test again with the runtime built with -DRC_POISON, which overwrites freed memory so a use after free shows up. It refuses to run when there is a link.local.cfg, since it writes its own for the poisoned pass, and removes it again however the pass ends.

items.title: Time
items.text:
stdlib/time.kod has two clocks, a Duration type, sleep, and a Time type for timestamps.

import "time"
import "time" { Duration }

let started = time.monotonic_ns()
time.sleep(Duration(ms: 250))
let took = Duration(ns: time.monotonic_ns() - started)
print(took.to_str())                       // 250.31ms

items.title: Clocks
items.text:
Function Returns monotonic_ns() nanoseconds from an unspecified origin that never go backwards; only differences mean anything. Use it to time things. unix_ns() nanoseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC by the wall clock. It can jump if the system clock is adjusted, so it is not for measuring elapsed time. monotonic_res_ns() the smallest step monotonic_ns() can take, in nanoseconds; at least 1.

Both are plain int64, which holds about 292 years of nanoseconds.

items.title: Duration
items.text:
A Duration is a length of time, kept as nanoseconds in an int64 (ns). Make one by naming the units you want; they add up, and each defaults to 0:

Duration(seconds: 5)
Duration(ms: 250)
Duration(minutes: 1, seconds: 30)
Duration()                       // zero

The units are hours, minutes, seconds, ms, us and ns, and labels go in that order, largest first, as in Duration(seconds: 1, ms: 500). Duration is a struct with a custom constructor, so Duration(...) is the only way to build one from units, and the units are labels, not types: Duration(seconds: 90) and Duration(minutes: 1, seconds: 30) are equal.

items.title: Arithmetic and comparison
items.text:
Duration defines the operators:

let a = Duration(seconds: 2)
let b = Duration(ms: 500)
a + b                  // 2.5s
a - b                  // 1.5s
a * 3                  // 6s
3 * a                  // 6s
a / 4                  // 500ms
-a                     // -2s
a > b                  // true
a == Duration(ms: 2000)   // true

A duration times or divided by an int64 is a duration, and Duration has no Duration * Duration or Duration / Duration: use a.ns / b.ns for a ratio.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Method Meaning as_ms() the whole milliseconds in it, truncated toward zero as_seconds() the whole seconds in it, truncated toward zero as_hours() the whole hours in it, truncated toward zero as_days() the whole 24-hour days in it, truncated toward zero ceil_ms() milliseconds, rounded up for a positive duration, so that a short timeout never becomes 0 (which most timeouts treat as none) to_str() a short reading, such as 1h2m3s, 1.5s, 250ms, 12.5us, 40ns or 0s

to_str writes hours and minutes only when the duration has them (a duration of an hour or more always shows minutes and seconds, as in 1h0m0s), seconds with a fraction when it has one, and below a second the largest unit that keeps the number at 1 or more. A negative duration starts with -.

items.title: Sleeping
items.text:
func sleep(anon d: Duration) -> none

waits at least d, to the resolution of the system clock, and a signal doesn't cut it short. A zero or negative duration returns at once.

items.title: Timestamps
items.text:
A Time is a moment: whole seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, negative before it, and nanos from 0 to 999999999 on top. It has no time zone of its own, and reads as UTC.

import "time"

let created = time.parse("2026-01-02T03:04:05+01:00")? or time.now()
print(created.to_str())                       // 2026-01-02T02:04:05Z
print(created.utc().year)                     // 2026
print((time.now() - created).as_days())       // how many days ago
Function Returns now() the wall clock's time parse(s) the Time of an RFC 3339 timestamp, or none if s isn't one parse_date(s) midnight UTC of a YYYY-MM-DD date, or none if s isn't one

parse takes what APIs send: 2026-01-02T03:04:05Z, with a fraction of a second as in 05.25Z, and an offset as in 05+01:00. A t and a z may be lowercase, as RFC 3339 allows. Digits past nanoseconds are dropped. It checks the calendar, so 2026-02-29 is none. A leap second, :60, is read as the first second after it, since a Time has no way to hold one.

Method Meaning t + d the Time a Duration later a - b the Duration from b to a, which panics past about 292 years, as a Duration does a == b, a < b and the like whether they're the same moment, or which comes first utc() a Utc with year, month (1 to 12), day, hour, minute and second to_str() RFC 3339 in UTC, with a fraction only if there is one, as in 2026-01-02T02:04:05.25Z

items.title: Durations in other modules
items.text: The timeouts and deadlines of net/tcp, net/tls and the HTTP client are Durations: Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15)).

items.title: Tuples
items.text:
A tuple is a few values together, of types of their own, that have no need of a name:

let p = (3, "three")            // a (int64, str)
print(p.0)                      // 3
print(p.1)                      // three

let (n, word) = p
print(f"{n} is {word}")         // 3 is three

Its type is the types of its elements in parentheses: (int64, str), [(int64, int64)], (str, (bool, float64))?. A tuple has two to eight elements; for more, or where the elements deserve names, declare a struct. (x) is just x.

items.title: Taking one apart
items.text:
let and mut take a tuple's elements as names of their own, with _ for what isn't needed. Tuples nest:

let (low, high) = bounds()
let (_, top) = bounds()
let ((a, b), c) = ((1, 2), "x")
mut (x, y) = (0, 1)
x += 1

So does a for:

let pairs = [(1, "one"), (2, "two")]
for (n, word) in pairs {
    print(f"{n} {word}")
}
for i, (n, word) in pairs {
    print(f"{i}: {n} {word}")
}

mut grid = Map[(int64, int64), str]()
grid[(0, 1)] = "a"
for (x, y), name in grid {
    print(f"{x},{y} {name}")
}

In an assignment the right side is worked out first, then its elements are stored from left to right, so this swaps:

mut a = 1
mut b = 2
mut xs = [5, 6]
(a, b) = (b, a)
(xs[0], xs[1]) = (xs[1], xs[0])

items.title: Elements
items.text:
p.0 is the first element, p.1 the next. One of a mut tuple can be assigned:

mut p = (1, "a")
p.0 += 1
p.1 = "b"
assert p == (2, "b")

A tuple is a value, as a plain struct is: assigning or passing it gives the other place the tuple as it is.

An array of tuples of two to four numbers, bools or payload-free enums keeps the elements' values in the array itself (see Arrays of small structs), so a [(int64, int64)] or a Set[(int64, int64)] costs no allocation per element.

items.title: Where a tuple goes
items.text:
Each element of a literal takes its type from where the tuple goes, as it would by itself:

let p: (int64?, [str]) = (none, [])
let found: [(str, int64 | str)] = [("a", 1), ("b", "x")]

func divide(anon a: int64, by b: int64) -> (int64, int64) {
    return (a / b, a % b)
}
let (q, r) = divide(17, by: 5)
assert q == 3 and r == 2

items.title: Patterns
items.text:
In a match and after is, (p, q) matches a tuple element by element. What stands for an element is any pattern, or a name to bind:

func where_is(anon p: (int64, int64)) -> str {
    match p {
        (0, 0) -> return "origin"
        (x, 0) -> return f"on the x axis at {x}"
        (0, _) -> return "on the y axis"
        (x, y) if x == y -> return "on the diagonal"
        (_, _) -> return "elsewhere"
    }
}

let o: (int64, str)? = (1, "a")
if o is Some((n, _)) {
    print(n)
}

A pattern of names alone always matches, so it covers the type.

items.title: Comparing, hashing and text
items.text:
As plain structs do (see Structs are values), two tuples of one type compare with == when their elements do, can be a Map's key or a Set's element when their elements can be hashed, and print when their elements do:

assert (1, "a") == (1, "a") and (1, "a") != (1, "b")
print((1, ("a", [true])))       // (1, (a, [true]))

Tuples are also ordered by <, <=, > and >= when their elements are: by the first element, and where those are equal by the next. So min, max and sort.sorted take them:

import "sort"

assert (1, 9) < (2, 0) and (2, "a") < (2, "b")
assert sort.sorted([(2, "b"), (1, "z"), (2, "a")]) == [(1, "z"), (2, "a"), (2, "b")]

items.title: Types
items.text:
Kod is statically typed. Every parameter needs a type annotation; a let without one takes the type of its value.

Naming a type that doesn't exist is an error wherever a type is written: an annotation, a parameter or return type, a struct field, an enum payload, an alias target or a type argument. The error carries a did-you-mean hint when a known type name is close.

An unannotated let takes the type of its value. If the compiler can't work out that type, the binding is an error (cannot infer the type of `x`; add a type annotation), and so is any other use of such a value, like a match subject or an argument. A value whose type is unknown because of an earlier error, such as a call to an unknown function or method, a misspelled field, an unknown variant or an unknown type, doesn't produce further errors where it's used.

items.title: Bindings and mutability
items.text:
A let binding is immutable: once set, reassigning the name is a compile error. Use mut for a binding you need to reassign. += and the other compound assignments count as reassignment, so they require mut too.

let max: int64 = 100
mut total: int64 = 0
total += max          // ok — total is mutable

max = 50              // error: cannot reassign immutable binding `max`

Mutability belongs to each binding. A let x in a block that hides an outer mut x (see Blocks and bindings) can't be reassigned inside that block, and after the block the outer x can be again. Likewise a mut x in a block leaves an outer let x immutable once the block ends. A for variable and the names a pattern binds, in a match arm, if … is or a let-else, can be reassigned without mut, whatever binding the name had in another block.

A local, whether a let, a parameter, a for variable or a pattern's binding, can't take the name of a type it can see: let str = 3 and for Circle in shapes are errors (`Circle` is the name of a type; give the local another name). In a pattern, a type's name is that type's pattern (see Type patterns).

Assigning to a name that was never declared is an error too (declare it with mut first), and so is assigning to anything other than a name, a field (p.x = 1) or an element (xs[0] = 1).

The value of an annotated let, of an assignment to a name and of an assignment to a field must have the declared type: let x: int64 = "s" is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), and so is storing an int64 in a bool or an [int64] in a [str]. A T is accepted where a T? is declared and is checked as a T: with type Words = [str], let w: Words? = [] is fine and let w: Words? = [1] reports the element (expected `str`, got `int64`), while let x: int64? = "s" names the declared type (expected `int64?`, got `str`). none is accepted wherever an optional or none is declared, a struct or primitive other than bytes where an interface is, and [] as any array type. A T? isn't accepted where a T is declared; unwrap it first with must x or x? or default. An optional is passed on as it is, so a T? where a U? is declared needs T to be U: like an [Sq] isn't a [Shape], an Sq? or int64? isn't a Shape? even when Sq and int64 implement Shape; rewrap it instead, as in match sq { Some(v) -> v none -> none }. A function value must match a function type exactly, since a function is never adapted: a function taking a struct isn't a func(SomeInterface) -> ..., and one returning int64 isn't a func() -> int64?. Without an annotation, let x = none and let xs = [] are errors, since their type can't be inferred.

Function and method arguments, struct constructor fields and enum payloads are checked the same way (see Argument types), so m.set(5, 1) on a Map[str, int64] is an error. So are element stores (xs[i] = v, m[k] = v, see Indexing) and return values (see Return values).

Parameters are immutable too. A mut parameter is the caller's variable, passed with mut at the call site, and the caller sees what the function assigns to it (see mut parameters):

func bump(anon mut x: int64) -> none {
    x = x + 1
}

mut n = 1
bump(mut n)       // n is 2

A struct's fields are assigned only through a mut name, as an array's elements are; a shared struct's fields through any name that holds it (see Field mutation).

items.title: Module-level constants
items.text:
A let at the top level of a module names a constant. It needs a type, and mut isn't allowed there:

let MAX_BLOCK: int64 = 65535
let SECONDS_PER_DAY: int64 = 24 * 60 * 60
let GREETING: str = "hello, " + "world"
let PRIMES: [int64] = [2, 3, 5, 7]
let DEFAULT_MODE: Mode = Mode.Fast

The value is built only from literals, operators, array literals, enum variants without a payload, and other constants. A call, a constructor, an f-string, a match or anything else is an error (this can't be part of a module-level constant), so a constant never has a side effect, and a constant that refers to itself, directly or through others, is an error (constant `A` refers to itself).

A constant is used by its name. Another module's is import "limits" { MAX_BLOCK } or limits.MAX_BLOCK, like a function's. A local variable or parameter of the same name hides it, as it does a function, and a constant and a function can't share a name in one module. A constant can't be assigned, and neither can its elements (`PRIMES` is a constant and can't be assigned; a module-level `mut` can be).

Each use of an array constant is an array of its own, so changing one changes nothing else: after mut p = PRIMES and p[0] = 1, PRIMES[0] is still 2. A use that can't change the array, indexing it, len of it or a for over it, reads one copy that the program builds the first time and keeps, so a lookup table read in a loop allocates nothing.
