Indexing an array of arrays still makes a new array, since the element read could be changed. A string can't be changed, so a string constant is built once.

An int64 or bool constant whose value is literals and the operators +, -, *, &, |, ^, << and >> on them, like MAX_BLOCK and SECONDS_PER_DAY above, is worked out when the program is compiled and put in place at each use, and so is a float64 constant that is one literal: reading one costs what the literal would.

items.title: Module-level variables
items.text:
A mut at the top level of a module names a variable that every function of the program shares. Like a constant, it needs a type:

mut calls: int64 = 0
mut seen: Map[str, bool] = Map[str, bool]()
mut log_lines: [str] = []

func remember(anon name: str) -> bool {
    calls += 1
    if seen.contains(name) {
        return false
    }
    seen.set(name, true)
    log_lines += [name]
    return true
}

The value can be any expression, calls included. It is worked out once, the first time the program uses the variable (reads it or assigns it), so a variable nothing uses costs nothing, and the order in which modules are declared or imported doesn't matter. A value that needs its own variable to be worked out first, directly or through a function it calls, stops the program with panic: `calls` is used while its value is being worked out. Once it is worked out, a read is a few instructions and no call: a look at whether it is, and a load.

Another module reads a variable the way it reads a constant (import "stats" { calls } or stats.calls), but only the declaring module assigns it: `calls` can only be assigned in stats.kod, and only it changes an array, map or struct the variable holds (seen.set(...)). A shared struct the variable holds can be changed through its fields from anywhere, as with any shared struct. A name that starts with _ keeps the variable private to its module. A local of the same name hides it, and a variable, constant or function can't share a name in one module. A constant can't use a variable, since a constant has no side effects (a module-level constant can't use the variable `calls`). A variable or constant that holds a function is called like one: mut on_error: func(str) -> none = log, then on_error("disk full").

Tests run in one program, one after another, so a test sees what the tests before it left in a module-level variable.

items.title: Primitive types
items.text: Type Description Example int64 64-bit signed integer 42, -7 float64 64-bit IEEE 754 float, see Floating point 1.5, 2e9 str UTF-8 string "hello" bool Boolean true, false none No value (unit type) —

items.title: Integer literals
items.text:
let n: int64 = 42
let m: int64 = -1

Base prefixes for non-decimal forms:

let hex: int64 = 0xff           // 255
let oct: int64 = 0o755          // 493
let bin: int64 = 0b1010         // 10

Decimal literals may use a space as a thousands separator. The grouping is strict — a head of 1-3 digits followed by space-prefixed groups of exactly 3 digits each:

let pop: int64 = 1 000 000      // ok
let bad: int64 = 1 23 456       // error — `23 456` isn't a group of 3, so it's another literal

A literal must fit in int64, in any base: 9223372036854775808 or 0x8000000000000000 is an error at the literal, not a value that wraps around. The one exception is the smallest int64, written as a prefix - and its digits, with or without a space between them: -9223372036854775808 or - 9223372036854775808. In x - 9223372036854775808 the - subtracts, and in -9223372036854775808.to_str() it negates the call, so in both the literal stands alone and is an error; the second suggests (-9223372036854775808).

Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, %. A compound assignment, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, &=, |=, ^=, <<= or >>=, updates a variable, field, or array element in place: n -= 3 is n = n - 3, and n *= a + b is n = n * (a + b). An assignment binds looser than every operator, so ok = a and b assigns a and b. A prefix - negates the whole call, field access, index or ? after it, and binds tighter than any binary operator: -xs[0] is -(xs[0]), -p.get() is -(p.get()), and -a * b is (-a) * b. That includes an unwrap's default, so -x? or 3 is -(x? or 3) and gives -3 for a none. It also makes -n.to_str() the negation of a str, an error whose hint suggests (-n).to_str().

Integer / rounds toward zero and % takes the sign of its left operand, so -7 / 2 is -3 and -7 % 2 is -1, and (a / b) * b + a % b is always a. For a remainder that counts as a clock does, (-7).mod(2) is 1 (see n.mod(m) below). Dividing by zero, with / or %, panics: panic: integer division by zero, with a backtrace.

A result of +, -, * or / that doesn't fit in an int64 panics too: panic: integer overflow. That includes negating the smallest int64 and dividing it by -1, the one quotient that doesn't fit (its remainder is 0). Where wrapping around is what is wanted, as in a hash or a random number generator, n.wrapping_add(m), n.wrapping_sub(m) and n.wrapping_mul(m) keep the low 64 bits of the result instead. A constant whose value overflows panics when it is read. The checks cost one instruction and one branch for + and -, a few for *, and two for a / whose divisor isn't a literal.

let big: int64 = 9223372036854775807
print(big.wrapping_add(1))              // -9223372036854775808
print(big + 1)                          // panic: integer overflow

A loop counter needs no check when the loop's condition bounds it: in a for whose condition has i < e (or i > e), alone, joined by and or in a chain, a body whose only write to i is one i += 1 (or i -= 1), not inside a loop within the body, can't take i past e. for i in a..b counts that way. With ..= or another step the counter steps with a wrapping add, and a step that wraps ends the loop, so for i in n..=MAX stops after MAX.

>> shifts in zeros, so it treats an int64 as 64 bits rather than a signed number, and so do the counting methods here. Each method is a few instructions at most:

Method Gives n.leading_zeros() how many zero bits are above the highest one bit; 64 for 0 n.trailing_zeros() how many zero bits are below the lowest one bit; 64 for 0 n.count_ones() how many bits are one; 64 for -1 n.mod(m) n % m moved into 0..m (or m..0 for a negative m): (-1).mod(100) is 99, where -1 % 100 is -1; panics for m 0 as % does n.abs() n without its sign; panics for the smallest int64, whose positive twin doesn't fit n.wrapping_add(m) n.wrapping_sub(m) n.wrapping_mul(m) n + m, n - m and n * m wrapped around to 64 bits, where the operators panic n.mul_high(m) the top 64 bits of the 128-bit product of n and m as unsigned numbers; n.wrapping_mul(m) is the bottom 64 n.carry_add(m) 1 when n + m doesn't fit in 64 bits as unsigned numbers, so n.wrapping_add(m) lost a carry, else 0; with no branch n.borrow_sub(m) 1 when n is below m as unsigned numbers, so n.wrapping_sub(m) borrowed, else 0; with no branch 
print(1.leading_zeros())                // 63
print(40.trailing_zeros())              // 3
print(0xff.count_ones())                // 8
print((1 << 62).mul_high(8))            // 2
print((-1).carry_add(1))                // 1: 2^64 - 1 plus 1
print(1.borrow_sub(-1))                 // 1: 1 is below 2^64 - 1

items.title: Boolean literals
items.text:
let flag: bool = true
let other: bool = false

Logical operators: and, or, not. Comparison: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Comparisons, and/or/not and is always produce a bool, so let ok = a < b is a bool binding and f"{a < b}" prints true or false.

not binds looser than comparisons and is, and tighter than and and or: not a == b is not (a == b), not x is .Red is not (x is .Red), and not a and b is (not a) and b. Its operand must be a bool; test an optional with x is none.

and and or don't mix without parentheses: a and b or c is an error that suggests (a and b) or c and a and (b or c), since either could be meant. A run of one of them, a or b or c, needs none, and neither does the or of x? or default, which is no boolean operator.

bool and int64 don't mix, and nothing else stands in for a bool. Both operands of and and or must be bool, and so must the condition of an if, a for loop and an assert: test a number with n != 0 and an optional with x is not none. Arithmetic, bitwise and ordering operators don't take bool operands, and ==/!= compare a bool only with another bool, so b == 1, true + 1 and if flags & 1 are errors. &, ^ and | bind tighter than comparisons, as in Python and Rust rather than C, so a bit test needs no parentheses: flags & 1 != 0 is (flags & 1) != 0, and a == b | c is a == (b | c). Among them & binds tightest and | loosest, and shifts and arithmetic bind tighter still: a | b & c << 1 is a | (b & (c << 1)).

Chained comparisons are supported Python-style: a < b < c is (a < b) and (b < c) with b evaluated once. The operands are evaluated left to right, and a chain stops at the first comparison that is false, so in a < b < f() f isn't called when a < b is false. Any comparison chain works — 0 <= i < len(xs) is the canonical bounds check.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
An operator never converts its operands; both must be of a type it takes, and of the same type:

Operator Operands Result + two int64, two float64, two str, two bytes or two arrays of one type the operands' type - * / two int64 or two float64 the operands' type % two int64 int64 & \| ^ << >> two int64 int64 < <= > >= two int64, two float64, two str or two bytes bool == != two int64, two float64, bool, str or bytes, two values of an enum or of a plain struct, an enum value and a variant, two arrays of one type, an optional and none, a T? and a T? or T, or a union and a value that goes into it, where what they hold has an == bool in not in a value and an array of its type, two str, or a value and a type with a contains method that takes it, such as Map and Set bool and or two bool bool

So "n = " + 5 is an error (cannot add `str` and `int64`); write "n = " + str(5) or f"n = {5}". s - t on two strings, xs * "2" on an array (an array repeats by an int64: see Repetition), -s on a string, s + b with b: bytes and red < blue on an enum are errors too. A compound assignment follows the rules of its operator. An index, as in xs[i], s[i] and xs[i] = v, and the bounds of a slice must be int64, so xs["a"] and xs[true] are errors, and so is an int64? index; unwrap it first.

== and != compare str and bytes by content, enums by variant (see Equality), arrays by their elements (see Comparing) and plain structs by their fields (see Structs are values). Nothing else has an ==: comparing two interface values, function values or shared structs without an op_eq is an error. Comparing values of two different types, like an int64 with a str or values of two different enums, is an error too.

x in c says whether c has x: an array an element == to it, a str the substring x, and anything else what c.contains(x) gives, so a Map the key x and a Set the element x. x not in c is its negation. in binds like the comparisons, and doesn't chain with them, so not x in c is not (x in c):

assert 2 in [1, 2, 3]
assert "ell" in "hello"
assert "a" not in seen

items.title: none
items.text:
none is the unit value. Functions that return nothing are declared -> none:

func say_hi() -> none {
    print("hi")
}

items.title: Optional types
items.text:
Append ? to any type to make it optional:

let x: int64? = none
let y: int64? = 42

The ? goes after the whole type, so [str]? is an optional array and Box[int64]? an optional generic struct. names? or [] is the array, or an empty one when there is none.

Test with is and destructure with Some(binding):

if x is none {
    print("nothing")
}
if y is not none {
    print("got something")
}
match y {
    Some(v) -> print_int(v)
    none -> print("nothing")
}

is not Pat reads as one operator — is negated by the trailing not — and works anywhere is Pat does (expression context and the if … is … form). It's the predicate spelling of "does this not match"; for the if form, the body runs when the pattern does not match.

is and is not bind like comparisons, tighter than and and or, so if ready and x is none reads as ready and (x is none). A pattern that binds a name, like Some(v), works in an if or for condition and in an and chain, where v is in scope for the operands after it: x is Some(v) and v > 0 (see if X is …). Under or or not it is an error, since v could be unset. Some(_) or Some(_v) binds nothing and works anywhere.

Or peel off the Some with let .Some(v) = y else { ... }:

let .Some(v) = y else { return -1 }
// v is in scope and has type int64

An optional of an optional is that optional, since T? is T | none and a union is a set: with type MaybeInt = int64?, MaybeInt? is int64?, and so is T? in a generic function where T is int64?. So none means one thing. A Map[str, int64?]'s get returns none both for a missing key and for a stored none; contains tells them apart. Where the difference matters, an enum that names both cases says it better.

items.title: Unwrapping: x? or default and must x
items.text:
x? or default on a T? value evaluates to T, or to the default when x is none. must x evaluates to T, and stops the program on none with the position of the value, as it stops on a failed T or Error:

let n: int64? = "hello".find("l")
let idx: int64  = n? or -1     // -1 if none
let idx2: int64 = must n       // stops if none

? is always the safe side: it goes before or or . (see Optional chaining), and a bare x? is an error that says to write must x or x? or default. Whatever can stop the program is spelled must. must takes the expression and its ., [...] and (...) steps, so must m.get(k) unwraps what get returns, and indexing the unwrapped value needs parentheses: (must m.get(k))[0].

The default is evaluated lazily (only when the value is none), and its type must match the unwrapped T, unless it's a call that never returns, such as panic(...) or a helper that ends in one (see Return values). It's built as a T: with T an interface, a struct default becomes an interface value, and with T an enum, .Up names T's variant. x? or d on a value that isn't optional is an error. A following or outside the unwrap stays a boolean operator: x? or 1 substitutes 1 for none, but (must x) or some_bool is a boolean-or on the unwrapped value (and a type error unless T is bool).

== and != compare an optional with none, with another optional of its type, or with a value of its type: with n: int64?, n == 3 holds when n has 3, n == none when it has nothing, and two optionals are equal when both are none or both hold equal values. That needs a T that has an ==. Other operators don't look inside an optional: n < 4 and n + 1 are errors; unwrap first, as in (n? or 0) + 1.

items.title: Optional chaining
items.text: On a struct T?, x?.field and x?.method(...) evaluate to an optional of the field or return type, and to none without touching the field when x is none. x?.method(...) works on any T? whose T has methods: n?.to_str() on an int64?, s?.find("l") on a str?, or a method of an interface value. A field or return type that is already optional stays one level deep, so chains read through: with a: A? whose b: B? has n: int64?, a?.b?.n is an int64?. The rest of a chain after ?. runs on the unwrapped value, so x?.name.upper(), x?.items[0] and json.parse(s)?.get("k").as_str() reach past the first step and are none as soon as x is; a ?. is needed again only where a step gives an optional itself, as a?.b?.n does. The chain ends at a ? that isn't followed by ., so x?.name.upper()? or "" defaults the whole chain. x?.method(...) takes arguments like an ordinary method call: arguments it leaves out take the method's defaults, and none of them is evaluated when x is none. A T? doesn't stand in for a T: returning t?.name from a function declared -> str or -> str or Error is an error, so unwrap it first with t?.name? or t?.name? or "", or declare the function -> str?. t?.name = v isn't an assignment; unwrap first. For a shared struct that is if t is Some(u) { u.name = v }; a struct is a value, so change a mut copy and store it back: mut u = must t, u.name = v, t = u.

items.title: Arrays
items.text:
[T] is a resizable array of element type T:

let nums: [int64] = [1, 2, 3]
let names: [str] = ["alice", "bob"]

See Arrays for indexing, slicing, and concatenation.

items.title: Structs
items.text:
Named product types:

type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64
}

See Structs.

items.title: Enums
items.text:
Tagged unions:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

See Enums.

items.title: Generics
items.text:
Type-parametric structs are monomorphised at compile time:

type Pair[A, B] = struct {
    first: A
    second: B
}

let p: Pair[str, int64] = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42)

The type arguments of a constructor call pick the instantiation, so let p = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42) needs no annotation. A generic struct always needs them: a bare Pair(first: "hello", second: 42) is an error that says to write Pair[A, B](...). A generic struct's method signatures are always checked, but a method body is compiled only for each instantiation, so the body of a struct that nothing instantiates isn't checked. An error in a body is reported once, for the first instantiation that hits it, and names that instantiation, like Pair[str, int64]. A type argument is a name (str, ast.Expr), an array ([str]), an optional of either (int64?, [str]?) or another instantiation (Map[str, Pair[int64, str]]()). Function types (func(int64) -> str) and optional instantiations (Pair[str, int64]?) aren't accepted. Passing the wrong number of type arguments, or type arguments to a struct that isn't generic, is an error, and so is a Type[A, B] that isn't followed by (. The same goes for a generic written as a type: let m: Map = ... is an error that says to write Map[K, V], and Map[str] is one for the missing type argument.

Map[K, V] (in builtins) is the canonical example.

Functions can be generic too, with their type arguments usually inferred from the call: see Generic functions.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text:
Method-based contracts that types can opt into by declaring the right methods. Primitives implement them implicitly via boxing.

interface Printable {
    func to_str(self) -> str
}

func show(anon x: Printable) -> none {
    print(x.to_str())
}

show(42)        // works — int64 implements Printable via primitives/int64.kod
show(true)      // same for bool

A call on an interface value must name one of the interface's methods, with arguments that match its signature; an unknown method is an error. A trailing argument the call leaves out takes the default the interface declares for it (func greet(self, times: int64 = 2) -> str), so give each implementation the same default.

A struct, an enum, int64, str or bool becomes an interface value wherever one is expected (a bytes value or a union can't be one): an annotated let, an argument, a field, an array element, a value stored with m[k] = v, and a return value, including the value of a -> Shape? or -> Shape or Error function.

The type must declare every method of the interface, with the same parameter and return types (labels and defaults may differ). Otherwise using it as the interface is an error at that spot, such as struct `P` doesn't implement interface `Shape`: missing method `area` (enum `E` ... for an enum) or method `area` is `func(int64) -> int64`, not `func() -> int64`. throw counts too, since it makes its value an Error.

items.title: Provided methods
items.text:
A method in an interface can have a body. It is provided: every type that implements the interface has it, without declaring it:

interface Reader {
    func read(self, anon max: int64) -> bytes or Error

    // Read until the end of the stream.
    func read_all(self) -> bytes or Error {
        mut out: bytes = kod_str_to_bytes("")
        for true {
            let chunk = try self.read(4096)
            if len(chunk) == 0 {
                return out
            }
            out += chunk
        }
    }
}

let f = try posix.open_read("data.bin")     // a posix.Fd, which has `read`
let data = try f.read_all()                  // the Reader's `read_all`
  • In the body, self is the interface: it can call the interface's methods, provided or not, be passed where the interface is expected, and be downcast with is. It has no fields, and the implementing type's other methods aren't reachable through it.
  • Only the methods without a body are required: a type with read is a Reader, and has read_all too.
  • A type that declares a method of the same name overrides it; the signature must match the interface's, and calls through the interface run the type's own method.
  • On a value of the type itself, as f.read_all() above, a method the type doesn't declare is looked up among the provided methods of the interfaces it implements that the calling module can see: its own and those of the modules it imports, directly or not. When more than one of them provides a method of that name, the call is an error that names them; convert the value to the one you mean, as in let r: Reader = f.
  • The body runs once for all types: its calls on self go through the method table, as for any interface value.

An interface value converts to another interface that declares only methods the first one has, with the same parameter and return types, in any order. It goes wherever a struct would (an argument, an annotated let, a field, a return value), and a downcast still works on the result:

interface Reader {
    func read(self) -> int64
}
interface ReadCloser {
    func close(self) -> none
    func read(self) -> int64
}

func drain(anon r: Reader) -> int64 {
    return r.read()
}

let rc: ReadCloser = File(n: 7)
drain(rc)                      // 7
let r: Reader = rc
if r is File(f) {              // still the File
    print_int(f.n)
}

The second interface's provided methods don't have to be in the first. For each one the first lacks, the converted value gets its type's own method of that name, when the type declares one with the same parameter and return types, as it would have been boxed straight into the second interface; else the body in the second interface. (An instance of a generic type is the one exception: it gets the second interface's body, since only the methods it uses are compiled.) A method the first interface has keeps what that table holds, except that a provided body the value got from an earlier conversion is looked up again the same way. A method the first interface provides can't stand in for one the second requires: that converts nothing, and is the usual expected `B`, got `A` error.

Converting builds the new interface's method table when it runs, so it costs a small allocation. Arrays and optionals of interface values don't convert element by element: a [ReadCloser] is not a [Reader].

items.title: Union types
items.text:
A | B holds a value of any one of its member types. A match or is says which one it holds:

type Id = int64 | str

func show(anon id: Id) -> str {
    match id {
        int64(n) -> return f"#{n}"
        str(s) -> return s
    }
}

let id: Id = 42
if id is str(s) {
    print(s)
}

A member can be any type: a primitive, a struct, an enum, an interface, an array, a generic instance or a function type. See Pattern matching for the patterns.

A union is a set, so order, repeats and nesting don't matter. int64 | str and str | int64 are one type, in every module, and with type Id = int64 | str, Id | bool is int64 | str | bool. A union with only one member left is that member.

none in a union makes it optional: T | none is exactly T?, and A | B | none is the optional of A | B, which can also be written (A | B)?. An optional member counts the same way, so A? | B is that type too. Its arms sit side by side, with no Some: A(a), B(b) and none.

In a type, | binds tighter than or, so int64 | str or Error is a fallible int64 | str. A function type's return type takes every member after the ->, so func() -> int64 | str returns a union. To put such a function in a union, put it in parentheses: (func() -> int64) | str. Parentheses group any type this way, and a ? after them makes the group optional.

A value goes into a union by being written where the union is declared, as a T goes into a T?. It goes to the member of its own type. Without one, a struct, enum or primitive goes to an interface member it implements, and implementing two of them is an error, since it could be either. An enum's .Variant goes to the one enum member that declares that variant, and [] to the one array member. A value with no member reports the mismatch (expected `int64 | str`, got `bool`).

A union goes where a union with all of its members is declared: an A | B is accepted as an A | B | C, and holds the same member there. Only the value itself widens. An [A | B] isn't an [A | B | C], as an [Sq] isn't a [Shape], and an (A | B)? isn't an (A | B | C)?; match those and put each member in instead. Nor is a union accepted where one of its members is declared.

A union prints as the member it holds, with print(x), f"{x}" or str(x), when every member can be printed. == and != compare two unions, or a union and a value that goes into it (x == 3, x == "a", x == .Red): they're equal when they hold the same member and those members are ==. Every member needs a == of its own, so a union with a function or a shared struct without op_eq as a member can't be compared. A union widens for == as it does elsewhere, so an A | B compares with an A | B | C. A union whose members can all be hashed can be hashed and be a Map key: Map[int64 | str, V] (see hash). Otherwise a union has no fields, methods or operators of its own.

A union can mention a type parameter, in a generic function, struct or enum:

func label[T](anon x: T | str) -> str {
    match x {
        str(s) -> return f"text {s}"
        T(t) -> return f"other {t}"
    }
}

print(label(3))                  // other 3
print(label[int64]("a"))         // text a

Each instance is the union of what the parameters stand for, as a set. With T = int64 the parameter above is an int64 | str; with T = str it is just str, so label[str]("a") takes the first arm that matches, text a; and with T = int64 | bool it is bool | int64 | str, where T(t) matches an int64 or a bool and binds it as an int64 | bool (see type patterns). A call infers T from an argument for such a parameter: T is the argument's members that the parameter doesn't list, so label(3) is label[int64], and an argument of type int64 | str makes it int64 too. When that leaves nothing, as in label("a"), the type arguments have to be written.

A union alias can't refer to itself, so a recursive type such as a JSON value is still an enum.

items.title: Type aliases
items.text:
type Name = T gives an existing type a second name. An alias is transparent: a value of the alias type is a value of T, with all of its methods, fields and operators. The target can be any type, including one declared further down the module or one from the module's own imports (type Num2 = dep.Num, usable as mid.Num2 from a module that imports only mid, or type Num = dep.Num to pass the name on as mid.Num). Each module's aliases are its own: two modules may declare aliases of one name whether or not they stand for the same type, and a module's alias may take the name of a struct, enum or interface another module declares (see Modules):

type Name = str
type Ids = [int64]
type MaybeNode = Node?
type Callback = func(int64) -> int64
type StrMap = Map[str, str]
type Outcome = int64 or Error
type Key = int64 | str

type Node = struct {
    label: str
}

let n: Name = "kod"
print_int(n.char_count())    // 3

An alias of T or Error works wherever T or Error does, including as the return type of a function or of main, so throw, try and must behave the same through it. That holds for an imported alias too, written dep.Outcome or listed in import "./dep" { Outcome }.

An alias whose target names an unknown type is an error, and so is one that refers back to itself through other aliases (type A = B with type B = A). So is a target that gets a generic's type arguments wrong, such as type B = Map[str], type P = Pair or type D = [Box[int64]] for a Box that isn't generic. Each of these is reported once, at the alias.

items.title: Fallible types: T or Error
items.text:
A function declared -> T or Error returns a Result cell — either an Ok(T) or an Err(Error). Use try to propagate, must to panic, or pattern-match the result directly.

try and must take a T or Error value, and try only works inside a function that returns T or Error itself; anything else is an error. must also takes a T? (see Unwrapping). Either can appear anywhere a value can, as in out += [try parse(s)] or xs[try first(xs)..]; on an Err, try returns from the function there. An explicit Result[T, E] with an E other than Error doesn't count, since its error isn't an Error to report or pass on; match it instead.

A call whose result is a T or Error can't be used as a statement on its own, because that would drop an error without a word:

file.close()               // error: the `none or Error` result of this call is dropped
try file.close()           // propagate it
must file.close()          // panic on it
let _ = file.close()       // ignore it, on purpose

try r or must r on its own line, with r a plain name, narrows r for the rest of the block: it is let r = try r, so r is the T from there on. must o narrows a T? the same way. Like the other narrowing in Narrowing, this doesn't apply when the rest of the block assigns to r, and after the block r has its declared type again:

func size_plus(anon path: str) -> int64 or Error {
    let size = file_size(path)
    try size                    // size is an int64 from here on
    return size + 1
}

let _ = expr evaluates expr, whatever its type, and keeps nothing: it binds no name, so it can be written any number of times in a block, and _ can't be read afterwards. It is for fallible calls whose failure doesn't matter, like closing a connection that already failed. Any other value can be dropped by calling it as a statement, as before.

A none or Error function that ends without a return, or with a bare return, returns Ok(none), as return none does.

A T goes where a T or Error is declared as its Ok, the way a T goes into a T?. That holds in a return, an annotated let, an assignment, an argument, a struct field, an array element, and an arm of a match whose value goes to one of them:

let r: int64 or Error = 3                // Ok(3)
let rs: [int64 or Error] = [1, read_size("a.txt")]

A value that is already a T or Error goes as it is, and a nested result wraps as often as it takes: let r: (int64 or Error) or Error = 3 is Ok(Ok(3)). Without the parentheses, int64 or Error or Error is just int64 or Error. A failure is never implicit. An Error where an int64 or Error is declared is an error that says to throw it, or to write .Err(error: e). Only when T itself takes the value, as with Error or Error, is it the Ok. .Ok(value: 3) still works, and so does .Err(error: e).

Error is the only type that can follow or: -> int64 or IoError is a parse error. Throw a struct or enum that implements Error instead, and recover it with a downcast (see below). throw takes an Error value, so throwing an array, an optional, or an enum without a to_str is an error, such as enum `Color` doesn't implement interface `Error`: missing method `to_str`.

type IoError = struct {
    message: str
    func to_str(self) -> str { return self.message }
}

func read_size(anon path: str) -> int64 or Error {
    throw IoError(message: f"file not found: {path}")
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let n: int64 = must read_size("missing.txt")  // panics on Err
    return n
}

To inspect a result instead of propagating or panicking, pattern-match it with Ok / Err (the two-armed analog of Some / none). Ok's binding has the result's value type; Err's is the Error interface (on an explicit Result[T, E], it's an E):

match read_size("missing.txt") {
    Ok(n)  -> print_int(n)
    Err(e) -> print(e.to_str())
}

A type pattern on a result tests what it holds when it succeeded, so a result matches like the value it carries. Error(e) is another way to write Err(e):

match parse(s) {                         // -> int64 | str or Error
    int64(n) -> use(n)
    str(t) -> show(t)
    Error(e) -> print(e.to_str())
}

T(t) matches an Ok whose value matches T(t) as a pattern on the success type: a member of a union, a union or optional of several, the success type itself (any Ok), a downcast when it is an interface, and none when it is optional. A type pattern never looks inside the error, even for a type that implements Error: NotFound(nf) on an int64 or Error is an error that points at Err(NotFound(nf)), which downcasts it.

The same patterns work with if … is and the bare is operator, which is handy in tests:

let r = read_size("missing.txt")
assert r is Err(_)              // it failed
if r is Err(e) { print(e.to_str()) }

items.title: A default for a failure: ? on a result
items.text:
r? or default, r?.field and r?.method() work on a T or Error as they do on a T?. Each takes the success value, and on a failure gives up the error right there, where the code says so:

let n = read_size("a.txt")? or 0
let name = load(path)?.name? or "?"

r?.field and r?.method() give an optional, none for a failure, so a chain ends in ? or default as an optional's does. When T is itself optional, a failure and a none look the same, as for a T??. To stop on a failure, write must r, which prints the error's message.

items.title: Recovering the concrete error type
items.text:
Err(e) binds e as the Error interface. To get back the concrete error struct, downcast with is StructType(binding) — a general interface downcast that tests the boxed type and, on a match, binds the typed value:

match read_size(path) {
    Ok(n)  -> use(n)
    Err(e) ->
        if e is NotFound(nf) {
            print(f"missing: {nf.path}")
        } else {
            print(e.to_str())
        }
}

It works in match, if … is, and the bare is operator (a match on an interface needs an else, since its set of implementors isn't enumerable). A struct that doesn't implement the interface can never be in one, so naming it is an error: `Point` doesn't implement `Shape`, so a `Shape` is never a `Point`. x is T and a T(b) pattern hold only for a value of exactly that declaration, or that generic instance, whichever module boxed it, so an error struct that an imported function throws matches its type in the caller. T may be an alias of a struct or of a generic instance (type IntBox = Box[int64]), written dep.T through another module. Naming a generic type itself (is Box) is an error: `Box` is generic; downcast to one of its instances through a type alias such as `type IntBox = Box[int64]`. The pattern names such a struct through its module (e is errs.NotFound(nf), which needs errs to declare NotFound) or, when it is imported as an item, by its own name (e is NotFound(nf)). Either way it binds one name, the struct, whose fields are read from it. A local or parameter named like the module hides it, so errs.NotFound(nf) after let errs = 3 is an error.

items.title: Calling C with unsafe
items.text:
stdlib/unsafe.kod lets Kod code call C functions that take buffers, write results through pointers, or deal in C strings. It reads and writes raw memory, so nothing checks what it does: a wrong address or size corrupts the program or crashes it, without an error that says why. Code that uses it says so with import "unsafe", and the rest of the program doesn't need it.

import "unsafe"

extern func pipe(anon fds: int64) -> int64
extern func getenv(anon name: int64) -> int64

func make_pipe() -> [int64] {
    let fds = unsafe.alloc(8)               // room for two C ints
    if unsafe.c_int(pipe(fds)) < 0 {
        panic(f"pipe failed: errno {unsafe.errno()}")
    }
    let ends = [unsafe.load32(fds), unsafe.load32(fds + 4)]
    unsafe.free(fds)
    return ends
}

func home() -> str {
    let name = "HOME"
    let value = getenv(unsafe.c_str(name))  // a `char *`, or 0
    if value == 0 {
        return ""
    }
    return unsafe.str_at(value)             // a copy in a Kod `str`
}

items.title: The libc module
items.text: stdlib/libc.kod declares the C library functions the standard library calls (read, write, close, pipe, kill, waitpid, posix_spawnp and its file actions, getenv, setenv, and so on), with pointers as int64. Import it to call one as libc.read(fd, buf, n) instead of declaring it again; that also keeps the C name out of the module's own names, so a module can have a kill or poll of its own.

items.title: Addresses
items.text:
An address is an int64, and arithmetic on it is ordinary arithmetic: fds + 4 is four bytes further on. Pass one to an extern parameter of type int64 where C takes a pointer, and take one back the same way. 0 is C's NULL.

Function Meaning alloc(size) size bytes of zeroed memory, from C's heap; a program that runs out of memory panics free(addr) give back what alloc returned; 0 does nothing load8(addr) the byte at addr, 0 to 255 load32(addr) the 4 bytes at addr as a signed C int load64(addr) the 8 bytes at addr store8(addr, v), store32(addr, v), store64(addr, v) write the low 1, 4 or 8 bytes of v at addr copy_out(addr, n) the n bytes at addr as a new bytes copy_in(addr, data) write the bytes of data at addr

Memory from alloc isn't counted or freed for you: free it when C is done with it. Loads and stores are single instructions; 4- and 8-byte ones should be at an address that is a multiple of their size, as C would place them.

items.title: Strings and bytes
items.text:
Function Meaning c_str(s) the address of the bytes of the str s, followed by a 0 byte: a char * for C to read data(b) the address of the bytes of the bytes b, for C to read str_at(addr) a copy of the C string at addr, up to its 0 byte, as a str

c_str and data don't copy: the address is good only while s or b is, so keep the value in a variable for as long as C uses the address, and don't let C change the bytes. A str with a 0 byte inside looks shorter to C; check for one first where that matters. To give C a buffer it writes into, alloc one and copy_out what it wrote.

items.title: C's int and errno
items.text:
Function Meaning c_int(x) the low 4 bytes of x as a signed C int errno() C's errno for this thread, as the last failed call left it

A C function that returns int leaves the upper half of the 8-byte result undefined, so wrap its result in c_int before comparing it: -1 may otherwise read as 4294967295. A function returning long, ssize_t, size_t or a pointer fills all 8 bytes. Read errno() straight after the call that failed: anything else in between, a print too, may change it.

items.title: Callbacks
items.text:
c_function(f) is the address of the top-level function f, for a C function that calls back, such as qsort's comparison:

extern func qsort(anon base: int64, anon count: int64, anon size: int64, anon compare: int64) -> none

// C passes the addresses of two of the int64s being sorted.
func by_value(anon a: int64, anon b: int64) -> int64 {
    let x = unsafe.load64(a)
    let y = unsafe.load64(b)
    if x < y {
        return -1
    }
    if x > y {
        return 1
    }
    return 0
}

qsort(nums, count, 8, unsafe.c_function(by_value))
  • f is a function's name, f or module.f: not a function literal, a local holding a function, a method or a generic function.
  • Its parameters and its result are int64, bool or, for the result, none: C calls it with machine words and nothing to count.
  • A C int parameter arrives with its upper half undefined, as a C int result does; wrap it in c_int before using it.
  • C calls it on whatever thread C runs, and Kod's heap isn't safe to use from two threads at once, so a callback C makes from a thread of its own must not allocate. Inside a signal handler, likewise, it may only load and store.

items.title: What doesn't fit
items.text:
• Variable arguments, as printf takes them, are only int64 and bool: declare the function with ... (see Extern functions) and pass numbers and addresses, but no double.
  • A C function that takes or returns a struct by value, or a float or double. Pointers to structs are fine: alloc the bytes C's layout needs and load/store the fields at their offsets.
  • A function value, a closure, as a callback: only a named top-level function can be one (see Callbacks).
